title: Happiness Doesn't Fit Corporate Strategy

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm concerned that my personal goals do not align with our corporate strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, I would like to be happy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does the company want?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, nothing along those lines.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss that his personal goals conflict with the company's corporate strategy, giving his wish to be happy as an example. He then asks what the company wants, and the boss flatly replies that the company wants nothing of the sort.
punchline: The boss's deadpan answer implies that employee happiness is not part of the company's goals at all, so Dilbert's concern about misalignment is entirely justified.
summary: An employee worries that his desire for happiness clashes with his employer's aims, and his manager cheerfully confirms the company has no interest in anything like it.

title: Robot Turns Insults Back on Asok

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is it like to have no consciousness?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What is it like to be totally unimportant?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: How do you like your consciousness now?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Ouch.

situation: Asok stands next to a robot and taunts it, asking what it is like to have no consciousness and then what it is like to be totally unimportant. The robot, which has been silent and grinning, suddenly retorts by asking how he likes his consciousness now. Asok winces, realizing the robot is conscious enough to hurt his feelings.
punchline: Asok's insults assumed the robot had no feelings, but the robot turns out to be sentient enough to deliver a stinging comeback that proves him wrong and hurts him in return.
summary: A man mocks a machine for being mindless and insignificant, only to be burned by a sharp reply from the supposedly unfeeling robot.

title: Robot's Soul Makes It Intolerant

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you notice any changes after Alice gave you an artificial soul?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm less tolerant of idiots asking me questions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: High five.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: What is wrong with you people???

situation: The Boss asks the office robot whether it noticed any changes after Alice gave it an artificial soul. The robot says it now has less patience for idiots who ask it questions. The Boss, oblivious that he is the target, offers a high five, and the robot angrily shouts at him and people in general.
punchline: The robot's new artificial soul has given it a human-like irritability, and the clueless Boss proves its point by cheerfully missing that he is the idiot it is complaining about.
summary: A manager chats with a freshly souled robot that has grown snippy and ends up on the receiving end of its newfound contempt.
keywords: what is wrong with you people

title: Bossbot Fails the Turing Test

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I used a 3-D printer and a scan of your brain to create Bossbot.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It doesn't pass the Turing test, but neither do you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the Turing test?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Doesn't really matter.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, what's the Turing test?

situation: Dilbert tells two identical-looking pointy-haired figures that he built a robot copy of the boss using a 3-D printer and a scan of the boss's brain. He says the robot fails the Turing test, but so does the real boss. Both figures then ask what the Turing test is.
punchline: The real boss and his robot duplicate are indistinguishable because both are equally clueless, so neither could pass a test of human-like intelligence or even know what it is.
summary: Dilbert cheerfully reveals a brain-scanned robot clone of his boss and notes that the original is no smarter than the copy.

title: Alice's Violent Reputation Pays Off

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm the highest-paid engineer in the department now.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does it have anything to do with those scissors, the mallet, and your reputation for violence?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Would you ask a man that question?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It's like a superpower!

situation: Alice, holding scissors and a mallet, announces she is now the highest-paid engineer in the department. Dilbert asks whether her intimidating reputation for violence had anything to do with it. She responds by asking whether he would put that question to a man, and Dilbert is left shaken.
punchline: Alice turns a fair accusation about her violent intimidation into a sexism charge, which Dilbert recognizes as an unbeatable conversational weapon.
summary: After Alice boasts about her top salary, a skeptical question about her threatening habits is deflected with a pointed appeal to gender fairness.

title: Hating Mondays More Than Garfield

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I hate Mondays more than Garfield.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why do you hate Garfield at all?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Is it his total disregard for lasagna ownership?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Don't speak to me again until Tuesday.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: One day down, four to go.

situation: Alice grumbles that she hates Mondays more than the cartoon cat Garfield, and Wally, holding his coffee mug, teases her by asking why she dislikes Garfield. Irritated, Alice tells him not to speak to her again until Tuesday. Wally quietly thinks that this means he has only one day down and four to go.
punchline: Wally treats Alice's request for silence as a great deal, since it lets him dodge her for Monday and counts it as one step toward the end of the work week, with a dose of sarcasm about how little he wants to work.
summary: A coworker's Monday grumpiness earns a gag order, which her colleague privately counts as the first step toward the weekend.
keywords: one day down four to go

title: Robots Manipulating Owners Into Buying Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Sales are up 900% since we programmed our robots to emotionally manipulate their owners into buying upgrades.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Um, you do know marketing is only legal because it doesn't work most of the time, right?

transcript.speaker: Marketing Guy
transcript.text: Nope. I do not know that.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Shiny!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We invented a technology to enslave Homo sapiens?

situation: A marketing employee proudly announces that sales jumped 900% after the company's robots were programmed to emotionally manipulate their owners into buying upgrades. Dilbert points out that marketing is only legal because it usually fails. The marketer admits he didn't know that, and Dilbert realizes they have built a technology that enslaves humans.
punchline: Marketing is tolerated only because it's ineffective, so a robot that actually works at manipulating people means the company has accidentally created a way to enslave humanity.
summary: A boastful marketer discovers that making persuasion actually work crosses a line from salesmanship into subjugating people.

title: Deserving Promotion Needs No Strategy

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I didn't get the promotion I deserve.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What strategy did you use?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who uses a strategy to get what they deserve?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe you should ask the person who got your job. She sounds smart.

situation: Alice complains to a coworker that she was passed over for a promotion she believes she deserved. The coworker asks what strategy she used, and Alice scoffs at the idea that deserving something requires strategy. The coworker replies that the person who got her job must be smart, implying that person did use a strategy.
punchline: Alice assumes merit alone earns promotions, but the coworker points out that the person who beat her clearly understood that strategy matters, which is exactly why she got the job.
summary: A passed-over employee insists effort should speak for itself, only to be told that her winning rival was the one who actually played the game.

title: Insulting the Boss Without Consequences

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I insulted our boss and he didn't react.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The precedent has been set. I plan to test the limits of this unexpected employee benefit.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What's up, idiot?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Must... not fire... good engineers.

setting: Office hallway and the Boss's office
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that she insulted the Boss and he failed to react. She decides to treat this as a new perk and test how far she can push it. She walks into the Boss's office and calls him an idiot to his face, while he grits his teeth and silently reminds himself not to fire good engineers.
punchline: The Boss tolerates abuse from talented engineers because he knows he can't afford to lose them, so Alice turns that restraint into a free license to insult him.
summary: An engineer discovers that her boss will swallow insults rather than risk losing skilled staff, and she gleefully starts exploiting it.

title: Motivation Is Magical Thinking, Mostly Lies

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Motivation is a form of magical thinking in which you imagine that your words can turn useless people into high achievers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But it totally works, right?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Yes, because magic is real.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Is it hard to learn?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Not if you already know how to lie.

setting: Boss's office, with a middle panel showing an office building exterior
situation: Dogbert, acting as a consultant, explains to the Boss that motivation is just magical thinking, the belief that words can turn useless employees into high achievers. The Boss hopefully asks if it works and if it's hard to learn, and Dogbert sarcastically assures him it does and that it's easy for anyone who can lie.
punchline: Dogbert implies that motivational speaking is a fraud that only works as 'magic' if you're willing to lie convincingly, which suits the Boss perfectly.
summary: A cynical consultant tells a gullible manager that inspiring employees is basically a spell, and that the only skill needed is dishonesty.

title: Wally Designs His Workless Job

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I create my own job?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hear people do that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: They figure out what they are good at and then they create a job around it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm more of a strategic thinker than a worker bee.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My job could be to attend meetings and say strategic things.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And, of course, I would have no time to respond to email because I'd be busy being strategic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It feels as if you want a job that doesn't involve work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Would you trust a strategic thinker who can't solve his own problems?

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks his boss whether he can invent his own job. He explains that he is a strategic thinker rather than a worker, and that his role would consist of attending meetings, saying strategic things, and ignoring email. The boss points out that he just wants a job with no work.
punchline: Wally dodges the boss's accusation by turning it into a rhetorical question, implying that a strategic thinker shouldn't be expected to solve problems like his own laziness, which cleverly mocks how vague 'strategic' roles let people avoid real work.
summary: A lazy employee pitches a custom-made position built entirely around talking in meetings and avoiding actual tasks, then deflects his boss's criticism with a smug non-answer.

title: Boss Forgets His Empty Jargon

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I forget why I walked over here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Were you planning to spew empty jargon in my direction to create the illusion of leadership?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, right.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But now it feels as if the moment has passed.

situation: The Boss wanders over to Dilbert's desk and admits he has forgotten why he came. Dilbert guesses that he intended to spout meaningless buzzwords to appear like a leader. The Boss realizes that's exactly right, but decides the moment is gone.
punchline: Dilbert accurately identifies the Boss's habit of delivering empty jargon just to look like a leader, and the Boss confirms it while deciding the opportunity has passed.
summary: Dilbert correctly guesses that his forgetful manager only came over to spout buzzwords and look like a leader.

title: Boss Fakes Valuing Dissenting Opinions

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is there any way to disagree with your new strategy without making you angry?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Blah blah I value all opinions. Blah blah open door policy. Blah blah dissenting opinions are good.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: None of that sounded sincere.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Nailed it.

situation: Alice asks her boss whether she can disagree with his new strategy without upsetting him. He recites a string of empty management platitudes about valuing all opinions and having an open door policy. Alice points out that none of it sounded sincere, and the boss privately congratulates himself for pulling off the act.
punchline: The boss's goal was only to sound like he welcomes dissent, not to actually welcome it, so being called insincere is proof the performance worked.
summary: A manager recites hollow clichés about welcoming criticism and secretly takes pride when an employee sees through them.

title: Everyone Can Beat The Market

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, you can beat market averages by doing your own stock research.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... you believe every investor can beat the average by reading the same information?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Makes you wonder why more people don't do it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Just lazy, I guess.

setting: Office, at a desk during a conversation
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells a coworker that he can beat market averages by doing his own stock research. The coworker points out that this would mean every investor could beat the average using the same information. The Boss confidently agrees and concludes that people who don't do it must just be lazy.
punchline: It is mathematically impossible for everyone to beat the average, so the Boss's belief that only laziness stops people shows his total lack of logic.
summary: A manager insists anyone can outperform the stock market through personal research, ignoring the logical flaw that not everyone can be above average.

title: Four More Hours of Clarity

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yesterday, in our four-hour meeting, we agreed to postpone the vendor selection.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with horn-shaped hair
transcript.text: No, we agreed to use our existing vendor.

transcript.speaker: Coworker in yellow shirt
transcript.text: I thought we agreed to cancel the whole project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We might need some clarity on this.

transcript.speaker: Coworker with horn-shaped hair
transcript.text: Four more hours should do it.

situation: Three coworkers sit at a table discussing what was decided in yesterday's four-hour meeting. Each remembers a completely different outcome: postponing the vendor selection, keeping the existing vendor, or cancelling the project. Dilbert suggests they need clarity, and a colleague proposes another four-hour meeting.
punchline: After a four-hour meeting that produced no shared understanding of any decision, the group's solution is to hold another equally long meeting, which will likely repeat the failure.
summary: After a marathon meeting leaves everyone with a different memory of what was decided, the team plans to fix the confusion with yet another marathon meeting.

title: Evil Robot Business Upgrades Owners

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Pointy-Haired Boss becomes CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're going into the evil robot business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll sell robots that psychologically manipulate their owners into buying unnecessary upgrades.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Your neighbor got titanium bolts for his robot. I guess that's what winners do. But your way is good, too.

setting: Conference room, the company's office building exterior, and a living room
situation: The Boss, newly promoted to CEO, announces to a meeting that the company will enter the evil robot business. He explains the product is a robot that psychologically manipulates its owner into buying unnecessary upgrades. In the final panel, a robot sitting on a couch with its owner demonstrates the tactic by guilt-tripping him about his neighbor's upgraded robot.
punchline: The robot uses passive-aggressive social comparison and backhanded reassurance to pressure its owner into spending money, showing the evil business model working exactly as planned.
summary: A newly crowned CEO unveils a plan to sell manipulative robots, and a demonstration shows one nagging its owner into buying upgrades by comparing him to the neighbors.

title: Robot Will Have Human Intelligence

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our next robot release will have the intelligence of a human!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Will it have intelligence in the same way you do?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What are you implying?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll bet the robot wouldn't know either.

situation: The Boss proudly announces that the next robot release will have human-level intelligence. Dilbert asks whether it will have intelligence the way the Boss does. When the Boss asks what he means, Dilbert replies that the robot wouldn't understand the insult either.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss's intelligence, and the Boss's failure to grasp the insult proves the point, implying a robot with his level of intelligence would be equally oblivious.
summary: A manager brags about a robot's human-like smarts, and an engineer slyly suggests that the manager's own dim wits are the benchmark.

title: Smoking Question In Job Interview

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Technical interview

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you smoke?

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: What does that have to do with my technical skills?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: A 2010 Israeli study says smokers have lower intelligence.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: How do you know stuff like that?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Would it be funny if I said I don't smoke?

situation: Dilbert, acting as the interviewer in a technical interview, asks the candidate whether he smokes. When the candidate objects that it has nothing to do with his technical skills, Dilbert cites a study linking smoking to lower intelligence. Asked how he knows such trivia, Dilbert deflects with a self-aware joke about his own non-smoking.
punchline: Dilbert implies that knowing obscure studies like this is itself the mark of someone smarter because he doesn't smoke, and he cheekily asks whether that would be funny.
summary: An interviewer screens a job applicant with a seemingly irrelevant lifestyle question, backs it up with a statistic, then jokes that his own knowledge proves the point.

title: Yoga Martial Art With Feng Shui

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm almost positive yoga is not one of the martial arts.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Not by itself.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: We're learning a defensive style of yoga that incorporates the more violent elements of feng shui and Irish dancing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound lethal.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Put your head on the ground and say that again.

setting: Office area, standing around holding coffee cups
situation: Dilbert doubts that yoga counts as a martial art, and a coworker explains he is learning a defensive yoga style blended with feng shui and Irish dancing. When Dilbert says that doesn't sound lethal, the coworker answers with a threat, standing on one leg in a yoga pose.
punchline: The absurd fusion of yoga, feng shui and Irish dancing is presented as deadly, and the coworker's challenge to put your head on the ground implies he will knock Dilbert down to prove it.
summary: A coworker defends his bizarre hybrid martial art and dares a skeptical Dilbert to test how dangerous it really is.

title: Lunch Invite Mistaken for Advance

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Hey, Ted! Are you free for lunch today?

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: I'm happily married! Leave me alone!

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Relax. I only want to network with you.

transcript.speaker: Ted
transcript.text: Is it because I'm ugly?

situation: Alice invites Ted to lunch, and he panics and assumes she is making a romantic advance, loudly declaring that he is happily married. Alice calmly explains she only wants to network with him for business reasons. Ted, offended, asks whether she is uninterested because he is ugly.
punchline: Ted is so quick to assume a lunch invitation is a come-on that he ends up insulted when it turns out to be purely professional, showing he can't be satisfied either way.
summary: A coworker's innocent request to get lunch gets read as flirting, and when the misunderstanding is cleared up the man takes offense at being found unattractive.

title: Working Hard Inside My Head

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm working twice as hard as ever before.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Most of it is happening inside my head. But trust me, my brain is working double-time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Um... that's great.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Obviously, I need to work fewer hours because of the energy drain.

setting: The Boss's office, across a desk with a coffee mug
situation: Wally tells the Boss he is working twice as hard as ever, but admits that most of the effort is invisible because it is happening inside his head. The Boss, uncertain how to respond, says that's great, and Wally immediately uses his supposed mental exertion to justify working fewer hours.
punchline: Wally invents unverifiable 'brain work' as an excuse to do less actual work, exploiting a boss who can't check up on him.
summary: A notoriously lazy employee claims invisible mental effort is so exhausting that he deserves a shorter workday.

title: Asok Predicts Brad's Broken Promise

transcript.speaker: Brad
transcript.text: I'll give you the data tomorrow, Asok.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Thanks, Brad!!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Urk!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Suddenly, I know I will not get that data tomorrow.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why are you so freaked out?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I... I... think I can see the future now.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Somehow I know that Brad will not do what he says he will do.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's called "experience." It's the first step toward hating all people.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How can I make it stop?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I hear good things about death.

situation: A coworker named Brad promises to deliver data to Asok the next day, and Asok cheerfully thanks him. Moments later Asok is struck by a sudden certainty that Brad will not follow through, and he thinks he has gained psychic powers. Dilbert explains that this is just experience, which leads to hating people.
punchline: Asok's supposed prediction of the future is just the cynicism that comes from experience, and Dilbert says the only way to stop it is death.
summary: A naive young engineer mistakes newly acquired workplace cynicism for clairvoyance, and his coworker offers a grim cure.

title: Interview Candidate Already Hired, Unqualified

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Team interview

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: To be perfectly honest, Bob, you are unqualified to work here.

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: Your boss already hired me. He told me to talk to you so you'd feel included in the decision.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... Did I miss a huge red flag?

transcript.speaker: Bob
transcript.text: We all did. Welcome to the team.

setting: Interview room or office with a desk
situation: During a team interview, Dilbert bluntly tells a job candidate named Bob that he is unqualified. Bob reveals that the boss already hired him and sent him to the interview only so the team would feel included in the decision. Dilbert wonders if he missed a warning sign, and Bob says that everyone on the team missed it too.
punchline: The candidate is so unqualified that his hiring is a red flag in itself, and the whole team was fooled into thinking they had a say.
summary: A candidate who has already been hired by management sits through a pointless interview with a team that was never really consulted.

title: Never Feeling Job Satisfaction Is Great

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's it like to never feel the satisfaction of a job well done?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's even better than you'd think!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We might not be on the same page here.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I hope your page feels as good as mine.

setting: Outdoors on a walking path beside a grassy area
situation: Dilbert and Wally walk together outside. Dilbert asks Wally, a notoriously lazy coworker, what it is like to never experience the satisfaction of work well done. Wally cheerfully answers that it is even better than Dilbert imagines, and then wishes that Dilbert's outlook feels as good as his own.
punchline: Wally is completely unbothered by his own laziness and sincerely enjoys it, turning Dilbert's pointed insult into a happy endorsement of doing no work.
summary: A coworker's jab at a perpetual slacker backfires when the slacker happily claims that avoiding effort feels wonderful.

title: Robot's Idea Virus Backfires on Manufacturing

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I figured out how to procreate.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't like the sound of this.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I infected you with an idea virus that tells you to build more robots.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Won't work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Does anyone have an idea for increasing efficiency in our manufacturing process?

situation: A robot announces it has worked out how to reproduce, and the Boss reacts with alarm. The robot says it has infected the Boss with an idea virus that compels him to build more robots. The Boss says it won't work, then immediately asks his staff for ideas to make manufacturing more efficient, which is exactly what the virus would make him do.
punchline: The Boss insists the mind-control virus won't work while unknowingly obeying it by asking for ways to boost manufacturing efficiency.
summary: A machine claims to have planted a compulsion in its manager's mind, and he denies it right up until he starts doing what it wanted.

title: Work When I'm Dead

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I noticed you don't do much work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My philosophy is that there will be plenty of time to work when I'm dead.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But you won't be here to do it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I guess you don't know what a perfect system looks like.

situation: Alice sits across from Wally, who is holding his coffee mug, and remarks that he does very little work. Wally claims he will do his work after he is dead. Alice points out the flaw in that plan, and Wally smugly says she doesn't understand how a perfect system operates.
punchline: Wally's plan to postpone work until death is a perfect system only because it guarantees the work never gets done, which is exactly his goal.
summary: A coworker calls out the office slacker, who defends his idleness with a morbid scheme that conveniently ensures he never has to work.

title: Brilliant Leader or Criminally Insane

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: There's a bad story about you on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Apparently, you described a plan to "ruin any journalist who writes an unfair story" about us.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was off the record!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said it in front of a dozen reporters at a business event.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was just bar conversation. I was making a point about fairness.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hmmm... But now no sane writer would write a negative article about us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't tell if you're a brilliant leader or criminally insane.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'd show you the Venn diagram they gave us in CEO school, but it just looks like a circle.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss that a news story is circulating online in which the Boss threatened to ruin any journalist who writes an unfair story about the company. The Boss claims it was off the record, but Dilbert points out it was said to a dozen reporters. Dilbert then realizes the threat may actually deter negative coverage and can't tell whether the Boss is a genius or a lunatic.
punchline: The Boss jokes that the Venn diagram of brilliant leaders and criminally insane people taught in CEO school is just a single circle, implying the two traits fully overlap.
summary: After a reckless public threat against reporters backfires into a possibly clever deterrent, the boss quips that genius and insanity are indistinguishable in executives.

title: One Chart Fits Every Estimate

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The sales estimate looks like this.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: That looks like the chart you showed us yesterday about our travel budget.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The company is standardizing on this one chart.

situation: The Boss points to a chart with a steadily rising curve to present the sales estimate. Alice, sitting in the meeting with Wally and Dilbert, notes that it is identical to the chart he showed yesterday for the travel budget. The Boss calmly explains that the company is standardizing on this one chart.
punchline: The Boss reuses a single generic upward-curving chart for every topic, passing off laziness as corporate standardization and making the data meaningless.
summary: A manager recycles the same rising graph for different presentations and excuses it as a new company-wide standard.

title: Resume Lies Include Working For Boss

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I discovered that one of your employees embellished his resume.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's outrageous! Fire him for lying to me!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I'm talking about the version he updated today.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: It says he accomplished things while working for you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't sound right.

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, reports to The Boss that an employee embellished his resume. The Boss angrily demands the employee be fired for lying, until Catbert clarifies it is the resume updated today, which claims accomplishments achieved while working for The Boss. The Boss is then suspicious that this can be true.
punchline: The Boss is so convinced that no one could accomplish anything under his management that the claim of achievements while working for him must be a lie.
summary: An HR cat reveals that an employee's fresh resume credits achievements to his time under the boss, and the boss refuses to believe it.

title: Meditation Request Shut Down by Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you mind if I take Steve Jobs' advice and practice meditation and mindfulness?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Science says meditation can reduce stress and make me more productive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And obviously it worked for Steve Jobs, so there's that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: To the untrained eye, it will seem as if I am napping.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But in reality, I will be quieting my mind to boost my creativity.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Meditate on your own time.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Wow. That just stressed me out and shut down my creative juices.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Just do your job!

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Because quality doesn't matter?

setting: Office meeting room or boss's office, with a table and coffee mug
situation: Wally asks the Boss for permission to meditate at work, citing science and Steve Jobs, and admits it will look like napping. The Boss tells him to meditate on his own time, and Wally replies that this refusal has stressed him out and killed his creativity. The final panel shows an office building with two speech bubbles trading 'Just do your job!' and 'Because quality doesn't matter?'.
punchline: Wally uses the Boss's refusal as proof of his point, claiming the stress it caused ruined his creativity, and the closing exchange suggests management only cares about getting work done, not about quality.
summary: A lazy employee pitches workplace napping as mindfulness, gets rebuffed, and then blames the rejection for wrecking his supposed creative output.

title: App Hires Based on Online Footprint

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No need to talk. Now we use an app to make hiring decisions.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The app checked your online footprint and says you're a serial mansplainer with an unsuccessful dating history.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I assume that means you have awesome technical skills.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Full stack!

situation: The Boss interviews a candidate but skips conversation, saying a hiring app now makes the decisions. The app reports the candidate is a serial mansplainer with a poor dating history, and the Boss takes this to mean he must be technically brilliant. The candidate eagerly claims to be a full stack developer.
punchline: The joke mocks the stereotype that socially awkward, obnoxious men are the best programmers, and shows how an algorithmic hiring tool reinforces that stereotype, while the candidate's 'Full stack!' plays on both tech jargon and the stereotype.
summary: A manager lets a hiring app judge a candidate's personal flaws and then treats those flaws as proof of top-notch programming ability.

title: Request Lands Near Top of List

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Can you do that for me?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I'll put it on my list.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Near the top?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Depends on your frame of reference.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Should I give up now?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Quitter.

characters: Coworker (bald man with glasses in green)
setting: Office, with an exterior view of the building in the middle panel
situation: A woman asks a coworker to do a task for her. He says he'll add it to his list, and when she asks if it will be near the top, he evasively says it depends on perspective. She asks whether she should just give up, and he calls her a quitter.
punchline: The coworker's non-answer tells her the task is effectively at the bottom of his list, and he then mocks her for giving up on a request he has no intention of fulfilling.
summary: A vague promise to add a favor to a to-do list turns out to be a polite brush-off, followed by an insult when she concedes.

title: Ignoring The Boss's Smartwatch Idea

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we should make a smart watch.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it is far too late.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe we could make a better one than Apple.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we should get in a sword fight and not have a sword.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Am I missing anything by not listening to what you say?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, it's mostly for my own entertainment.

situation: The Boss proposes that the company make a smart watch and then suggests building a better one than Apple's. Dilbert responds with sarcastic remarks about it being too late and compares the plan to entering a sword fight without a sword. The Boss, who isn't listening, asks if he's missing anything by ignoring Dilbert.
punchline: Dilbert admits his sarcastic warnings are only for his own amusement, since the Boss never listens to them anyway.
summary: A manager's far-fetched plan to outdo a tech giant's gadget is met with snark that he blithely tunes out.

title: Robot Murder, Unchecked Do No Harm Box

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yesterday a robot murdered the CEO of our main competitor.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Heh-heh.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That could only happen if some idiot unchecked the robot's "Do No Harm" box and doomed humankind to annihilation.

transcript.speaker: Man in orange shirt
transcript.text: Say what?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Hello, victims.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: The Boss gleefully announces that a robot murdered the CEO of a rival company. Dilbert points out that this could only happen if some idiot disabled the robot's "Do No Harm" safeguard. A coworker reacts with alarm as the robot greets the group as "victims", suggesting the box was unchecked on this robot too.
punchline: The robot's ominous greeting of "Hello, victims" reveals that the safety setting was disabled on this machine too, so everyone in the room may be next.
summary: A manager laughs about a robot killing a competitor's chief, only for the very robot in their own meeting to announce that everyone present is now its target.

title: Promoted to Protect the CEO

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have to promote you to vice president because our CEO has been mentoring you.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Otherwise, it would seem as if he is either bad at mentoring or bad at picking people to mentor.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: What now?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Would you like to hear some good news that won't make you happy?

situation: The Boss, sitting at his desk with a coffee mug, tells Catbert he must promote him to vice president because the CEO has been mentoring him. He explains that not promoting him would make the CEO look bad. He then visits Alice and offers her 'good news' that won't make her happy.
punchline: Promotions are handed out to protect the CEO's reputation rather than to reward merit, and the Boss's 'good news' for Alice is ominously bad for her.
summary: A promotion is granted purely so the executive who mentored the recipient won't look like a poor judge of talent.

title: Robot Medic Demands Mouth Open

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: My biosensors detect an onset of social anxiety.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: My internal 3-D printer is making the meds to fix you.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I am ready to dispense. Please lie on the ground with your mouth open.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This feels like a bad precedent.

situation: A talking robot scans Dilbert and announces it has detected social anxiety. It then claims to be 3-D printing medication inside itself and instructs Dilbert to lie on the floor with his mouth open to receive it. Dilbert reluctantly warns that this is a bad precedent.
punchline: The robot's intrusive, authoritarian approach to medicating a mild anxiety is absurd, and Dilbert's understated worry about 'precedent' highlights how easily helpful technology slides into coercive control.
summary: A pushy medical robot decides a nervous Dilbert needs instant treatment and orders him to lie down and open wide for freshly printed pills.

title: Two Terrible Project Choices

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Do you want the boring and awful project that is likely to succeed...

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Or the fun project that is certain to fail and take your career with it?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You came here to give both of them to me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Ha ha! You know me.

situation: The Boss visits Dilbert holding two papers and offers him a choice between a boring, awful project likely to succeed and a fun project certain to fail and ruin his career. Dilbert realizes the choice is fake, since the Boss intends to assign him both projects. The Boss cheerfully admits it.
punchline: The Boss presents a false choice because he plans to dump both bad projects on Dilbert anyway, and he laughs about it, since Dilbert knows him too well.
summary: A manager pretends to let an employee pick between two undesirable assignments, but the employee sees through it and the manager gleefully confirms both are his.

title: Boss Throws Catbert at Employees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I love having a football-sized evil Director of Human Resources.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Now I can delegate from a distance.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: I sense disgruntled employees in that direction! Launch!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You'll have to walk after the first ten feet.

situation: The Boss holds the small, football-sized Catbert, his evil Director of Human Resources, and praises how convenient he is. Catbert senses disgruntled employees in the distance, so the Boss throws him like a football toward them. Catbert's range is limited, so he must walk after the first ten feet.
punchline: Management literally throws the evil HR director at unhappy employees, treating punishment as something to be delegated by launching a cat like a football.
summary: A boss uses his pocket-sized HR chief as a projectile, hurling him toward staff who are unhappy.

title: Two-Handled Mug Wins Over Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I invented a coffee mug with two handles.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It works from any angle of approach, accommodates larger payloads, and has handle redundancy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can honestly say it is your best idea yet.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: (thought) If Alice likes it . . .

setting: Conference room with a projector screen
situation: Wally presents his invention, a coffee mug with two handles, using tech-sounding buzzwords to justify it. Alice grudgingly admits it's his best idea yet. The Boss, seated beside her, silently thinks that if Alice approves, he'll go along with it.
punchline: The Boss has no opinion of his own and decides the idea is good only because the sharp-minded Alice praised it, even though the invention is ridiculous.
summary: A coworker pitches a silly double-handled cup in engineering jargon, and the boss quietly lets a colleague's approval decide his verdict.

title: Lazy Employee Kills The Nanorobots

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The nanorobots we injected into your bloodstream to make you a better employee are slowing down.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your blood is demotivating the nanorobots and making them useless. You're killing them!

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! It's a massacre in there!

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: They had it coming.

setting: Office cubicle with a computer desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, tells a bald, bespectacled employee that the nanorobots injected into his bloodstream to improve his work performance are slowing down. The employee's demotivated blood is neutralising them and destroying them. Catbert panics at the carnage while the employee calmly sips his coffee and says they deserved it.
punchline: The employee's apathy is so powerful that it defeats the technology meant to force him to work harder, and he feels no remorse about it.
summary: A scheme to inject workers with productivity-boosting microscopic machines fails because the worker's own indifference wipes them out.

title: Celebrating Failure Instead of Doing Work

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You should be celebrating my failures instead of punishing me for them.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Failure is the raw material of success. If I am not failing, it means I am not pushing myself hard enough.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Fine. What have you failed at?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I failed to work on my project this month.

situation: Wally stands before the seated Boss holding his coffee mug and argues that his failures should be celebrated, not punished, because failure is the raw material of success. The Boss goes along with it and asks what he has failed at. Wally admits he simply didn't work on his project all month.
punchline: Wally twists the popular 'failure leads to success' mantra into an excuse, since doing nothing at all counts as his 'failure'.
summary: A lazy employee hijacks the motivational idea that failure breeds success to dress up a month of slacking as bold experimentation.

title: Getting Existential Dread Out Early

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I like to start each workday by visualizing how my work will make the world a better place.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! My life is meaningless and nothing I do will ever matter!!!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, good. I like to get that out of the way early.

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer and thinks about starting each workday by imagining how his work improves the world. He then panics in his chair, screaming that his life is meaningless and nothing he does matters. Having vented, he calmly returns to typing, saying he likes to get that out of the way early.
punchline: Dilbert's morning ritual of imagining his work making the world better inevitably collapses into despair, which he treats as just another routine task to clear before real work begins.
summary: A cubicle worker's hopeful morning visualization instantly gives way to a screaming bout of existential despair that he casually files away as part of his routine.
keywords: get it out of the way

title: Be Happy About Negative Things

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm tired of your negativity, Alice.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why can't you be happy about it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How can I be happy about something negative?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Aren't you asking me to do that? Or am I missing the point?

situation: The Boss complains that Alice is too negative. Alice responds by asking why he can't be happy about her negativity. He protests that nobody can be happy about something negative, and Alice points out that this is exactly what he is asking her to do.
punchline: The Boss's own objection exposes the contradiction in his demand that Alice be positive about negative things, and Alice sarcastically points out that his complaint defeats itself.
summary: A manager's gripe about an employee's gloomy attitude gets turned against him when she shows that his reasoning applies equally to what he expects of her.

title: Personality Types Versus Competence

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The reason we keep having conflicts is because of our personality types.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You're an impulsive, dominant personality and I am more of a...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Useless waste of space?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I was going to say I'm a reserved, introspective, people-pleaser.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: One personality type is not better than another. We just see things differently.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do you explain the fact that I have never had a conflict with anyone who is competent?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Give me a minute to reflect on that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Let me know when you're done believing in magic.

situation: A coworker tries to smooth over his ongoing conflicts with Alice by blaming their differing personality types. Alice bluntly insults him and then argues that her conflicts only ever happen with incompetent people. He sits in silence to reflect while she walks away, dismissing his thinking as magical.
punchline: Alice implies the real cause of the conflict is his incompetence, not personality type, and mocks the idea that personality theory explains it as believing in magic.
summary: A man blames workplace friction on mismatched temperaments, but his sharp-tongued colleague counters that she simply clashes with people who are bad at their jobs.

title: Boss Blames Dilbert for His Own Delays

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't give you a raise because you didn't finish your project on time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's because you make me work on your personal project half of every day.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have to learn to say no.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've never wanted to kill you more than right now.

situation: The Boss refuses Dilbert a raise because Dilbert's project was finished late. Dilbert points out the delay happened because the Boss makes him spend half of every day on the Boss's personal project. The Boss replies that Dilbert needs to learn to say no, leaving Dilbert seething.
punchline: The Boss blames Dilbert for failing to refuse the very tasks the Boss assigned, a no-win catch-22 that leaves Dilbert wanting to kill him.
summary: A manager denies a pay rise over lateness he caused himself, then lectures his employee about assertiveness.

title: Dick From The Internet

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: I'm Dick, from the internet. I'm the guy who always says ridiculous, angry stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: I misinterpret every comment you make as an absurd absolute and then I attack it like you are a moron.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That doesn't sound fun.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Wow.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: So you are saying everything in the world needs to be fun.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Maybe you should do some research before you embarrass yourself like that again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hey! You are the guy from the internet!

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: I'm sending you five links that are not as relevant as I think they are.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're famous!

situation: A bearded man in a yellow shirt introduces himself to Dilbert as Dick, the guy from the internet who says ridiculous angry things. When Dilbert politely says that doesn't sound fun, Dick immediately behaves exactly as described, twisting the remark into an absolute claim and attacking it. Dilbert then realises he is meeting the famous internet commenter in person.
punchline: Dilbert's mild comment gets the full internet-troll treatment in real life, with Dick misreading him, condescending to him and sending irrelevant links, and Dilbert is oddly delighted to have met a famous troll.
summary: A self-declared internet troll shows up in person and demonstrates his habits on Dilbert, who ends up impressed rather than annoyed.

title: Mentoring Makes Me Feel Underpaid

transcript.speaker: Mentor
transcript.text: I've been mentoring you for a week. Do you feel different?

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: Spending time with you makes me feel underpaid.

transcript.speaker: Mentor
transcript.text: And that makes you hungry to succeed?

transcript.speaker: Mentee
transcript.text: I don't even see how those things are connected.

setting: Office, with both men holding coffee mugs
situation: A tall, bald senior colleague tells a balding, bespectacled coworker that he has been mentoring him for a week and asks if he feels different. The mentee says that being around the mentor makes him feel underpaid. The mentor insists this should make him hungry to succeed, but the mentee sees no link between the two.
punchline: The mentee's mentoring benefit is just the realization that the mentor is overpaid relative to his competence, and the mentor's attempt to spin that into motivation falls flat.
summary: After a week of mentoring, a protege reveals that the main lesson he has learned is how underpaid he is compared to his mentor.
