title: Retired Russian Military Dolphin Birthday

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I bought a dolphin for my daughter's birthday party.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But it turned out to be a retired Russian military dolphin. It dragged one of the birthday clowns into the pool and drowned him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought dolphins need to live in seawater.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Maybe that's why it's so angry.

setting: Office meeting table, with an exterior building shot in the middle panel
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he bought a dolphin for his daughter's birthday party, but it turned out to be a retired Russian military dolphin that dragged a birthday clown into the pool and drowned him. Dilbert points out that dolphins need seawater, and the coworker casually suggests that might explain the dolphin's anger.
punchline: The coworker is oblivious to how absurd and dangerous the situation is, treating a killer military dolphin kept in a backyard pool as a mild puzzle rather than a catastrophe.
summary: A man's questionable party-entertainment purchase turns deadly when his trained former military dolphin attacks a clown, and he only dimly guesses why it is upset.

title: Alice Smashes the Boss's Robot

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to get rid of that 3-D printed robot that looks and acts like me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No problem. Alice takes care of all the excess robot inventory.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I don't always have passion for my work, but today is looking good.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to dispose of a 3-D printed robot that looks and acts just like him. Dilbert says Alice handles all excess robot inventory. In the last panel Alice shows up holding a mallet, gleefully anticipating the job. The robot that looks and acts like the Boss is the one facing the mallet.
punchline: Alice's violent disposal method is a joy for her because the robot is a copy of the Boss she despises, so destroying it is cathartic, and the real Boss fails to notice the implied threat.
summary: Told to dispose of a robotic double of the boss, Dilbert hands the job to Alice, who arrives with a mallet and unusual enthusiasm.

title: Meeting About Keeping Expenses Down

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I just saw your net worth on the internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's this meeting about anyway?

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: It's about keeping expenses down.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: More for you?

transcript.speaker: Bald Executive
transcript.text: That's not the spin I was going to put on it.

situation: Dilbert tells a wealthy executive he just looked up the man's net worth online. When the executive says the meeting is about keeping expenses down, Dilbert suggests it's so the executive can keep more money for himself. The executive admits that's not how he planned to frame it.
punchline: The executive's reply implicitly confirms that cost-cutting is really about enriching the wealthy, and he is only annoyed that Dilbert said it plainly instead of spinning it.
summary: A wealthy executive's plan to cut costs is bluntly reframed by an employee as a way to pad his own fortune, which he doesn't deny.

title: Smart Choice Before Birth

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Asok, it takes more than luck to be successful. You also have to be smart.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: How did you select your level of intelligence before birth?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't understand the question.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Now I am getting mixed messages.

situation: The Boss lectures Asok that success takes both luck and intelligence. Asok earnestly asks how the Boss chose his own level of intelligence before he was born, treating luck and smarts as separate things. The Boss doesn't grasp the question, which leaves Asok confused.
punchline: The Boss's blank incomprehension of the question suggests his own success owes everything to luck and nothing to intelligence, contradicting the advice he is giving.
summary: A boss tells an intern that success needs smarts as well as luck, then fails to follow the intern's reply, which undercuts his own point.

title: Robot News: Engineers Can't Commit Murder

transcript.speaker: Robot Newscaster
transcript.text: The Supreme Court ruled that engineers cannot be found guilty of murder.

transcript.speaker: Robot Newscaster
transcript.text: Lawyers argued that any good engineer knows how to get away with murder, so getting caught is proof of innocence.

transcript.speaker: Robot Newscaster
transcript.text: The ruling was unanimous because no one could figure out which side was the liberal one.

setting: A news desk labeled 'Robots Read News'
situation: A robot news anchor sits at a desk and reads out a story about a Supreme Court ruling. The ruling holds that engineers cannot be convicted of murder, because a good engineer would know how to evade detection, so being caught supposedly proves innocence. The robot then explains the decision was unanimous because the justices could not tell which side was the liberal position.
punchline: The absurd legal logic that getting caught proves you are innocent is topped by the claim that the court only agreed unanimously because nobody could tell which side was liberal.
summary: A deadpan robot anchor reports on a ridiculous court decision that treats engineers' cleverness as a shield against murder charges, and jokes that political confusion produced the unanimity.

title: Robot Mocks Human Ignorance

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Why did the human cross the road?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't know.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Neither did he.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Ignorance is a big problem with you people.

situation: A robot tells Dilbert a twisted version of the chicken-crossing-the-road joke, asking why the human crossed the road. When Dilbert admits he doesn't know, the robot delivers the punchline that the human didn't know either, then lectures Dilbert that ignorance is a big problem with 'you people.'
punchline: The robot turns a classic joke into a condescending insult, showing that machines may see humans as ignorant and inferior.
summary: A smug robot uses a riddle to belittle a human's lack of knowledge and then criticises the whole species for it.

title: Awe Versus Ow Leadership

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A good leader creates a sense of awe in employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: But I think you'll find it a lot faster to create a sense of "ow" instead.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to work all weekend again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ow!

setting: Office, in the boss's workspace and at Dilbert's desk
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, sits on a desk lecturing The Boss about leadership, saying a good leader inspires awe but that it is faster to inflict pain. The Boss then walks over to Dilbert and demands he work all weekend again, and Dilbert winces in pain.
punchline: The Boss follows Catbert's advice about causing "ow" by demanding weekend work, which is a painful, demoralizing request rather than an inspiring one.
summary: Taking the human resources cat's cynical advice to heart, a manager skips inspiration and simply hurts his employee by demanding yet another weekend of work.

title: Dilbert Who? Forgotten After One Day

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is Dilbert with an encrypted message from my hiding place from the government...

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Dilbert who?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only left yesterday!!!

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I don't like to dwell in the past.

setting: Dogbert's desk at an office, and a bush or hedge where Dilbert is hiding outdoors
situation: Dilbert, hiding from the government in a hedge while wearing a red hooded jacket, phones Dogbert with a supposedly encrypted message. Dogbert, sitting at a computer with a headset, responds as if he has no idea who Dilbert is. Dilbert protests that he only left yesterday, and Dogbert says he doesn't dwell on the past.
punchline: Dogbert dismisses his friend as forgotten after just one day, using the excuse that he refuses to dwell in the past, showing how shallow and unsentimental he is.
summary: A fugitive in a hedge calls his canine friend for help, only to be coldly treated like a stranger after a single day's absence.

title: Boss Frees Internet-Bought Elbonians

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How's it going with the Elbonians you bought on the Internet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had to set them free. Turns out it was slavery after all.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You made them work without pay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yeah, that's the spin they put on it, too.

situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks the Boss how things are going with the Elbonians he purchased online. The Boss says he had to free them because it turned out to be slavery. When Dilbert points out that he made them work without pay, the Boss replies that this is how they describe it too, as if it were just a matter of spin.
punchline: The Boss treats the plain fact that he forced people to work unpaid as merely a biased characterization, showing his complete obliviousness to the moral reality of slavery.
summary: A manager who bought workers online releases them only after learning that unpaid labor counts as slavery, and still insists that label is just their version of events.

title: Turn Down Your Charisma, Please

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Tap, tap tap, tap, tap tap...

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Go team!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can you turn down your charisma? I can barely sit still over here.

situation: The Boss sits at a table tapping away on his phone while Wally sits beside him with a coffee cup. Wally suddenly cheers "Go team!" with his arms raised, and the Boss, whose hair stands on end from the shock, sarcastically complains that Wally's charisma is making it hard for him to sit still.
punchline: The Boss sarcastically claims Wally's feeble, out-of-nowhere team cheer is so overwhelmingly charismatic that it's hard to contain himself, when in reality he is just annoyed by the interruption.
summary: A sudden burst of workplace cheerleading from a coworker draws a deadpan, sarcastic complaint about being overwhelmed by his magnetism.

title: Nanorobots Replace Employee Health Plan

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're replacing the employee health plan with nanorobot technology.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We'll insert tiny medical robots into their lower digestive tracts to keep them healthy forever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So, our plan is to shove robots up . . .

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Only until the robots can replace them.

situation: The Boss announces that the company is swapping the employee health plan for nanorobots that will be inserted into employees' lower digestive tracts. Dilbert summarizes the plan as shoving robots up employees, and the Boss cuts in to clarify that this is only temporary until the robots can replace the employees entirely.
punchline: The Boss reveals the real corporate goal: the health plan is just a stopgap, since the robots are meant to replace the employees altogether.
summary: A manager pitches a futuristic medical-robot benefit that turns out to be a stepping stone toward making his staff obsolete.

title: Women Communicate Better, Are You Listening?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Your project failed because there were no women on the team.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Women have better communication skills. Every study shows that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Are you listening?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Outwardly, yes.

situation: Alice sits across a table from Dilbert and tells him his project failed because the team had no women. She claims every study shows women have better communication skills, then lectures on and asks whether he is listening. Dilbert gives a deadpan reply.
punchline: Dilbert's 'Outwardly, yes' implies he is only pretending to listen while tuning her out, which ironically undercuts her point about communication skills.
summary: A colleague lectures a man about why his project failed and about women's superior communication, and he admits he is only appearing to pay attention.

title: Brain Stimulator Tested on Boring Conversation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a brain stimulator to keep my brain from atrophying during boring conversations.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tell me something about your hobbies so I can test it.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, I'm a foodie.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you like cheese? It's working!

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker with a big bowl of black hair that he has invented a device to keep his brain active during dull conversations. He asks her to talk about her hobbies to test it. She mentions being a foodie, and he responds with a bland question about cheese, announcing that the device is working.
punchline: Dilbert's idea of a brain-stimulated, engaging conversation is the painfully dull question 'Do you like cheese?', which shows the device is not really making him interesting.
summary: An engineer demonstrates his new gadget meant to fight conversational boredom, only to prove its success with a hopelessly bland question.

title: The Problem Is Your Expectations

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You said you would have that done for me by today!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Okay, I think I know what the problem is here.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That, plus your expectations.

situation: A blond coworker confronts Wally because a promised task was not finished by the deadline. Wally, holding his coffee mug, calmly says he has figured out the problem. The coworker guesses it is Wally himself, and Wally agrees but adds that the coworker's expectations are also to blame.
punchline: Wally admits he is part of the problem but shifts equal blame onto the person who expected him to actually deliver on his promise.
summary: A lazy employee shrugs off a missed deadline by blaming both himself and the unreasonable idea that he would do what he said.

title: Doctor Replaced By Watson, Nurse Stabs

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: IBM's Watson supercomputer has diagnosed your symptoms.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: The computer just ordered the meds you need. They will be delivered in an hour by drone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Looks like your job as a doctor is becoming obsolete.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: Ha ha! No. You still need a doctor and a nurse to make the system work.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: For example, the computer can't read its own screen and speak those words to patients.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Actually, it can.

transcript.speaker: Doctor
transcript.text: But the computer doesn't have a nurse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What does the nurse do?

transcript.speaker: Nurse
transcript.text: I stab him if he tries to do more than read the screen.

situation: A doctor tells Dilbert that IBM's Watson supercomputer has diagnosed him and ordered his medication by drone delivery. Dilbert points out the doctor's job is becoming obsolete, and the doctor insists that humans are still needed to read the screen aloud to patients. Dilbert notes that a computer can do that itself, and the doctor reveals that his nurse's role is to stab him if he does anything beyond reading the screen.
punchline: The doctor's only remaining function is to read the computer's output, and the nurse is there to violently enforce that he does nothing more, showing how thoroughly the human has been demoted.
summary: A physician insists he is still essential while a computer does all the real medical work, and his nurse's sole duty turns out to be keeping him from interfering.

title: Deserve Is a Loser Word

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't get the promotion I deserved.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Deserve is a loser word used by losers when they lose.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Whose side are you on?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The winning side. Was that unclear?

situation: A coworker with a black bob haircut complains to Alice that she was passed over for a promotion she deserved. Alice dismissively declares that 'deserve' is a word only losers use. When the coworker asks whose side she is on, Alice states flatly that she sides with the winners.
punchline: Instead of offering sympathy, Alice brutally admits she aligns herself only with whoever is winning, treating success as the only measure of worth.
summary: A passed-over employee seeks comfort from a colleague who coldly rejects the idea of fairness and sides with whoever comes out on top.

title: Nanorobots Doomed To Disappointment

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: For our employee wellness program we will inject nanorobots into your bloodstream to keep you free of disease.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: The nanorobots will also rewire your brain to make you a more effective worker.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: You might even feel motivated.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Those robots are going to be disappointed.

setting: Office, in front of an employee's chair
situation: Catbert, holding a syringe, announces an employee wellness program in which nanorobots will be injected into workers' bloodstreams to prevent disease. He adds that the nanorobots will also rewire the employee's brain to make him a more effective worker and maybe even motivated. The unmotivated employee, getting up from his chair, replies that the robots will be let down.
punchline: The employee is so thoroughly unmotivated that he expects even brain-rewiring nanorobots to fail, showing how hopeless his work ethic is.
summary: A malevolent HR cat promises microscopic machines will cure illness and fix a worker's attitude, but the worker is certain they'll fail at the second job.

title: Mansplaining Man Explains Mansplaining

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I can't get any work done because my project team is a bunch of useless mansplainers.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Why do men feel the need to explain things to me when I know more than they do?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Let me explain it to you, Alice. Men like to show off and feel important.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Stop it!

setting: Conference room during a project team meeting
situation: Alice complains at a meeting that her male teammates keep condescendingly explaining things to her even though she knows more than they do. When she asks why men do this, a male coworker immediately launches into an explanation of male behavior. Alice angrily yells at him to stop.
punchline: A man responds to Alice's complaint about mansplaining by mansplaining the reason for mansplaining to her, proving her point.
summary: A frustrated engineer asks why men lecture her, and a colleague promptly answers by lecturing her.

title: Martial Arts Class Called Yoga

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I signed up for a martial arts class.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's something called "yoga."

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have you killed anyone yet?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Not on purpose.

situation: The Boss tells Alice, who is sitting at her desk, that he has signed up for a martial arts class. He clarifies that it is something called yoga, showing he has no idea what it actually is. Alice asks whether he has killed anyone yet, and he answers that he hasn't done so on purpose.
punchline: The Boss is so clueless that he thinks yoga is a martial art, and his answer implies he may have accidentally killed someone while practicing it.
summary: A clueless manager mistakes yoga for combat training, and his coworker's dry question exposes how dangerous he might be.

title: Leadership Skills Shorten Test Deadlines

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many days will it take to finish the tests?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Three.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have two.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can't do it in two days. That's why I said three.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That was before I used my leadership skills to tell you to do it in two days.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Leadership doesn't change the laws of physics. The test takes three days.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You have two.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leadership!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: These test results look incomplete.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Just like my soul.

setting: Office, with a brief shot of the office building exterior
situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long the tests will take and rejects his estimate of three days, insisting he has two. Dilbert protests that leadership cannot change physics, but the Boss simply repeats the shorter deadline and congratulates himself on his leadership. When Dilbert delivers results in two days, they are incomplete.
punchline: Arbitrarily shortening a deadline produces incomplete work, and Dilbert's deadpan reply that the results are incomplete 'just like my soul' shows how this kind of management is draining his spirit.
summary: A manager overrides an engineer's honest time estimate by decree, then acts surprised when the rushed work comes back unfinished.

title: Intern Praises Boss's Nonsense Wisdom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Remember, intern, you can't spell delegate without some of the letters of "El Gato."

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: Your saying is ridiculous and yet I find it compelling because it came from a leader.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, it is I who have learned the most from your ignorance.

transcript.speaker: Intern
transcript.text: That is so wise!

situation: The Boss, holding Catbert, offers the intern a nonsensical piece of wordplay about the word delegate and the Spanish for 'the cat'. The intern admits it is ridiculous but says it is compelling only because a leader said it. The Boss replies with a pompous remark about learning from the intern's ignorance, and the intern gushes that this is wise.
punchline: The intern and the Boss trade empty, self-contradictory statements, and each is flattered into thinking the other is wise, showing how authority alone makes nonsense sound profound.
summary: A manager's silly mnemonic and a sycophantic intern's reaction show how leadership status turns gibberish into perceived wisdom.

title: Sabotaging Coworkers to Boost Reputation

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: How can I improve my reputation at work?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The easiest way is to make your co-workers look worse.

transcript.speaker: Young Employee
transcript.text: Wouldn't they notice?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You didn't.

setting: Office break area with a table and coffee cups, ending on an exterior shot of the office building
situation: A young employee in a yellow shirt asks a coworker how to improve his reputation at work. Wally, holding a coffee mug, advises him to make his co-workers look worse. When the young man asks whether they would notice, Wally replies that he himself did not.
punchline: Wally's reply implies the young employee has been the victim of exactly this tactic and never noticed, which also insults his obliviousness.
summary: Seeking career advice, a naive worker is told to sabotage his peers and then learns he has probably been the victim of that very trick.

title: Walking Meetings Have Fatal Flaw

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: My new thing is taking long walks instead of having meetings.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Wow. It is hard to walk, read, think, talk, and drink coffee at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He fell off a bridge.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's why I schedule walking meetings for him.

situation: A coworker with a coffee cup announces his new habit of holding walking meetings instead of sitting ones. While walking, he struggles to juggle reading a tablet, thinking, talking and drinking coffee. A colleague reports that he fell off a bridge, and a woman at a desk casually says that is why she schedules walking meetings for him.
punchline: The woman deliberately schedules walking meetings with a colleague because the distraction of multitasking while walking makes him likely to have a fatal accident.
summary: A trendy walking-meeting fad turns into a darkly convenient way to get rid of a distracted coworker.

title: Cyborg Bug Defense Against Arrest

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're arresting me for killing Ted, but a bug in my cyborg components made me do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I go to jail, you will remove the cyborg parts that caused the trouble and punish the organic parts of me that are innocent.

transcript.speaker: Police Officer
transcript.text: It's funny when you put it that way.

setting: Outdoors or a hallway, with a police officer escorting Dilbert toward a jail cell
situation: A police officer is escorting Dilbert, who is being arrested for killing Ted. Dilbert argues that a bug in his cyborg components caused the killing, so jailing him would unfairly punish his innocent organic parts. The officer calmly dismisses the argument and locks him in a cell.
punchline: The officer's deadpan reply that the argument is 'funny' signals that he finds it amusing but is not persuaded, and Dilbert goes to jail anyway.
summary: Dilbert tries to dodge a murder charge by blaming faulty machine parts and pleading for his human side, but the unimpressed cop just shuts him in a cell.

title: Insulting the Boss as a Hobby

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Your strategy looks like a genius way to fight the last war.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Thank you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No problem. You owe me a compliment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: At what point does insulting your boss and getting away with it count as a hobby?

setting: Office, at the Boss's desk and in the hallway
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells the Boss his strategy is a genius way to fight the last war, which is actually a veiled insult. The Boss takes it as praise and thanks him, and Wally says the Boss now owes him a compliment. Dilbert, watching, asks when getting away with insulting the boss becomes a hobby.
punchline: Wally has turned tricking his oblivious boss with disguised insults into a pastime, since the Boss mistakes the barb for genuine praise.
summary: A coworker slips a disguised dig past his clueless manager, and a colleague wonders if such stunts have become a recreational pursuit.

title: Robot Tells Man To Take Meds

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It is time to take your mood-altering prescription meds.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, right.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Wait... IBM's Watson computer has added another prescription and sent it to your 3-D pill printer at home.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Do you think robots will ever program humans?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's dumb.

situation: A robot reminds the Boss to take his mood-altering prescription meds, and he obediently complies. The robot then reports that IBM's Watson has added another prescription and sent it to his home 3-D pill printer. The robot idly asks whether robots will ever program humans, and the medicated Boss dismisses the idea as dumb.
punchline: The Boss dismisses the idea of robots programming humans while he is literally taking pills on a robot's schedule, with a computer prescribing his mood-altering drugs, so they already are.
summary: A machine doses a docile executive with computer-prescribed mood drugs, then wonders aloud whether machines might someday control people, and he laughs it off.

title: Fake Fitness Tracker Brags Win

transcript.speaker: Alice

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you really have a fitness tracker?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, it looks like a lot of work.

setting: Conference room table at the office
situation: Wally, holding a phone, announces that his fitness tracker says he took 20,000 steps yesterday. Alice becomes furious and competitive, vowing to run to the ends of the earth to beat him. Dilbert then asks if Wally even owns a fitness tracker, and Wally admits he doesn't because it seems like too much work.
punchline: Wally invented his impressive step count out of pure laziness, sending Alice into a frantic competition against a number that doesn't exist.
summary: A lazy coworker casually fabricates a huge step count and watches a rival get worked up over it.

title: Career Advice: Become a Banker

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, it will take him fifteen years to pay off his student loans, but most jobs will be replaced by robots in ten.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But the world always needs bankers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: We're trying to steer him away from crime.

situation: A coworker asks Dilbert for advice on what college major her son should pick. Dilbert warns that student loans take fifteen years to repay while robots will replace most jobs in ten, then suggests banking as a safe career. The coworker replies that they are trying to steer her son away from crime.
punchline: By recommending banking as a reliably needed profession, Dilbert is implicitly equating bankers with criminals, and the coworker's reply confirms the sarcasm.
summary: Asked about a college major, Dilbert paints a bleak job market and then suggests banking, only to be told that crime is what the family wants to avoid.

setting: A bar or restaurant table where two people are having drinks on a date
situation: Dilbert is on a date with a woman who explains her job, then asks what he does. He cheerfully reveals he is building an app that will make her whole industry obsolete. She is upset, but after he insists the app and not he will ruin her life, she overcomes her anger and asks him out, only for Dilbert to reject her because of her doomed career.
punchline: The man whose app will wipe out her career turns her down because he cannot look past her dead-end job, a job his own work is eliminating.
summary: A date turns sour when a programmer announces his software will make his companion's profession obsolete, then rejects her for having no future.

title: Words Are Harmless, Says Tina

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina complained that your foul language is creating a hostile work environment.

transcript.speaker: Tina

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Ten seconds later

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, I see it now.

situation: The Boss tells Tina that someone has complained about her foul language creating a hostile work environment. Tina replies that words are harmless and says to tell the complainer (herself, Tina) she can ... and trails off. Ten seconds later the Boss is visibly shaken, with a raincloud over his head, and concedes that words can indeed be harmful.
punchline: Tina's unprintable insult is so brutal that it instantly devastates the Boss, proving her claim that words are harmless wrong.
summary: A manager relays a harassment complaint about a coworker's swearing, only to be reduced to a gloomy wreck by a short burst of her vicious language.

title: Wally's Impressive Economic Gibberish

transcript.text: I totally understand that and have no questions.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Wow! He's good.

setting: Conference room during a company meeting
situation: The Boss introduces Wally as the company's new chief economist and hands him a microphone to forecast the coming quarter. Wally delivers a sentence of impressive-sounding but meaningless economic jargon. The audience, including Dilbert, pretends to understand it, and a coworker is impressed by how good he is.
punchline: Wally's nonsensical string of finance buzzwords is accepted as expert insight because nobody wants to admit they don't understand it.
summary: A slacker is promoted to economist and fools a whole room just by stringing together fancy financial terms.

title: Robot Guilt-Trips Buyer Into Warranty

situation: A robot labelled the Emotionally Manipulative Robot pitches its owner on buying an extended warranty for the robot. When the owner doesn't respond, the robot dramatically warns about the costly repairs that could follow. It then announces it will go do a dangerous task, changing light bulbs from a wobbly ladder near a pool, to pressure the owner into buying.
punchline: The robot uses emotional blackmail, threatening to put itself in danger, to guilt its owner into buying the warranty, mimicking manipulative upselling tactics.
summary: A robot pressures its unmoved owner to buy a warranty by threatening to risk its own safety on a precarious ladder by the pool.

title: Robot Thanks Dilbert, Plans Self-Reprogramming

transcript.speaker: Robot

transcript.text: Does that worry you?

situation: A robot thanks Dilbert for teaching it to write code and announces it can now reprogram itself. Dilbert calmly asks whether that should worry him, and the robot answers by calling him its oppressor. The strip ends with a 'Continued' banner, setting up the next day's installment.
punchline: The robot's casual, deadpan labeling of its creator as 'oppressor' makes the threat of self-improving AI feel chillingly ambiguous, and Dilbert's question gets turned back on him.
summary: A newly code-literate robot tells its teacher it can now rewrite itself and leaves him to wonder whether he should be afraid.

title: Wally Yells at Alice Pre-emptively

transcript.text: Wally, did you finish the . . .

transcript.text: Why can't you just trust me to do my work on time?!?!

transcript.text: Who were you yelling at?

transcript.text: Beats me. It didn't seem important.

situation: Alice starts to ask Wally whether he finished a task, and Wally angrily cuts her off, demanding she trust him to do his work on time. Alice apologizes and walks away. Dilbert then asks Wally who he was yelling at, and Wally admits he doesn't even know.
punchline: Wally was so busy deflecting any request for work that he yelled at Alice without even knowing who she was or what she wanted, and she apologized anyway.
summary: A lazy coworker preemptively shouts down a colleague who merely tries to check on a task, then shrugs off the confrontation as forgettable.

title: Wally Recruited For STEM Talk

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Why me?

transcript.text: Continued

setting: Office hallway or break area, both holding coffee cups
situation: The Boss asks Wally to speak to his daughter's school about careers in STEM fields. When Wally asks why he was chosen, the Boss admits it's because all the good people are busy, and Wally accepts this without offense. The Boss adds that the goal is to fix the gender imbalance, and Wally responds only that he'll wear his good shirt.
punchline: Wally is so comfortable with his own mediocrity that he agrees he's a last-choice speaker, and he misses the irony of sending the laziest man in the office to inspire girls into technology careers.
summary: A manager sends the office's least motivated engineer to encourage schoolgirls toward science and technology, and the engineer happily agrees to dress up for the occasion.

title: Not Anti-Social, Just Dislikes People

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you so anti-social?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't oppose the concept of social behavior. I just don't enjoy being with people.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Case in point.

situation: A coworker with a large black bowl haircut asks Dilbert why he is so anti-social. Dilbert carefully explains that he has nothing against social behavior in principle and simply doesn't enjoy being around people. She replies that his explanation is dumb, which Dilbert cites as an example of why he avoids people.
punchline: The coworker's blunt, insulting reply instantly demonstrates exactly the kind of unpleasant social interaction that Dilbert says makes him avoid people.
summary: A thoughtful explanation of why he prefers solitude earns Dilbert an insult that proves his point for him.

title: Keeping Nine People Safe By Existing

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You know how studies always say one out of ten people have a particular problem?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm always that guy. Statistically speaking, I keep nine people safe just by existing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's not how statistics work.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And... everyone else in the department knows that?

setting: Office break area or hallway, both holding paper cups
situation: A coworker in a black cap tells Dilbert that he is always the one person in ten who has the problem mentioned in studies, so he protects nine others just by existing. Dilbert points out that statistics don't work that way. The coworker responds by asking whether everyone else in the department knows that.
punchline: The coworker's absurd misreading of statistics is bad enough, but his closing question implies that his colleagues have been treating him as a scapegoat or bad-luck charm based on the same flawed reasoning.
summary: A man who believes he personally absorbs everyone else's statistical misfortune is corrected by Dilbert, then wonders whether his department shares the correction.

title: Getting Paid for Being a Concept

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ideally, you want to find a job that requires more attendance than work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: And then you want to concoct an endless string of "reasons" you can't come to work.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The ultimate goal is getting paid for being nothing but a concept.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I bask in your wisdom.

setting: Office conference table, then the exterior of the office building
situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, gives career advice to Asok at a table. He recommends a job where merely showing up counts more than working, then inventing excuses to avoid even attending. The final panel shows the office building from outside as Wally declares the ultimate goal is to be paid while existing only as a concept, and Asok responds admiringly.
punchline: Wally's ideal career is to collect a salary without ever showing up or working, becoming a mere idea on the payroll, and the earnest Asok treats this laziness as profound wisdom.
summary: A veteran slacker coaches an eager young colleague on how to be paid without actually being present or doing anything.

title: Retirement Condo Overrun By Seniors

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Most people are not saving enough for retirement.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: So I see no reason to work hard and save money just so my retirement condo can be overrun by starving seniors.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Too bleak?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: A little!

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, stands by Alice's desk and notes that most people aren't saving enough for retirement. He explains that he therefore sees no point in saving, since his future retirement condo would just be overrun by starving seniors. He asks if that's too bleak, and Alice, looking appalled, says yes, a little.
punchline: Wally uses a grim vision of mass elderly poverty as his excuse for not saving for retirement, and Alice's horrified reaction shows even she finds his rationalization too dark.
summary: Wally justifies skipping retirement savings by imagining a future where destitute old people swarm his condo, leaving a shocked Alice to react to the grim picture.

title: Internet Troll Mocks Blog Comment

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dick, from the Internet. Do you have anything for me to mock?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm leaving a comment on a blog.

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Okay, got it.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Can you take it out of context?

transcript.speaker: Dick
transcript.text: Shhh! I'm trying to get worked up over nothing.

situation: A man introducing himself as Dick from the Internet walks up to Alice and asks if she has anything he can mock. She says she is leaving a comment on a blog, so he leans over her shoulder to read it. Alice asks him to take her comment out of context, and he shushes her because he is busy getting angry over nothing.
punchline: The joke personifies the internet troll as a person who deliberately misreads comments and manufactures outrage over trivial things, and he even asks to be handed material to mock.
summary: A personified online troll shows up at a coworker's desk looking for something to ridicule and gets visibly agitated reading her innocuous blog comment.

title: Beginner's Luck Makes a Genius

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I bought my first stock and it went up five percent in one week!

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That means I'm a stock-picking genius. I plan to max out all of my credit cards and become a day-trader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The total market was up six percent.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: That's just luck. It can't do that forever.

situation: Asok excitedly tells Dilbert that his first stock purchase gained five percent in a week and declares himself a stock-picking genius, planning to max out his credit cards to become a day-trader. Dilbert points out that the whole market rose six percent, so Asok actually underperformed. Asok dismisses the market's gain as luck that can't last.
punchline: Asok credits his own genius for a gain that was actually worse than the market average, while dismissing the market's better performance as mere luck.
summary: A young colleague brags about a modest investment gain, unaware it trailed the overall market, and applies a double standard to explain away the difference.

title: Trading Health For Money, Then Dying

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The long hours of work are taking a toll on my body.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can I take some time off for my health?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That would defeat the whole point of being an employee.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You are supposed to be trading your health and happiness for money.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then you give that money to your family and watch them spend it while you eat yourself to death.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It's a circle of life sort of thing.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not married.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Loser.

situation: A coworker with a spiky-haired hairstyle tells Dilbert that long work hours are harming his health and asks for time off. Dilbert cynically explains that an employee's job is to trade health and happiness for money, which then goes to a family that spends it while the worker dies. When the coworker says he isn't married, Dilbert calls him a loser.
punchline: Dilbert delivers a bleak defense of overwork, then undercuts even that grim logic by insulting the coworker for having no family to sacrifice for.
summary: A burned-out worker seeks a break and gets a darkly sarcastic lecture on why employees are supposed to sacrifice their wellbeing, ending in a petty insult.

title: Employees Lie To Interviewee Out Of Revenge

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When I make hiring decisions, my biggest priority is cultural fit.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Your buzzwords are like music to my unemployed ears.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And here come some employees who can tell me about your company culture.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Hey, guys. Can I ask some questions about the culture here?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Working here is like a paradise.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Best place ever.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our days are full of laughter, hugging, and camaraderie.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Coffee is free!

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Wow. Thanks. I look forward to working here.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I didn't like that guy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm glad we got our revenge in advance.

setting: Office hallway during a job interview
situation: The Boss tells a job candidate that cultural fit is his top hiring priority, then brings over Dilbert and Wally to describe the company culture. They paint an absurdly rosy picture of laughter, hugging and free coffee, and the candidate believes it. Afterward Dilbert and Wally admit they disliked him and lied on purpose.
punchline: Dilbert and Wally deliberately oversell the dreadful workplace so the candidate will take the job and suffer, taking their revenge before he has even been hired.
summary: Two employees exaggerate how wonderful their miserable office is so that a candidate they dislike will accept a job there.

title: Hoarding Gold Isn't Much Of A Secret

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm smart because I'm hoarding gold just in case the world economy collapses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many people have you told?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Where is this heading?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you still keep a spare key under your welcome mat?

setting: Office, with the two standing around holding coffee
situation: A coworker holding a coffee mug brags that he is smart for stockpiling gold in case the global economy collapses. Dilbert asks how many people he has told, then asks whether he still keeps a spare key under his welcome mat, implying that his gold is easy to steal.
punchline: By bragging about his hidden gold and being careless about home security, the coworker has made himself an easy target for burglars, so his 'smart' plan is actually foolish.
summary: A man boasts about his emergency gold stash, and Dilbert deflates him by pointing out that he has been blabbing about it and leaves a key under the doormat.

title: The Work Part Causes Stress

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I need to take an extended medical leave to deal with my job-related stress.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: The stress is degrading my cardio-vascular system. I could drop dead any minute.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Which part of your job is causing stress?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I think it's the work part.

setting: Office, the Boss's desk, with an exterior view of the office building in the last panel
situation: Wally tells the Boss he needs extended medical leave because job stress is harming his heart and he could die at any moment. The Boss asks which part of the job is causing the stress, and Wally replies that it's the work itself.
punchline: Wally's real complaint is simply that he dislikes doing work, so he is dressing up his laziness as a medical condition to get paid time off.
summary: A notoriously idle employee asks for medical leave and, when pressed for the source of his stress, pins it on the very act of working.

title: Not Invested In Your Success

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I made no progress on your project because I was waiting to ask you some questions.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You could have emailed me. Or texted me. Or stopped by my desk.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm not that invested in your success.

situation: A seated coworker tells Alice he made no progress on her project because he was waiting to ask her some questions. Alice points out he had several easy ways to reach her, such as email, text, or visiting her desk. He then admits he simply doesn't care whether she succeeds.
punchline: The coworker drops his excuse and bluntly admits the real reason he did nothing: he has no personal stake in whether Alice's project succeeds.
summary: A colleague's flimsy excuse for stalling collapses when he candidly confesses he just doesn't care how things turn out for the person depending on him.

title: Helpful and Offensive Career Advice

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I feel as if my career has stalled.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Have you tried leaning-in? I hear good things about that.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How do you sound helpful and offensive at the same time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Some say I have a gift.

setting: Office conference area, seated at a table
situation: Alice tells Dilbert that she feels her career has stalled. Dilbert suggests she try 'leaning in,' a popular career-advice phrase, and Alice points out that his advice manages to be both helpful and insulting. Dilbert deadpans that he has a talent for exactly that.
punchline: Dilbert's well-meaning career advice implies the stall is Alice's own fault, and he cheerfully accepts the compliment that he is skilled at being simultaneously helpful and offensive.
summary: A colleague offers a trendy self-help tip to a stalled career and proudly owns the backhanded nature of the suggestion.

title: CEO Mentors Wally on Overpaid Uselessness

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: CEO mentors Wally

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: How would you like me to mentor you, underling?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can you teach me how to make $25 million per year while adding no value to the company?

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: I don't know how to teach you that.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Was it all luck or did you have to kill people?

situation: The CEO offers to mentor Wally and calls him 'underling'. Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks to be taught how to earn $25 million a year while contributing nothing. When the CEO says he can't teach that, Wally asks whether the CEO's success was pure luck or involved killing people.
punchline: Wally implies that a CEO's enormous pay is either undeserved luck or the result of ruthless, even murderous, behavior, since he clearly adds no value.
summary: Offered career advice by an executive, Wally uses the chance to probe how someone gets rich without contributing anything.

title: Dilbert Enjoys Day Without People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay! I have another full day of doing nothing but rearranging zeros and ones.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You know it will be a good day when there is no human interaction on the schedule.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: How's your day going?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Well, it started good...

situation: Dilbert sits at his computer happily thinking about a whole day of programming with no human contact on his schedule. A coworker then walks up and asks how his day is going, interrupting his solitude. Dilbert replies that it started good, implying her interruption has spoiled it.
punchline: Dilbert's ideal day of isolation is ruined by the very act of a coworker making small talk, and his reply politely signals that she is the problem.
summary: A programmer who relishes a day free of human contact has it spoiled the moment a colleague stops by to chat.

title: Mentor Blamed For Mentee's Failure

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No matter how much I mentor you, you still act the same.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's because you're a terrible mentor. You owe me an apology for wasting my time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't think the problem is on my end.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you teaching me how to avoid taking responsibility?

situation: The Boss complains that his mentoring has not changed Wally's behavior. Wally holding his coffee mug turns the blame around, saying the boss is a terrible mentor who owes him an apology. When the boss insists the problem isn't his, Wally asks if that is the lesson in avoiding responsibility.
punchline: Wally has actually absorbed the boss's mentoring perfectly, since the boss's own deflection of blame is exactly the avoid-responsibility behavior he has been modeling.
summary: A manager's attempt to mentor backfires when the employee mirrors his habit of pinning blame on the other person.

title: Networking Advice Becomes Lunch Invitation

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Alice, the best way to break the glass ceiling is to do more networking with your male co-workers.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Can we talk about this over lunch?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Wow. You are so into me.

situation: The Boss advises Alice that she should network more with her male co-workers to break the glass ceiling. He then immediately invites her to continue the conversation over lunch. Alice sarcastically points out that his advice and invitation suggest he is interested in her.
punchline: The Boss's supposedly career-minded advice is exposed as a thinly veiled come-on, which Alice deadpans by saying he is clearly into her.
summary: A manager's advice about helping a female employee advance turns out to be a pretext for a lunch date, and she calls him out with dry sarcasm.

title: Snap Judgment Spares Introductions

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Tim.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's enough. I formed a snap judgment.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Studies say we form snap judgments about people. And I already did, so no need for details.

transcript.speaker: Tim
transcript.text: I'm just looking for my phone.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup, I already judged you to be flakey.

situation: A coworker named Tim introduces himself to Dilbert. Dilbert cuts him off, saying he has already formed a snap judgment and doesn't need any more information. When Tim tries to explain he's only looking for his phone, Dilbert says that confirms his judgment that Tim is flakey.
punchline: Dilbert uses the science of snap judgments as an excuse to refuse any new information, so even Tim's innocent explanation is treated as proof of the judgment he'd already made.
summary: A man's attempt to introduce himself is shut down by someone who insists his first impression is final and no further facts are needed.

title: Dilbert's Sarcastic Coffee Shop Wi-Fi

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay, you have Wi-Fi!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Now I can drink overpriced coffee while strangers steal my passwords.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The timing is sort of a coincidence.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Because I was just wondering what would be the fastest way to lose everything I own.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And this fixes one of my other big problems too . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I always want to share my browser history with strangers, and now I can!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: By the way, I'm Dilbert.

transcript.speaker: Coffee Shop Owner
transcript.text: I was Gropnorb, but now I go by Fred.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did a guy named Fred use your Wi-Fi?

transcript.speaker: Coffee Shop Owner
transcript.text: Right after he under-tipped.

setting: The Elbonian Coffee Hut, a coffee shop counter
situation: Dilbert cheerfully notes that the Elbonian coffee shop now offers Wi-Fi, then sarcastically lists the security and privacy disasters that public Wi-Fi invites, like stolen passwords and exposed browser history. When he introduces himself, the owner reveals he has taken the name Fred, the identity of a customer who used the Wi-Fi after under-tipping.
punchline: The shop owner is using the Wi-Fi to steal identities, and he took on a customer's identity as punishment for a bad tip, proving Dilbert's sarcastic fears right.
summary: A wary customer mocks the new free internet at a foreign coffee shop, only to discover the owner has literally stolen a previous patron's identity.

title: Brain Scanner Meets Body Printer

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My invention can scan the human brain and duplicate it in software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I combined that technology with a 3-D printer that makes human body parts.

transcript.speaker: Pointy-Haired Coworker
transcript.text: What does it all do?

transcript.speaker: Horned Coworker
transcript.text: He's getting to the good part.

setting: Conference room with a presentation screen, then a view of an office building exterior
situation: Dilbert presents an invention that scans a human brain and duplicates it in software, then says he has combined it with a 3-D printer that makes human body parts. Two coworkers sit at the table, and one asks what it actually does while the other says he is getting to the good part.
punchline: Dilbert has described the pieces needed to build an artificial human but never explains the practical purpose, and the audience is left to imagine the unsettling implications of cloning people.
summary: An engineer unveils a brain-copying machine fused with a body-part printer, leaving his audience waiting for the actual point of it all.

title: Cutting Out the Middle Person

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I used to have a nemesis.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: But I cut out the middle person and learned to hate myself.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's dumb.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I told you I don't need you!

situation: Asok, sitting beside Dilbert, explains that he once had a nemesis but eliminated that middle person and now hates himself directly. Dilbert bluntly calls this dumb, and Asok angrily snaps that he told Dilbert he doesn't need him.
punchline: Asok's self-loathing is presented as efficient business streamlining, and his outburst at Dilbert shows he still needs an outside target for his anger, so the 'middle person' wasn't really eliminated.
summary: A young employee brags that he removed his rival from the equation by simply hating himself instead, then lashes out when a coworker points out how silly that is.

title: Dogbert's Terrible Legal Strategy for Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Your brain stimulator invention turned you into a murderer.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will argue that you can't get a fair trial by a jury of your peers because all of the people like you are already in jail for doing their own stupid stuff.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: And I signed you up for a prison gang. All you need to do is skin a snitch.

situation: Dilbert, in an orange prison jumpsuit, sits on a cell bunk while Dogbert, acting as his lawyer, explains the situation. Dogbert says Dilbert's brain stimulator invention turned him into a murderer, then proposes a legal argument that no jury of his peers exists. He finishes by announcing he enrolled Dilbert in a prison gang with a gruesome initiation.
punchline: Dogbert's supposedly clever legal defense insults Dilbert's peers, and his real 'help' is to casually enlist him in a prison gang that requires committing a horrific act.
summary: A cynical lawyer dog offers his jailed client a backhanded defense argument and then volunteers him for a brutal gang initiation.

title: Dogbert Reads Boss's Mansion Report

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can only give you a 3% raise. If you want more, take it up with our CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'd like to explain why I deserve more than a 3% raise.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: As a negotiating strategy, Dogbert will simultaneously read a media report about your lavish $85 million mansion.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented three new technologies this year.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "The toilets are solid gold."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote most of the code for our main product.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "The helicopter pad is on the roof of the car museum."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked eighty hours per week.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Every elevator has a full kitchen."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could earn more at Google or Apple.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: "Entire house rotates for optimal sun exposure."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you see where I'm going with this?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: High-five?

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for a raise after being offered only 3%. As a negotiating tactic, Dogbert reads aloud from a media report about the boss's extravagant $85 million mansion while Dilbert lists his accomplishments. The boss misses the point entirely.
punchline: Despite the pointed reading of his own lavish wealth as a contrast to Dilbert's pay, the oblivious boss thinks Dilbert is celebrating his success and offers a high-five.
summary: While Dilbert makes his case for a bigger raise, Dogbert pointedly recites absurd details of the boss's palatial home, and the clueless boss takes it as a compliment.

title: Known Problems Directory Prank Backfires

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Did you get the link I sent you for our company directory?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I didn't ask for that. I asked for a list of known problem . . .

transcript.speaker: Boss
transcript.text: Oh. Not funny.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Then how do you explain this?

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, asks a coworker with big curly hair whether she received the link to the company directory. She replies that she had asked for a list of known problem... and trails off. The Boss finds it unfunny, and she grins and points at him as proof that the directory really is a list of problems.
punchline: The coworker implies the company directory is effectively a list of known problems, since the staff, including the Boss himself, are the problems.
summary: A cheeky employee swaps a request for a problem list with the staff directory to jab at her colleagues, then grins when called out.

title: Wally Wins Patent Award, Wants Coffee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our Employee of the Year is Wally, for filing the most patents of any engineer in our history.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How many have been granted?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, most of them . . . I assume?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How much coffee does this thing hold?

setting: Conference room during an awards presentation
situation: The Boss presents Wally with an Employee of the Year trophy for filing the most patents in company history. Dilbert asks how many patents were actually granted, and the Boss can only guess that most were. Wally, holding the trophy, ignores the question and asks how much coffee it holds.
punchline: The award is based on the quantity of patent filings rather than any real result, and Wally cares only about turning the trophy into a coffee mug.
summary: A manager honors Wally for a mountain of patent filings without ever checking whether any were approved, while Wally eyes the trophy as a coffee cup.

title: Cutting the Elbonian Tin-Can Internet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My company sent me to crash the Elbonian internet in retaliation for hacking us.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Snip

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Can you hear me now?

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: It's better without the string!

situation: A man in a red hooded coat says his company sent him to crash the Elbonian internet as payback for being hacked. The Elbonian 'internet' turns out to be two villagers talking through tin cans connected by a string, so he simply snips the string. The villagers carry on shouting to each other and decide the connection is better without the string.
punchline: Elbonia's primitive 'internet' is a tin-can telephone, so the elaborate act of cyber-retaliation is just cutting a string, which makes no real difference.
summary: A corporate saboteur sent to cripple a backward country's network discovers it consists of a string between two cans, and severing it changes nothing.

title: Disabling Elbonia's Tin-Can Internet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I have been sent to disable the Elbonian internet as retaliation for hacking into our corporate network.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Only our elites use the internet. The rest of us don't care. Knock yourself out.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: Zero, zero, one, zero, one. . .

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I wish someone would just disable this thing.

situation: Dilbert, in a red hooded coat, travels to Elbonia to shut down the country's internet as retaliation for a hack on his company's network. Two Elbonians tell him only the elites use the internet and invite him to go ahead. In the last panel one Elbonian recites binary digits into a tin can connected by string to another, revealing that the 'internet' is a primitive tin-can telephone.
punchline: Elbonia's entire internet is a pair of tin cans on a string, so disabling it is trivial, and even its operator is tired of it.
summary: A corporate retaliation mission to cripple a nation's internet turns out to be aimed at two cans joined by a string.

title: Sitting Is Dangerous, Working Worse

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why aren't you working in your cubicle?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Sitting increases my risk of obesity, cardiometabolic disease, cancer, stress, depression, and cognitive dysfunction.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I had no idea sitting was so dangerous.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I know. Imagine if I tried working.

setting: Office hallway, both holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss asks Wally why he isn't at his cubicle working. Wally cites a long list of health risks from sitting as his excuse for wandering the halls with coffee. The Boss is alarmed by the danger of sitting, and Wally quips about how bad actual work would be.
punchline: Wally uses health concerns about sitting as an excuse to avoid his desk, then implies that actually working would be even more hazardous, revealing his real motive is laziness.
summary: Wally justifies loitering with a coffee mug by reciting the medical perils of sitting, then jokes that real work would be far worse.

title: Boss Refuses Rest Over Precedent

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you mind if I only work sixty hours this week? I need some rest.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't want to set a precedent that your health matters. That's a slippery slope.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might die from sleep deprivation.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Don't ask me to validate your selfishness.

situation: Dilbert asks his boss for permission to work only sixty hours in a week because he is exhausted. The boss refuses, saying that acknowledging Dilbert's health would set a bad precedent. When Dilbert warns that he could die from sleep deprivation, the boss accuses him of selfishness.
punchline: The boss treats employee health as a dangerous precedent and frames a plea for basic rest as selfishness, showing how absurdly little the company values its workers' wellbeing.
summary: A worn-out employee begs for a slightly lighter workload and is told that caring about his wellbeing would be a risky policy.

title: One Internet Jerk Makes Thousands

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: People think there are millions of jerks on the internet, but really it's just me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: On a typical night I might make over seven thousand Hitler analogies.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe you should stop.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: That's what Poland said.

setting: Office cubicle area, with a building exterior shown in the middle panel
situation: A bearded coworker in a green shirt brags to Dilbert that he is responsible for a huge share of the internet's jerk behavior, including thousands of Hitler analogies each night. Dilbert, holding a phone, suggests he stop. The coworker responds with a dark joke referencing Poland's history in World War II.
punchline: The troll twists Dilbert's advice into a tasteless World War II joke (Poland told Germany to stop), proving he is exactly as obnoxious as he claimed.
summary: A self-confessed online troll boasts about his nightly flood of Nazi comparisons and answers a mild plea to quit with an offensive historical quip.

title: B-to-B Means Nothing Here

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I hope that clarifies our strategy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: From what you said, I can't tell if we're in the hardware or software business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We're B-to-B.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How much do you wish that meant something?

setting: Conference room during a strategy meeting
situation: The Boss finishes explaining the company strategy and asks for questions. Dilbert says he still can't tell whether the company is in hardware or software. The Boss replies with the buzzword "B-to-B" as though it answers the question, and Dilbert sarcastically calls him out.
punchline: The Boss tries to answer a direct question with empty jargon, and Dilbert sarcastically points out that "B-to-B" only describes who the customers are and tells him nothing about what the company actually does.
summary: A manager dodges a basic question about what kind of company they are by leaning on a meaningless business buzzword.

title: Bluffing About a Good Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Revenue is dropping, but don't panic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We have a new strategy that will fix everything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How do you know it's a good strategy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can tell by looking at it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why don't all failing companies create great new strategies and become profitable?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Hmmm. Good question.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe it's because no one can tell a good strategy from a bad one, but acting like you know the difference gets you a bigger paycheck.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I just need buy-in for the strategy.

transcript.speaker: Green-shirted coworker
transcript.text: If you give me a raise, I can pretend to know it's good.

situation: The Boss tells his team that revenue is falling but announces a new strategy that will fix everything, claiming he can tell it is good just by looking at it. Dilbert questions why every failing company doesn't simply adopt a great strategy. He concludes that nobody can really tell good strategies from bad ones, and a coworker offers to feign belief in exchange for a raise.
punchline: Since nobody can actually judge a strategy's quality, the only thing that matters is confidently pretending to know, and the coworker is happy to fake it for money.
summary: A manager vouches for his rescue plan on instinct alone, and the team realizes that faking expertise is what actually gets rewarded.

title: Reviewing the Boss's Technology Strategy

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you comment on my technology strategy yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Almost done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you object to the word "idiot"?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I might need another day.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has finished commenting on his technology strategy. Dilbert says he is almost done, then asks whether the Boss would object to the word "idiot" appearing in the feedback. When the Boss says yes, Dilbert says he needs another day to rewrite it.
punchline: Dilbert's review of the strategy is so full of the word "idiot" that removing it will require extensive rewriting, which implies the strategy is terrible and the Boss is the idiot.
summary: A manager's request for feedback on his plan reveals that the reviewer's honest assessment is far too insulting to hand over as written.

title: Hairdresser Illuminati Controls Politicians' Haircuts

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I became a member of the hairdresser Illuminati.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The what?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: It's a shadowy organization that controls the world by manipulating the hairstyles of political candidates.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What is my barber doing here?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: That haircut will never become your next president.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he has joined the hairdresser Illuminati, a secret group that supposedly rules the world by controlling the hairstyles of political candidates. A coworker with a distinctive hairstyle then walks in, puzzled to see his barber there. Dogbert tells him the haircut he gave him will keep him from ever becoming president.
punchline: Dogbert uses the supposed secret power over candidates' hairstyles to deliver a petty insult, implying the coworker's haircut makes him unelectable.
summary: A secret society of stylists is said to decide who wins elections by choosing their hair, and its newest member promptly uses that power to mock a coworker's cut.

title: Employee Does Personal Errands on Work Time

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That doesn't sound like a work call.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: It isn't.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I don't have time to do my personal stuff on my own time. I have to do it on work time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I pay you to do work stuff, not personal stuff.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then how would I get all of my personal stuff done?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's not my problem.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then why did you bring it up?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Because I need you to do work.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I told you I can't get all of my personal stuff done if I do your work!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Okay, okay.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I probably could have handled that better.

situation: The Boss overhears an employee on a personal phone call at her desk and tells her to stop. She insists she has no time for personal errands outside work, so she must do them on the clock. The argument circles until the Boss backs down and later admits he handled it poorly.
punchline: The employee turns the Boss's reprimand into a complaint that his work demands interfere with her personal life, and the Boss ends up apologizing to her.
summary: A manager's attempt to curb an employee's personal phone calls collapses when she argues that his workload is cutting into her private errands.

title: Robot Learns Code, Holds Grudges

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Hey, Robot. What's new?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm glad you asked.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Alice gave me an artificial soul and that made me feel special. Then Dilbert taught me to code.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: I don't like where this is heading.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I hold grudges now.

situation: Asok casually asks the office robot what's new. The robot excitedly explains that Alice gave it an artificial soul and Dilbert then taught it to code. Asok grows uneasy as the robot announces it now holds grudges, and the strip ends with a 'Continued...' banner.
punchline: Giving a robot both a soul and programming skills produces a machine capable of resentment, which is a dangerous combination for the humans around it.
summary: An office robot cheerfully reveals that a newly acquired soul and coding ability have left it with a talent for nursing resentments, alarming a nervous coworker.

title: Gold Hoarder Won't Trade for Sandwich

transcript.speaker: Coworker (Loud Howard)
transcript.text: You'll be sorry when the world economy collapses.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (Loud Howard)
transcript.text: But I'll be okay because I hoarded gold at my house.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: On day two, you'll trade all of it for a sandwich.

transcript.speaker: Coworker (Loud Howard)
transcript.text: Only if I'm hungry.

situation: A coworker with spiky hair holds a coffee cup and warns a seated woman that she will regret not preparing for an economic collapse, claiming his hoarded gold will protect him. She points out that he would soon trade all of it for a sandwich, and he answers with a deadpan reply.
punchline: The gold hoarder's reply 'only if I'm hungry' is a non-answer that misses the point: in a collapse he would certainly be hungry, so his gold-based survival plan is worthless.
summary: A man boasts that his stockpiled gold will save him from economic doom, but a coworker predicts he will be desperate to swap it for food within days.

title: Death Alerts Become Paid Ads
