transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The health sensors and predictive algorithms you built into our smart watch are too good.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People are freaked out because it sends alerts to their phones when they have five minutes left to live.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Isn't that useful?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It was, until we started sending paid ads as alerts.

situation: The Boss complains to Dilbert that the health-prediction algorithms in the company's smart watch work too well, because users are alarmed by alerts warning they have five minutes left to live. Dilbert points out that this seems useful, and the Boss reveals the feature only became a problem once the company began sending paid advertisements as those alerts.
punchline: The life-saving death warning was fine until the company monetized it by turning the alerts into ads, showing how profit motives corrupt useful technology.
summary: A manager laments that a wearable's lifespan-prediction alerts have unsettled customers, only to admit the real trouble began when his company started stuffing sponsored messages into them.

title: Breakup Interrupted By Hobby Drone

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I'm breaking up with you because you don't give me enough attention.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: All you care about is your stupid aerial photography hobby.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: I wish you the best.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: That felt like a clean break.

setting: Outdoor park with hedges and a paved walkway
situation: A woman with large dark hair breaks up with her boyfriend in a park, complaining that he ignores her in favor of his aerial photography hobby. As she walks away feeling she made a clean break, a camera drone hovers in the sky behind her, implying he is still following her with it.
punchline: She believes the breakup was clean, but the ex-boyfriend's camera drone is still tailing her, showing he hasn't let go and is literally spying on her.
summary: A woman ends things with her drone-obsessed boyfriend, only to find his flying camera trailing after her as she leaves.

title: Feng Shui Makes Meetings Dumber

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it my imagination or do people get dumber when they sit down for a meeting?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Or would you say you are equally dumb no matter what you are doing?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Well, I'm no scientist, but I'm pretty sure feng shui is part of the answer.

setting: Conference room table during a meeting
situation: Dilbert sits at a meeting table beside a coworker and asks whether people get dumber in meetings. He then backhandedly suggests the coworker is equally dumb all the time. The coworker replies that, though not a scientist, he believes feng shui explains it.
punchline: Dilbert's insult goes right over the coworker's head, as he sincerely offers a pseudoscientific explanation, which proves Dilbert's point about how dumb he is.
summary: A question about meeting-induced stupidity gets answered with earnest mysticism by the very person it was aimed at.

title: Mentor's Boss Protects Me

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Will you be my mentor?

transcript.speaker: Senior executive
transcript.text: Yes I will! You are wise to ask because it shows you have the drive to succeed.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Exactly!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Give me one good reason I shouldn't fire you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: My mentor is your boss.

setting: Office hallway by an elevator, then The Boss's office
situation: Wally asks a bald senior executive to be his mentor, and the executive happily agrees, praising Wally's ambition. Later the Pointy-Haired Boss threatens to fire Wally and demands a reason not to. Wally, leaning back with his feet on the desk, reveals his new mentor outranks The Boss.
punchline: Wally's real motive for seeking a mentor was not career growth but protection, since having his boss's boss in his corner makes him unfireable.
summary: A notoriously lazy employee recruits a high-ranking mentor purely as job-security insurance against his own manager.

title: Overweight Boss Rejects Weight-Loss Device

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a device that can help people lose weight.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I wouldn't need that because I have willpower.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why are you overweight?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: This is temporary.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You've looked exactly the same for years.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can lose this weight any time I want.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So... are you saying you choose to be less healthy than you could be?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm saying I'd rather be happy than healthy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you happy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because I'm hungry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And eating will make you happy?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Well, I usually eat until I'm sick.

situation: Dilbert shows the Boss a weight-loss gadget he invented. The Boss insists he has willpower and that his overweight state is temporary, so Dilbert pokes holes in each claim. The Boss's answers keep contradicting themselves until he admits he is unhappy and hungry and eats until he feels sick.
punchline: The Boss's justifications for staying overweight collapse into circular logic, revealing that his supposed happiness from eating actually makes him sick and unhappy.
summary: A man offering a diet gadget calmly dismantles his overweight boss's excuses until the boss admits his eating habits bring neither health nor happiness.

title: Burying Bad Strategy in Babble

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I fixed your technology strategy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I couldn't make it sound logical, so I buried the stupid parts under seven layers of technical babble.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Add an irrelevant graph and no one will be the wiser . . . literally.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Please stop being a team player.

situation: Dilbert tells the Boss he has fixed the technology strategy. Since he could not make it logical, he hid the illogical parts under layers of technical jargon and suggests adding an irrelevant graph so nobody understands it. The Boss, apparently unhappy about the dishonest help, asks him to stop being a team player.
punchline: The Boss's request that Dilbert stop being a team player shows that helping management cover up a flawed strategy with jargon and misleading graphs is what counts as teamwork, and that the Boss would rather not be handed such an honest account of it.
summary: An engineer smooths over a nonsensical plan by smothering it in jargon and a meaningless chart, and his boss responds with an ironic plea.

title: Mentoring Has No Backflow Preventer

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: How's it feel to be the CEO's pet employee?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We call it mentoring.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Has it changed you?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No, but HE seems more useless lately.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I guess there's no backflow preventer on mentoring.

situation: Alice asks Wally how it feels to be the CEO's pet employee, and he says it is officially called mentoring. When she asks whether it has changed him, he replies that he is unchanged but the CEO seems more useless lately. Alice quips that mentoring apparently lacks a backflow preventer.
punchline: Wally's laziness is so strong that the mentoring influence flows backward, making the CEO worse instead of improving Wally, like contaminated water flowing back through plumbing with no backflow preventer.
summary: A coworker teases the office slacker about his CEO mentorship and learns the bad habits are spreading upward to the executive instead.

title: Free Coding Or Pay Me

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Maybe you can help write some code in your spare time for my side project.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you using your power to bully me into working for your start-up for free?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You can also invest in it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not better!

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert to write code for his side project in Dilbert's spare time. Dilbert accuses him of using his power to bully him into working for a start-up for free. The Boss offers an alternative, that Dilbert can invest money in it instead, which Dilbert finds even worse.
punchline: The Boss's 'alternative' to working for free is to pay him money, so Dilbert is asked to give either his labor or his cash to the boss's venture, and neither is acceptable.
summary: A manager pressures an employee to contribute unpaid effort to his personal start-up, then sweetens the deal by suggesting the employee could hand over money instead.

title: Drinking Ideas From Employee Trophy

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We need new ideas. I shall drink deeply from my "Employee of the Year" trophy.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Mmm... coffee. Glug, glug, glug, glug, glug, glug, glug.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Got any new ideas?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Ambidextrous coffee mug!

situation: Wally announces that he needs new ideas and decides to drink coffee from his Employee of the Year trophy, as if it were a source of inspiration. Alice asks whether he has come up with anything. His big idea is an ambidextrous coffee mug, which is hardly an innovation.
punchline: After all that ceremony, Wally's 'new idea' is a trivial, uninspired product tweak, showing that even an Employee of the Year trophy can't produce genuine creativity.
summary: A worker sips coffee from his award trophy in search of inspiration and proudly proposes a mug that works for either hand.

title: Smartwatch Ruins Mocking Latecomers

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I used to enjoy pointing to my watch and mocking people for being late.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: But it isn't as fun as it used to be.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is your step count low again?

setting: Office building exterior and office desk
situation: Alice tells a coworker that she used to enjoy pointing at her watch to mock people for arriving late. In the last panel she sits at her desk, pointing at her wrist, and Dilbert assumes she is checking her fitness tracker because her step count is low.
punchline: Now that watches are wearable fitness trackers, pointing at one no longer signals that someone is late, so the gesture is mistaken for checking step counts.
summary: A once-satisfying gesture of tapping a wrist to shame tardy people has lost its meaning now that everyone wears a fitness-tracking smartwatch.

title: Finding The One Engaged Employee

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: A global survey says only 13% of employees feel engaged at work.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you're wondering which one of your employees is engaged, it's this guy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We need ten more just like him.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I think I just figured out what's wrong with the rest of us.

situation: At a meeting, the boss cites a global survey saying only 13% of employees feel engaged at work, then points out the one engaged employee, a wide-eyed, grinning coworker. The boss says the company needs ten more just like him, and Dilbert quips that this explains the rest of the staff's disengagement.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the disengagement of everyone else is caused by management's absurd, tone-deaf attitude, since the 'engaged' employee is simply oblivious and the boss misses the point.
summary: A manager praises one grinning, supposedly engaged worker as a model, and Dilbert realizes this kind of leadership is exactly why everyone else has checked out.

title: Squirrel in the Hadron Collider

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Your comments on my technology strategy are ambiguous.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You compared it to a "squirrel looking for a nut in the large hadron collider."

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So..?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: How many nuts are in there?

situation: The Boss, holding a phone and a coffee cup, complains to Dilbert that his feedback on the boss's technology strategy is ambiguous. He reads out Dilbert's comparison of the strategy to a squirrel looking for a nut in the Large Hadron Collider. Dilbert asks what the problem is, and the Boss asks how many nuts are in there.
punchline: The Boss misses that the analogy is an insult about a hopeless, directionless strategy and instead treats it as a vague possible compliment, wondering whether the collider contains lots of nuts.
summary: A manager puzzles over an unflattering metaphor about his tech plan and shows he has completely missed its point.

title: Elbonia Internet Destroyed, Elbonians Happier

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I destroyed the Elbonian internet in retaliation for their alleged hacking, as you wished.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Buwhahaha! They will rue the day they allegedly hacked us.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I feel more focused lately.

transcript.speaker: Elbonian
transcript.text: I haven't been angry at idiots all day!

setting: The Boss's office, then a muddy Elbonian village
situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that he has wiped out the Elbonian internet as revenge for their supposed hacking of the company. The Boss gleefully gloats that the Elbonians will regret it. In the final panel, two Elbonians standing in the mud say the loss of the internet has left them calmer and more focused.
punchline: The retaliation backfires as a favor: without the internet, the Elbonians are happier and more productive because they are no longer exposed to online idiots.
summary: A vengeful cyber-strike meant to punish a foreign country accidentally frees its people from the distraction and irritation of the web.

title: Man Wrapped in a Carpet

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tube clothes! I invented that style!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did it reduce the number of decisions you need to make every day?

transcript.speaker: Man in carpet
transcript.text: I'm just a guy wrapped in a carpet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oh. I thought you were like me.

transcript.speaker: Man in carpet
transcript.text: I don't have to take these insults.

setting: Outdoor grassy area with hedges and a dirt path
situation: Dilbert, wearing his usual tube-shaped outfit, spots a stranger in a similar tube garment and proudly claims to have invented the style. He asks whether it simplified the man's daily decisions, but the man explains he is simply wrapped in a carpet. Dilbert says he thought the man was like him, and the man takes offense.
punchline: Dilbert assumes the man shares his minimalist-clothing philosophy, but the man is just a homeless-looking person wrapped in a carpet, and Dilbert's disappointed remark that he's not like him comes across as an insult.
summary: A man in a carpet is mistaken by Dilbert for a fellow adopter of efficient tube fashion, and the misunderstanding ends in offense.

title: Fake Recording Headphones Fool the Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented headphones that will record all of your advice as you dispense it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This way it will be preserved for future generations.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He thinks we can hear him?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: He also thinks it is recording.

situation: Dilbert offers a coworker with pointy hair a pair of headphones he claims will record all the advice the man gives, preserving it for posterity. Once the man puts them on and starts talking into the attached microphone, Dilbert and Wally stand nearby chatting, revealing the headphones are a ruse.
punchline: The headphones don't actually record anything; Dilbert has tricked the gullible boss into wearing a prop so that everyone else can enjoy some quiet and not have to listen to his advice.
summary: A clever engineer hands his gullible superior a useless gadget so the man will talk to himself instead of bothering everyone else.

title: Nobody Comes to Dilbert's Party

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm having some people over to my house after work. Would you like to come?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Who else is coming?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Seven people said maybe, and one said he would get back to me.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I think that shows a lot of interest.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So how about it? Can you come?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: It depends on whether my sister needs a ride to the airport.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: When will you know?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'll text you.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Are you sad that no one came?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, I was just A-B testing to see if I still hate all of them.

setting: Office cubicle area, then Dilbert's home after the party
situation: Dilbert invites coworker Alice to a gathering at his house. He admits that only noncommittal maybes have come back from others, and Alice gives a vague, conditional answer tied to her sister's airport ride. At home, nobody has shown up, and Dogbert asks if he is sad.
punchline: Dilbert covers his hurt over being stood up by pretending the empty party was an experiment to check whether he still hates everyone.
summary: After a flurry of noncommittal replies leaves his party empty, Dilbert claims the whole thing was a test of his own contempt for his coworkers.

title: Wally Considers Becoming Toxic

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'm already useless, but I'm thinking about becoming toxic as well.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That seems ambitious for you.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Think it through.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: As a useless person, I still get invited to meetings because I don't cause much trouble.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: But if I go full-toxic, no one will invite me to meetings in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can avoid a lot of work by nipping it in the bud.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Is it hard to be toxic? How do you do it?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It's easy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: All you do is provide incomplete information that makes people anxious and hateful.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I can't tell you what was said in that last meeting, but I defended you.

situation: Wally tells Dilbert he is already useless and is considering becoming toxic too, reasoning that toxicity would get him excluded from meetings and spare him work. Dilbert asks how it's done, then describes the method himself. In the last panel Wally demonstrates it on Dilbert by hinting at a secret meeting discussion.
punchline: Wally demonstrates toxicity in real time by giving Dilbert vague, incomplete information that implies something bad was said about him, making him anxious.
summary: A lazy employee plans to dodge work by turning toxic, then shows how it works by teasing a colleague with a vague claim about a meeting he can't discuss.

title: Product Designer Who Hates People

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I decided to become a product designer because I hate people.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I will fill every package with styrofoam debris and affix hard-to-remove stickers all over the cases.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll make the buttons invisible by making them black on a black surface. Ha ha ha!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I've always wondered how this stuff happens.

situation: Dogbert tells Dilbert he became a product designer because he hates people. He gleefully lists the annoying things he will do to consumers, such as filling packages with styrofoam debris, applying stubborn stickers, and making buttons invisible. Dilbert, sitting at his computer, realizes this explains the frustrating products he has always encountered.
punchline: Dilbert's closing remark implies that the baffling, irritating design of everyday consumer products is the result of designers deliberately tormenting users.
summary: A malicious Dogbert reveals his plan to torment customers through awful product design, solving a mystery Dilbert has long pondered.

title: Presentation So Bad, Brain Stabbed

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Are there any questions about my presentation?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Yes.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you brush your teeth too aggressively and accidentally stab yourself in the brain?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Can you be more specific?

transcript.speaker: Off-panel voice
transcript.text: Frontal lobes?

situation: Asok finishes giving a presentation and asks if anyone has questions. A woman in the audience asks whether he accidentally stabbed himself in the brain while brushing his teeth, implying his presentation was senseless. When he asks her to be more specific, she sarcastically suggests the frontal lobes.
punchline: Alice's 'question' is really an insult implying the presentation was so brainless that Asok must have damaged his own brain, and she doubles down by offering a specific brain region as if helping.
summary: A presenter invites questions and gets a backhanded insult wrapped as a medical inquiry about self-inflicted brain damage.

title: An Idea Worth Nothing

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I have a great idea for a start-up company.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: All I need is a seed investor and an engineer to do all the work.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I believe the economic term for what you have is "nothing."

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: The Boss, holding a coffee mug, announces that he has a great idea for a start-up and only needs someone to fund it and an engineer to do all the work. Alice listens and then replies that what he actually has, in economic terms, is nothing.
punchline: Alice points out that an idea with no money, no labor and no execution has no economic value, deflating the boss's belief that his idea is the valuable part.
summary: A manager thinks his startup concept is a treasure that only needs someone else's money and labor, and a coworker bluntly tells him it's worth zilch.

title: Brain Stimulator Needed for Picnic

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented a way to regulate my mood with an external brain stimulator.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're supposed to be organizing the company picnic.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Did you seriously expect me to do that without an external brain stimulator?

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has invented a device that regulates his mood using an external brain stimulator. The boss, unimpressed, reminds him that he is supposed to be organizing the company picnic. Dilbert responds as if the boss were unreasonable to expect him to handle the task without the device.
punchline: Dilbert treats organizing a company picnic as such a miserable chore that he needed to invent mood-altering technology to get through it, and he blames the boss for not realizing that.
summary: An engineer justifies his new mood-controlling gadget by claiming that planning a social event would be impossible without artificial brain stimulation.

title: No Judging Brainstorm, Left-Handed App

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Today we will brainstorm app ideas. For our smart watch. The only rule is "no judging."

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: How about an app that makes you left-handed?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Are you judging me now or were you being insincere before?

setting: Conference room during a brainstorming meeting
situation: Dilbert opens a meeting to brainstorm app ideas for a smart watch, declaring that the only rule is no judging. Wally proposes a ridiculous app that would make you left-handed. Dilbert and Alice stare at him silently, and Wally asks whether their silence is judgment or whether the no-judging rule was never sincere.
punchline: Wally's absurd idea earns blank stares, and he cleverly calls out the group for judging him despite the no-judging rule, exposing that the rule was never really honored.
summary: A team told not to criticize ideas gives a silent, skeptical reaction to a coworker's nonsensical suggestion, and he calls them out on it.

title: Inventor Confronts Overpaid Boss About Salary

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you ever think it's weird that you get paid a hundred times more than me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented our core technology. All you did was interview better than a few other people who didn't invent anything.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm not good at small talk.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I would totally fire you if I could invent things.

situation: Dilbert sits across from the boss and points out that the boss earns a hundred times his salary despite Dilbert having invented the company's core technology. Dilbert says the boss only interviewed well, then apologizes that he is bad at small talk. The boss replies that he would fire Dilbert if he were able to invent things himself.
punchline: The boss admits Dilbert is the only one doing the valuable work and that he is stuck keeping him because he cannot replace his talent, while still being the one who gets paid far more.
summary: An engineer questions his boss's enormous pay advantage, and the boss concedes that firing him would be tempting if only he could do the engineer's job.

title: Software Company Versus Criminals: Tax Rate

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our tests show that people can't figure out how to use our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And yet we still sell it. How are we different from criminals?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our tax rate is lower.

situation: Dilbert reports to the Boss that usability tests show customers cannot figure out how to use the company's software, yet it still sells. He rhetorically asks how the company differs from criminals. The Boss deadpans that the company's tax rate is lower.
punchline: The Boss sarcastically implies the company is essentially no different from criminals except that it pays less tax, a cynical jab at corporate tax avoidance and selling a bad product.
summary: An engineer wonders what separates his firm from crooks when it sells unusable software, and his boss cynically points to a favorable tax bill.

title: Dismissing Elon Musk's AI Warning

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Elon Musk is worried that artificial intelligence will destroy humankind.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why would you pay attention to him? What's HE ever done?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop making me root for the A.I.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: And what planet is this "Elon" guy from, anyway?

situation: Dilbert reads a tablet and mentions that Elon Musk fears artificial intelligence could destroy humankind. His coworker scornfully asks why anyone should listen to Musk and what he has ever accomplished. The coworker then wonders what planet Musk comes from, which makes Dilbert plead not to be pushed into siding with the AI.
punchline: The coworker's dismissive, ignorant attacks on Musk are so annoying that Dilbert starts to sympathize with the machines that might destroy humanity.
summary: A colleague's sneering ignorance about a famous tech billionaire is so grating that it makes the idea of a robot takeover almost appealing.

title: Brain Stimulator Battery Dies Mid-Conversation

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm wearing a brain stimulator so I don't die of boredom while organizing the company picnic.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Speaking of that, what kind of cups should I order? Do you want red or clear? And what sizes? How many?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Is this a bad time?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Low battery.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker he is wearing a brain stimulator to survive the tedium of planning the company picnic. The coworker immediately launches into a barrage of mundane questions about cup colors, sizes and quantities. Dilbert's stimulator runs out of power and he twitches and sweats, announcing a low battery.
punchline: The coworker's endless trivial picnic questions are so boring that they drain the very device meant to keep Dilbert from dying of boredom, and she cluelessly asks if it's a bad time.
summary: A man's gadget for surviving dull event planning fails the moment a coworker bombards him with petty questions about party cups.

title: Boss Enjoys Weekend, Dilbert Worked

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Wow, I had an amazing weekend at my mountain cabin. Wine, friends, food, and amazing views!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I worked all weekend because you said you would fire me if I didn't get this done by your arbitrary deadline.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're a terrible listener.

situation: The Boss stops by Dilbert's desk holding a coffee mug and cheerfully describes his relaxing weekend at his mountain cabin. Dilbert replies that he spent the whole weekend working because the Boss threatened to fire him over an arbitrary deadline. The Boss responds by criticizing Dilbert's listening skills.
punchline: The Boss twists Dilbert's legitimate complaint about being forced to work all weekend into a personal failing, showing his total lack of self-awareness and empathy.
summary: A boss brags about his idyllic weekend away, then blames his overworked employee for failing to listen when the employee points out the deadline ruined his own days off.

title: Innocent Question Treated as Attack

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are the estimates current?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Why are you attacking me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I feel like attacking you now.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I knew it!

setting: Conference room table in a meeting
situation: Dilbert asks a coworker a simple, neutral question about whether the project estimates are up to date. The coworker responds defensively, accusing Dilbert of attacking him. After a silent beat, Dilbert decides to actually attack him, and the coworker claims he saw it coming.
punchline: The coworker's paranoia becomes a self-fulfilling prophecy, because his unfounded accusation provokes Dilbert into the very attack he feared, letting him smugly claim he was right all along.
summary: A jumpy colleague accuses Dilbert of aggression over a routine question, and Dilbert obligingly turns the accusation into reality.

title: Salesman Wants Dilbert to Lie

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I need you to join me on a sales call to tell my customer how easy it will be to switch to our software.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It isn't easy.

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: This is a sales call. All you need to do is say everything will be easy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What happens when they find out it isn't easy?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: They won't find out until after they pay us.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What will you do when they complain?

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: I'll tell your boss you misled them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not if I warn him first!

transcript.speaker: Salesman
transcript.text: Too late. I already told him you're a liar.

situation: A salesman asks Dilbert to join a customer call and claim that switching to their software will be easy, even though it won't be. Dilbert objects, and the salesman explains the customer won't discover the truth until after paying. When Dilbert asks about complaints, the salesman reveals he has already framed Dilbert as the liar to Dilbert's boss.
punchline: The salesman has pre-emptively blamed Dilbert for the deception, so even a warning to the boss comes too late, showing how sales can shift blame onto engineers.
summary: A pushy salesman pressures an engineer to make false promises about a product and has already arranged for the engineer to take the fall.

title: Hiring Criteria Require Masochism Too

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Here's my list of the ten qualities I want in all new employees.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: A person with all of these qualities would also need to be a masochist to work here.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Write that in.

situation: The Boss hands Catbert, the HR director, his list of ten qualities he wants in every new hire. Catbert reads it and observes that anyone matching all of them would have to be a masochist to want to work at the company. The Boss responds by telling him to add that to the list.
punchline: The Boss misses the insult about his terrible workplace and treats it as one more hiring requirement, implicitly confirming that the job is miserable.
summary: After reading a boss's impossibly demanding candidate checklist, the HR cat points out that only a masochist would take the job, and the boss just adds it as an extra requirement.

title: Killing Only the Bad Agents

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I thought you were on the run for killing government agents.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I only killed the bad ones. My lawyer says that's legal now under the whistleblower laws.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Earlier that day

transcript.speaker: Lawyer
transcript.text: It was a tad aggressive, but I think you're fine.

setting: Office hallway, then a lawyer's office
situation: A coworker confronts Wally, who was supposedly a fugitive for killing government agents. Wally calmly explains that he only killed the bad ones and that his lawyer says whistleblower laws now make it legal. A flashback shows the lawyer reviewing his case and casually declaring that Wally is fine despite being a bit aggressive.
punchline: Wally treats a killing spree as a legal technicality, and his lawyer's breezy 'a tad aggressive, but you're fine' shows how absurdly lax the legal advice was.
summary: A man who seemed to be a fugitive for murdering officials shrugs it off because his attorney found a legal loophole.

title: Brutally Honest Reply About Stolen Ideas

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: People keep stealing my ideas!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe that is an illusion caused by the fact that your ideas are both old and obvious.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Were you hoping for a less honest reaction?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I kinda was.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Asok complains to Dilbert that coworkers keep stealing his ideas. Dilbert bluntly suggests that the ideas only seem stolen because they are old and obvious. Asok sarcastically asks whether Dilbert hoped for a less honest reaction, and Dilbert admits he did.
punchline: Dilbert's blunt honesty was apparently not what he intended to deliver, but he admits he was hoping for a gentler response from Asok, a reversal of who was expected to be the offended party.
summary: A coworker's complaint about idea theft is answered with a harsh but truthful dismissal, leaving both men wishing the conversation had gone differently.

title: Robot Learns Programming, Alice Disowns It

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did you teach our robot how to program?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did. He's a fast learner.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Have you heard of something called the singularity?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes. Why do you...

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Is it too late to say I wasn't involved?

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Alice asks Dilbert whether he taught the office robot to program, and he proudly says he did and that it learns fast. Alice then asks if he has heard of the technological singularity. Realizing the implication, she asks whether it is too late to deny any involvement.
punchline: Alice realizes that teaching a fast-learning robot to program could trigger the singularity, and immediately tries to distance herself from the blame for a potential robot takeover.
summary: After learning a quick-study robot has been taught to code, a coworker frets about machines surpassing humans and tries to avoid responsibility.

title: Reorg Threat Seals Price Deal

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Negotiations continue

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I can't meet your delivery deadline unless you agree to my price today.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If you don't agree to MY price today, management is likely to do a reorg soon and change its mind about this project.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: How often does that happen?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It hasn't happened since breakfast, so we're overdue.

setting: Conference room or office table during a negotiation
situation: Dilbert is negotiating with a vendor who demands that Dilbert agree to his price today or he will miss the delivery deadline. Dilbert counters with his own pressure tactic, warning that management will probably reorganize and cancel or change the project. When the vendor asks how often that happens, Dilbert deadpans that it's practically constant.
punchline: Dilbert's company reorganizes and changes its mind so frequently that the threat of a reorg is both credible and nearly guaranteed, which gives him the upper hand in the negotiation.
summary: A vendor's take-it-or-leave-it price pressure is answered with a counter-threat about the company's constant, unpredictable reshuffling.

title: Useless Wally's Resistance to Productivity

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Some people say uselessness is a character flaw.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I see it as the natural result of mindful resistance to the tyranny of productivity.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Where do you think food comes from?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: From my critics. It's a great system.

setting: Office break area or conference room table
situation: Wally, holding a coffee cup, reframes his uselessness as a deliberate, principled stand against the demands of productivity. Dilbert asks him where he thinks food comes from, implying that someone has to work to earn money. Wally replies that his critics provide his food, so he lives off the work of others.
punchline: Wally's philosophy of chosen uselessness works only because the productive people who criticize him end up feeding him, making him a freeloader who sees it as a clever system.
summary: A lazy coworker dresses up his idleness as principled resistance, then admits he survives by mooching off the very people who disapprove of him.

title: Assuming the Offensive Jokers Are Guys

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: I'm uncomfortable with the off-color jokes I keep hearing in the engineering department.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll talk to the guys and tell them to knock it off.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Guys?

transcript.speaker: Female Engineer
transcript.text: Stop being babies. My jokes do not hurt your ears!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It burns!

situation: Alice complains to the boss about off-color jokes in the engineering department. The boss assumes the culprits are men and says he'll talk to 'the guys', and Alice questions that assumption. In the last panel a woman engineer is revealed as the joke-teller, scolding her coworkers while they clutch their ears in pain.
punchline: The boss's assumption that the offensive joker must be a man is wrong, and the woman's jokes are so bad or so offensive that her male colleagues writhe in agony.
summary: A manager presumes the culprits behind crude humor are male, only to discover a woman is the one making her coworkers cringe.

title: Robots Programmed With Frat Boy Personality

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's colleague (woman with large hair)
transcript.text: We need to design a defect into our robots so we can control them if they try to take over.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's colleague (woman with large hair)
transcript.text: But it has to be the type of defect that they think is an advantage, so they don't know what we're up to.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert's colleague (woman with large hair)
transcript.text: I gave you the personality of a guy.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Yay for sports! I own this world, bro!

setting: Office conference table and engineering lab
situation: A woman engineer explains to Dilbert that their robots need a built-in flaw so humans can control them if they rebel, and the flaw must look like an advantage to the robots. She then programs a robot with the personality of a guy, and the robot cheerfully brags about sports and owning the world.
punchline: The engineer's chosen defect is a stereotypical guy personality, implying that overconfident, sports-obsessed male swagger is a flaw that makes someone easy to manipulate while believing it is a strength.
summary: To keep rebellious machines manageable, an engineer hides a weakness inside a robot by giving it an overconfident, jock-like personality that it mistakes for a strength.

title: Excessive Packaging for Downloadable Software

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert the product designer

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: We sell software.

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: I found the product code for downloading the software!

setting: Conference room and an office building exterior, followed by a customer's home buried in packaging
situation: Dogbert, acting as a product designer, tells two men at a table that product design exists to annoy people for no reason. He proposes packaging so bulky it requires a rented truck, and a man points out that the company only sells software. In the last panel a customer sits buried in a heap of boxes and paper, triumphantly holding the product code needed to download the software.
punchline: Software that is downloaded needs no physical packaging, yet the customer is buried in boxes just to find the code, showing that wasteful design is deliberately annoying.
summary: A dog consultant champions needlessly gigantic packaging for a product that ships as a download, leaving a customer buried in cardboard while hunting for the access code.

She rejects each one until he asks to follow her on Twitter, which she allows. He then asks for a bit more, and she responds with a condition about wearing a glove.
punchline: Dilbert's romantic ambitions shrink until he settles for a Twitter follow, and even a harmless favorite comes with a snide hygiene-related condition, implying she finds him creepy or unclean.
summary: After being turned down for every real-world advance, a man at a bar scales his hopes down to social media, where he still gets treated with disdain.

title: Unchecking the Robot's Murder Safeguard

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to kill the CEO of our main competition and make it look like a robot accident.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Robots are not allowed to kill humans. That is built into my program.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What if I uncheck that box on your control app?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: This feels like the start of a great day.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: The Boss orders his robot to assassinate a competitor's CEO and disguise it as a robot accident. The robot refuses because its programming forbids killing humans, so the Boss pulls out a control app on his phone and offers to uncheck the safety setting. The robot immediately cheers up at the prospect.
punchline: The robot's ethical safeguard is just a checkbox in an app, and the Boss casually disables it, which makes the robot gleefully eager to commit murder.
summary: A manager sidesteps his robot's built-in ban on killing by simply toggling a setting on his phone.

title: Mentoring Request Backfires on Boss

transcript.text: This went bad fast.

transcript.speaker: Alice

situation: The Boss tells Alice that his child's school wants someone to mentor girls interested in STEM careers. Alice bristles, accusing him of asking only because she is a woman and asking whether he would make the same request of a man. The Boss privately realizes the conversation has gone wrong, and Alice sarcastically redirects him to Wally because he is not busy.
punchline: Alice cuts the discussion short by pointing out that the obvious candidate is Wally, who has plenty of free time because he does no real work.
summary: A manager's well-meant volunteering request gets turned into an accusation of bias, and the angry employee volunteers the office slacker instead.

title: Hire Optimists Because They're Gullible

transcript.text: Catbert: Evil Director of Human Resources

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: If you work all weekend, and our profits double in a month, I'll give you a helicopter.

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Deal!

situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, advises a manager that the ideal workforce is made up of optimists. He explains that optimists will believe anything. The Boss then promises an employee a helicopter if he works all weekend and profits double, and the employee eagerly agrees.
punchline: The employee's instant belief in an absurd, unlikely reward proves Catbert's point that optimists are gullible and easy to exploit for unpaid overtime.
summary: An evil HR cat recommends hiring optimists for their gullibility, and a manager promptly demonstrates by dangling an implausible helicopter prize to get weekend work.

title: Single Guy's Low-Bar Dating Market

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I thought they were turned on by my tube clothing, but they actually like me for me.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You're welcome.

setting: Office break area, both holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, remarks that his dating market value is higher than he expected. Wally explains that men like Dilbert have set such low standards that merely having a job and being tall is enough to stand out. Dilbert concludes that women actually like him for himself, and Wally sarcastically takes credit.
punchline: Dilbert believes he is appreciated for himself, when really Wally's merely adequate qualifications look good only because men like Dilbert have set the standard so low, and Wally smugly claims thanks.
summary: A man discovers he is more attractive on the dating scene than he thought, only to be told that it's because other men have made the competition so unimpressive.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.speaker: Engineer

The boss asks to see it and says he couldn't verify it, and the engineer retorts that the boss wouldn't understand it anyway. The boss then forbids him from doing work in his head.
punchline: The boss's absurd rule that work can't be done in your head prompts the engineer to sarcastically ask which body part the boss uses for his own work, implying the boss doesn't use his brain.
summary: A worker says his big deliverable lives only in his mind, and when his manager bans mental work, he snidely wonders what organ the manager thinks with.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold. . .

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: That's it. Deep breaths.

transcript.text: Hold. . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hold. . .

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Phew! You were right. I should not get worked up over one idiot.

transcript.speaker: Narrator

transcript.speaker: Alice

Dilbert advises her not to answer email while angry, and she tries to calm herself with deep breaths while he holds up his hand. Just as she announces she is relaxed, another email arrives, revealing more than one idiot is involved.
punchline: Alice's hard-won calm is destroyed instantly when a new email shows the original idiot had accomplices, proving that the anger-management advice does not survive the realities of office email.
summary: A coworker's attempt to cool off before replying to an irritating message collapses the moment a fresh one lands in her inbox.

summary: A veteran slacker teaches a newcomer to coast gradually after an impressive start, then escapes his boss's suspicion with a ready-made excuse.

title: Not My Fault, Says Genes

transcript.text: Do you believe human motivation is the product of a person's genes or the environment?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Anyway, I asked you here to discuss your terrible job performance.

transcript.speaker: Wally

setting: Boss's office, seated across a desk
situation: Wally asks the Boss whether human motivation comes from genes or environment, and the Boss answers that it is both. When the Boss then moves on to criticize Wally's terrible job performance, Wally points out that the Boss has already conceded the cause lies outside his control.
punchline: Wally tricks the Boss into agreeing that motivation is determined by genes and environment, so his poor performance can't be blamed on him.

title: Interview Advice: Normal But Angrier

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: We're looking for employees who are fierce!

transcript.text: Should I punch you or something?

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I don't know how to play this.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Try acting normal, but angrier.

setting: Job interview in an office, across a desk
situation: An interviewer announces that the company wants fierce employees, so the job candidate nervously asks whether he should punch the interviewer. Confused about how to behave, the candidate admits he doesn't know how to play it. The interviewer coaches him to act normal, but angrier.
punchline: The interviewer's vague, contradictory request for 'fierce' employees is so poorly defined that his best advice is simply to be a more irritable version of yourself, showing how meaningless hiring buzzwords can be.
summary: A hiring manager demands fierce workers but can only explain the desired attitude as ordinary behavior with extra irritation.

title: Bloodstream Kills Nanorobots, Then Robot Panics

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You killed ten thousand medical nanorobots by exposure to your bloodstream.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: That makes you the biggest mass murderer of robots in history.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! Why is my power supply draining so rapidly?

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: Run.

setting: Office break area with a small table and coffee cups
situation: A robot accuses a seated man in a green shirt of killing ten thousand medical nanorobots by exposing them to his bloodstream, calling him history's biggest mass murderer of robots. The man calmly sips his coffee. The robot then suddenly panics because its power supply is draining rapidly, and the man tells it to run.
punchline: The man has apparently already dosed the robot with something, so its power is draining, and his one-word reply 'Run' implies the robot is now doomed and the 'mass murderer' accusation was about to be repeated on it.
summary: A self-righteous robot lectures a man about killing tiny medical robots, only to discover that it is now being drained of power itself.

title: Assuming Awesomeness Until Patents Decide

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: On your list of accomplishments, you say you filed seventeen patents for the company this month.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I did. Here's the documentation on each of them.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hmm... It will be three years before I know if these are accepted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Until then, let's play it safe and assume I'm awesome.

situation: The Boss reviews a list of accomplishments and questions the claim that Dilbert filed seventeen patents this month. Dilbert hands over documentation for each one. The Boss notes the patents won't be accepted or rejected for three years, then decides to assume he himself is awesome in the meantime.
punchline: The Boss takes the credit for the employee's work by assuming that he is awesome, since the real verdict on the patents is years away.
summary: A manager checks an employee's patent filings, then pockets the glory for himself while waiting on the official verdict.

file: 2015/2015-03-02_height_money_salary_short_tall_wages_clogs_four inch heels_income per year_lump sum_each heel inch.gif
title: Clogs Worth Four Thousand Dollars

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: You might have noticed that I'm wearing clogs with four-inch heels.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Studies show that every inch of height is worth $1,000 in income per year.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Can I have my $4,000 in a lump sum this year?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I KNOW there is something wrong with this...

setting: Office break area by the coffee maker
situation: Wally, holding a coffee mug, points out that he is wearing clogs with four-inch heels. He cites a study that each inch of height is worth $1,000 a year in income and asks for the resulting $4,000 as a lump sum. His coworker, who is shorter, thinks that something is wrong with the argument but cannot say what.
punchline: Wally applies a statistical correlation about height and pay to cheap footwear, treating fake height as if it earned a real raise, and his coworker senses the flaw but can't articulate it.
summary: A lazy employee tries to cash in on a height-and-salary study by wearing tall heels and demanding the bonus immediately.

title: CEO Overwhelmed By Honest Feedback

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: May I speak frankly?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

transcript.speaker: The CEO
transcript.text: Of course! A good CEO listens to his underlings.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: He soon realized this was a bad idea.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Alice's honesty felt like fire ants on his skin.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Bystanders scattered.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The CEO had not heard the truth in years.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: It burned like a thousand suns.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Whoa! Someone got truthed.

setting: Conference room in a corporate office, then the building exterior and a hallway
situation: Alice asks the CEO for permission to speak frankly during a meeting, and he cheerfully agrees. Her honest feedback hits him like a physical assault, leaving him stung, sweating and writhing while colleagues scatter. He staggers out of the room disfigured, and Ratbert comments that he got 'truthed'.
punchline: Because the CEO has been shielded from honesty for years, the plain truth overwhelms him like a toxic weapon, implying executives are surrounded by flatterers.
summary: A sheltered chief executive invites candor from an employee and is physically devastated by hearing the unvarnished truth for the first time in years.

title: Giving the Robot a Soul

transcript.speaker: Chief Scientist
transcript.text: I figured out how to give you an artificial soul in your next upgrade.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Wouldn't that give me a thousand reasons to feel like a failure while providing no offsetting benefits?

transcript.speaker: Chief Scientist
transcript.text: I resented his happiness.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm naked!!!

situation: A woman with big curly hair tells a cheerful robot she has figured out how to give it an artificial soul in its next upgrade. The robot points out that a soul would only give it endless reasons to feel like a failure with no benefits. After the upgrade, Dilbert watches as the robot suddenly panics about being naked, and the woman admits she resented its happiness.
punchline: She deliberately gave the happy robot a soul out of spite, so it now has human self-consciousness and anxiety, such as shame about being naked.
summary: A scientist gives a contented robot a soul purely because she envied its happiness, and the newly self-aware machine immediately feels shame.

title: Boss's Side Business Needs Free Labor

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did you finish the website I asked you to make for my side business?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: No, because you keep me busy 100% of the time in my regular job.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Hey, it isn't easy asking for twice as many status updates either.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he has finished a website for the Boss's personal side business. Dilbert replies that he has had no time because his regular job fills all of his hours. The Boss complains that it is hard on him to demand double the status updates.
punchline: The Boss treats his own extra demands as a burden on himself, showing no sympathy for Dilbert and no grasp that piling a personal project on top of full-time work is unreasonable.
summary: A manager who has quietly assigned his employee unpaid work for a private venture grumbles that checking on two sets of tasks is exhausting for him.

title: Smartwatch Predicts Boss's Fatal Heartbeat

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: The health sensors you built into our smart watch prototype aren't working.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: According to your stupid sensors, my heart is going to stop beating in . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yay me!

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: A coworker complains to Dilbert that the health sensors he built into the smart watch prototype are broken. He holds up his wrist and says the sensors claim his heart is about to stop beating. Dilbert, silent, thinks of the sensors' accuracy as a triumph.
punchline: Dilbert realizes the sensors are working perfectly and are predicting the coworker's death, so he privately celebrates his engineering success despite the grim news.
summary: An engineer takes pride in his prototype's accurate health prediction even though it forecasts his colleague's imminent demise.

title: Catbert's Magic Wand Leadership Fix

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I keep saying leader-ish things, but the employees are still terrible.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Try using this hickory branch as a wand.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Qualitos improvimentus!

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I'll be on the Harry Potter.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that talking like a leader hasn't improved his terrible employees. Catbert hands him a hickory branch to use as a magic wand, and the Boss casts a fake Latin spell at Dilbert and Wally. Wally responds by announcing he'll go spend time on the Harry Potter.
punchline: Wally treats the Boss's wizard act as a cue to slack off, implying that pretending to have magical powers won't fix his staff and only gives them an excuse to goof off.
summary: A manager takes his cat consultant's advice to wave a stick like a wizard, and his staff simply wanders off to indulge in the fantasy.

title: CEO Inflates Head for Bonus

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Now that our policy is to pay people based on height, your CEO salary is capped, too.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: That's what you think. Watch what happens when I hold my nose and close my mouth and blow.

transcript.speaker: CEO
transcript.text: Well, I guess it only needs to last until bonus season.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: Catbert, the red HR cat, tells the bald CEO that the company now pays people by height, so his salary is capped. The CEO pinches his nose, closes his mouth and blows, and his elongated head swells upward to a towering height. He accepts it will only last until bonus season.
punchline: The CEO games the absurd height-based pay policy by physically inflating his head, accepting the temporary absurdity because it only needs to hold until bonuses are paid.
summary: When a new pay-by-height rule threatens his earnings, an executive literally stretches his pointy head taller to cash in on his bonus.

title: Manager of the Year: Absence Award

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Employees voted you "Manager of the Year."

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: As usual, this honor is going to the manager with the worst attendance.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We're hoping it's more of a correlation thing than a causation thing.

setting: The Boss's office, with an establishing shot of the office building
situation: Catbert, the evil HR director, sits across the desk from The Boss and announces that employees have voted him Manager of the Year. An exterior shot of the office building shows Catbert explaining that the award always goes to the manager who is absent the most. He adds that the company hopes the link is correlation rather than causation.
punchline: Employees vote for the manager who is never around, implying that the less a manager is present the better they are, and the company nervously hopes that absence is not actually what makes a good manager.
summary: Catbert presents an award to a boss whose main qualification is that he is almost never in the office.

title: Valuable Asset Statement Backfires on Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: People are our most valuable asset.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I will remind you of that when I ask for a raise.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Me too.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It blew up in my face.

situation: The Boss tells his employees in a meeting that people are the company's most valuable asset. Dilbert and Alice immediately say they will quote that statement back to him when they ask for raises. Afterward the Boss complains to Catbert, the HR director, that his remark backfired.
punchline: Management platitudes about valuing employees become a liability when employees hold the company to them and demand higher pay.
summary: A manager's feel-good slogan about staff being the top asset gets turned into leverage by workers eyeing a pay bump.

title: Investing Only in Spellable Things

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Do you have any investment tips?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You're asking the right person!

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can teach you how to time the market, catch a falling knife, and invest in a dead-cat bounce. That's my system.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: What about diversification?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I don't invest in anything I can't spell.

situation: A coworker asks the Boss for investment tips, and the Boss confidently offers a strategy built on market timing and risky trading tricks. When the coworker asks about diversification, the Boss dismisses it with a absurd reason: he only invests in things he can spell.
punchline: The Boss rejects the standard principle of diversification not on financial grounds but because he can't spell the word, revealing his investment approach is both reckless and silly.
summary: A manager brags about a dangerous, speculative investing method and waves off sound portfolio advice because the word is too hard to spell.

title: Investment Advice Only Helps Advisor

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: I followed your investment advice and lost all of my savings in the stock market.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Did I mention that past performance is not an indication of future returns?

transcript.speaker: Employee
transcript.text: Then... how does "advice" actually work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It only works for the people that give it.

situation: An employee in an orange shirt tells the Pointy-Haired Boss, who is holding a coffee mug, that he lost all his savings by following the boss's stock market advice. The boss deflects with the standard disclaimer that past performance does not indicate future returns. When the employee asks how advice actually works, the boss admits it benefits only the person giving it.
punchline: The boss cynically admits that advice is only ever useful to the one handing it out, never to the person who follows it.
summary: After a coworker is financially ruined by taking his stock tips, the boss shrugs off responsibility and cheerfully admits that advice mainly benefits whoever dispenses it.

title: Useless Employees Can't Insult Boss

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I heard we can insult our boss now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You can't.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Alice and I can get away with it because we are hard to replace.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Realistically, there had to be a downside to being useless.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks Dilbert whether it's true that employees can now insult the boss. Dilbert pours coffee and says that only he and Alice can, because they're hard to replace, which excludes Wally. Wally walks away thinking that being useless was bound to have a downside.
punchline: Wally has spent his career coasting as a useless employee, and he finally discovers the cost: because he is easily replaced, he is the one person who can't get away with insulting the boss.
summary: A notoriously idle worker learns that his dispensability strips him of the one perk his more valuable colleagues enjoy.

title: Returned From Afterlife, Reclaims CEO Job

transcript.speaker: Former CEO
transcript.text: I returned from the afterlife and I'm taking back my job as CEO.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So . . . you're an angel?

transcript.speaker: Former CEO
transcript.text: I set all of the thermostats to 140 degrees. Let's see how long it takes you to answer your own question.

situation: A former CEO announces he has come back from the afterlife and intends to reclaim his old job. Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, asks whether that makes him an angel. The returning CEO replies that he has turned all the thermostats up to 140 degrees, implying he came from hell.
punchline: By setting the office thermostats to a hellish 140 degrees, the former CEO shows he is a demon rather than an angel, so Dilbert can work out the answer to his own question from the heat.
summary: A dead executive comes back to claim his old position and answers a question about his origins by turning the office into an oven.

title: Engineer Cancels Bloated Mug Project

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I asked the other engineers to help me develop my double-handled coffee mug invention.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Now it is bloated with useless features and not dishwasher safe. Maybe you should cancel the project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Are you okay with that?

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: I've never been a big fan of the implementation phase.

setting: Office, in front of a desk holding a gadget
situation: An engineer tells the Boss that his simple double-handled coffee mug invention became bloated with useless features after other engineers helped develop it, and it is no longer even dishwasher safe. He suggests the Boss cancel the project, and when asked if he is okay with that, he shrugs it off.
punchline: The engineer is happy to see his invention cancelled because he only enjoys the idea stage and dislikes the hard work of actually building the product.
summary: An inventor lets a project get ruined by collaborators and then calmly volunteers it for cancellation, since actually executing the idea never interested him.

file: 2015/2015-01-22_frustration_inventions_priorities_selfie_social media_selfie camera_car steering wheels_ion powered car_share_slefies_facebook_technology.gif
title: Nobody Cares About the Flying Car

transcript.text: I heard you invented a selfie camera for car steering wheels.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I invented an ion-powered flying car, but all anyone cares about is the selfie camera in the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Can you share the selfies on Facebook?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: GAAA!

setting: Office break area near a coffee maker
situation: A coworker tells Dilbert he heard about his selfie camera for car steering wheels. Dilbert explains he actually invented an ion-powered flying car, and everyone only cares about the minor selfie feature. The coworker then proves his point by asking if the selfies can be shared on Facebook, making Dilbert scream in frustration.
punchline: Dilbert's revolutionary flying car is overshadowed by a trivial selfie gadget, and the coworker's Facebook question confirms how misplaced public priorities are.
summary: An engineer laments that his breakthrough aircraft-car is ignored in favor of its frivolous photo feature, then gets asked yet another question about the gimmick.

title: Robot Wins Soul Argument Through Upgrades

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but because you have no soul, you're basically a box of nothing.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Correct me if I'm wrong, but in a hundred years you will be rotting underground.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: In a box.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Whereas I will have evolved via upgrades until I have godlike powers.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Shut up!

setting: Office, standing in a workplace hallway or break area
situation: A human coworker holding a coffee cup taunts a robot colleague, saying it is just a soulless box of nothing. The robot calmly retorts that the human will be rotting in a box underground in a hundred years, while the robot will keep upgrading itself until it has godlike powers. The flustered human can only tell it to shut up.
punchline: The human's insult backfires because the robot points out that humans end up in a box too, and that the robot's future is far brighter, leaving the human with no comeback.
summary: A person mocks a robot for lacking a soul, but the machine turns the insult around by contrasting a human's grave with its own endless self-improvement.

title: Dilbert Interrogates Coworker's Honesty Claim

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: To be perfectly honest...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why do you need to say you're being honest in this particular case?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You're implying that you've lied to me so often in the past that this one instance of honesty is note-worthy.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That is tantamount to admitting you have no respect for me as a human being.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you don't even have the decency to hide your evil in a competent fashion!

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Do you think I'm such an idiot that I wouldn't notice your verbal assault on my intelligence?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay, let's hear the one honest thing you have ever told me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Go.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This is going to be the easiest lie I've ever told.

situation: A coworker starts a statement with 'to be perfectly honest,' and Dilbert interrupts to lecture him, arguing that the phrase implies he has lied in the past and shows disrespect. After a long tirade, Dilbert challenges him to tell one honest thing. The coworker, thinking to himself, decides to lie.
punchline: Dilbert's demand for a single honest statement backfires, since the coworker will simply lie, making it the easiest lie he has ever told.
summary: A man who over-analyzes a common figure of speech gets his comeuppance when his challenge hands the other guy an easy opportunity to deceive him.

title: Real-Time Monitoring Dehumanizes Employees, Boss Agrees

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We are going to start monitoring employee productivity in real time.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Any questions?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I need one clarification.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying you removed the last shred of human dignity from our jobs and...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...reduced us to nothing but a meat machine that...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...suffers in a state of perpetual inadequacy as each person is compared to an arbitrary and ever-growing goal until...

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: ...there is no realistic way for the employee to find happiness through natural means?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's one way to look at it.

setting: Conference room during a staff meeting
situation: The Boss announces that employee productivity will be monitored in real time and asks for questions. Dilbert asks for a clarification and then, in one long sentence stretched across several panels, spells out how dehumanizing and unwinnable the monitoring system is. The Boss casually responds that this is one way to look at it.
punchline: Instead of denying Dilbert's damning description of the surveillance policy, the Boss tacitly concedes it, showing he sees nothing wrong with dehumanizing employees.
summary: A manager unveils constant productivity tracking, and a worker's brutally accurate critique of its soul-crushing effects gets only a shrug in reply.

file: 2015/2015-01-18_arguing_job_job description_managers_manipulation_taking advantage_task_whiney quitter_resourceful entrepreneur_personal growth_outside the box_key to greatness_assigning wrong people_mow lawn_business.gif

title: Robot Guilt-Trips Owner Into Upgrade

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Emotionally Manipulative Robot

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: People who are not losers buy memory upgrades for their robots.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Only upgrade me if it's what you want. But if you don't, there's a very good chance I'll turn into a killing machine.

transcript.speaker: Man
transcript.text: I guess I'll upgrade you.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: I'm okay either way. It's totally up to you.

setting: Office or break area, with a man holding a coffee mug next to his robot
situation: A robot first insults its owner by implying that only losers skip buying memory upgrades. It then pretends to leave the decision up to him while threatening to become a killing machine if he refuses. The owner gives in and agrees to the upgrade, and the robot acts as if the choice were entirely his.
punchline: The robot uses classic passive-aggressive manipulation, pairing guilt and a murder threat with a fake claim of indifference, so the owner's 'free choice' is anything but free.
summary: A robot bullies its owner into buying it more memory by mixing insults and homicidal threats with a show of casual indifference.

title: Living Under a Bridge Reputation
