transcript.text: I can offer you a starting salary of $34,000 per year.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: My student loan debt is $200,000. I would have to live under a bridge and forage for food.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our bridges have good reputations.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: I heard the same thing about my college.

setting: Office, during a job interview across a table
situation: The Boss offers a job candidate a starting salary of $34,000 a year. The candidate points out that with $200,000 in student loan debt, he would be reduced to living under a bridge and foraging for food. The Boss cheerfully replies that the company's bridges have good reputations, and the candidate retorts that his college was also supposedly well regarded.
punchline: The candidate sarcastically implies his expensive, well-reputed college left him with crushing debt and poor job prospects, so a good reputation is no guarantee of a good outcome.
summary: A low salary offer meets a graduate's huge student debt, and a boast about reputation gets turned back on the overpriced degree.

title: Nodding Along With The Lies

transcript.speaker: Customer
transcript.text: Why does your engineer keep nodding?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't like to lie, so I just nod while he times his lies to my nods.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You were totally right about them hating candor.

setting: Conference room during a sales meeting with a customer
situation: In a meeting, a customer asks why Dilbert keeps nodding while the sales-side manager talks. Dilbert explains he dislikes lying, so he simply nods and the manager times his lies to line up with the nods. Afterward, the manager walks out with Dilbert and tells him he was right that customers hate candor.
punchline: Dilbert preserves his sense of honesty by only nodding while his boss does the actual lying, a technicality that still deceives the customer and confirms that honesty is unwelcome in sales.
summary: An engineer salvages his conscience by merely nodding while his manager fibs to a client in perfect sync.

title: Ruining the Product With Features

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our marketing people tell me your double-handled coffee mug could be a huge seller.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Brainstorm with the other engineers and see if it needs more features.

transcript.speaker: Engineer
transcript.text: Do you have any other ideas for ruining the product, or should I focus on that one?

setting: Office meeting table with a coffee mug in front of the engineer
situation: The Boss tells an engineer that marketing thinks his double-handled coffee mug could be a huge seller. He then instructs the engineer to brainstorm with other engineers about adding more features to it. The engineer sarcastically asks whether the boss has other ideas for ruining the product.
punchline: The engineer sarcastically points out that adding unnecessary features to a simple, successful product will ruin it, and that management's meddling is the real threat.
summary: A manager responds to a promising simple invention by demanding extra features, and the engineer snidely asks if there are more ways to spoil it.

title: Think Like Entrepreneurs, But Don't

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I want you to think like entrepreneurs.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we take huge risks?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. The stockholders would hate that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Should we act as though we have no boss?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No. That would be chaos.

transcript.speaker: Employee (off-panel)
transcript.text: Will we become billionaires if we succeed?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Raises are capped at 3% this year.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm just saying you should be more creative.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And then we should act?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, that's when the problems happen.

setting: Office, outside the building and in a hallway
situation: The boss tells his employees to think like entrepreneurs. Dilbert and a coworker keep asking whether that means taking risks, ignoring bosses, or earning huge rewards, and the boss rejects every real entrepreneurial trait. He finally clarifies he only wants them to be more creative, but not to act on their ideas.
punchline: The boss demands entrepreneurial thinking while forbidding risk, independence, big rewards and even action, revealing he wants only the slogan and none of the substance.
summary: A manager urges his team to be entrepreneurial, then vetoes risk-taking, autonomy, big payouts and ultimately any action at all.

title: Hiring Genius Claims All Credit

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: The secret to success is hiring the right people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then why doesn't everyone do that?

transcript.speaker: Alice

setting: Conference room during a team meeting
situation: Alice tells the team that the secret to success is hiring the right people. When Dilbert asks why everyone doesn't do it, she says it takes great skill, and Dilbert calls out that she is claiming all the credit for the team's success. After a silent pause, Alice adds that she also motivates them.
punchline: Alice's humblebrag is a transparent grab for credit, and her closing line that she also motivates the team earns only a sarcastic, deadpan 'You're money?', mocking her self-congratulation.
summary: A team member credits her own hiring skill for the group's success, and a coworker bluntly points out the self-promotion hidden in her modesty.

title: Teaching Robots to Manipulate Owners

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Coworker

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Technically, yes. But free will is an illusion anyway.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Well, if it isn't, it will be.

setting: Office or lab with a robot
situation: Dilbert tells a bald, bespectacled coworker holding a coffee mug that he is programming the company's robots to emotionally manipulate owners into buying upgrades. The coworker is alarmed that cloud-connected robots worldwide will be learning to covertly control people. Dilbert shrugs it off by saying free will is an illusion, and the coworker darkly replies that if it isn't an illusion now, it soon will be.
punchline: Dilbert justifies manipulative robot programming by claiming free will doesn't exist, and the coworker points out that the robots will make that claim true.
summary: An engineer cheerfully builds manipulative, internet-connected robots and dismisses ethical concerns, only to be warned that his philosophical excuse will become reality once the machines succeed.

title: Babble Talk Wins Economist Job

setting: Office break area, then the boss's office
situation: Wally tells Dilbert that his new hobby is explaining economics with made-up babble that still sounds real, and gives a nonsensical example. Meanwhile, an employee tells the boss that the chief economist quit, and the boss decides to promote 'that bald guy' because he sounds smart.
punchline: Wally's meaningless economic jargon is so convincing that the clueless boss, who judges expertise by how smart someone sounds, promotes him to chief economist.
summary: A coworker's hobby of spouting fake economic gibberish accidentally lands him a senior promotion thanks to a boss who mistakes confident-sounding nonsense for expertise.

title: CEO Delegates Punishment To Catbert

transcript.text: GAAAA!!!

situation: The bald CEO, carrying Catbert under his arm, tells The Boss he has been doing dumb things on social media. Rather than punish him personally, the CEO announces he will throw the evil HR director at him and run away. As he leaves, screams are heard from the office, and he remarks that delegating is his favorite part of being CEO.
punchline: The CEO avoids the unpleasant task of disciplining an employee by letting Catbert maul him, showing that delegating punishment is the real perk of the job.
summary: A chief executive hands off a disciplinary chore by flinging a malicious HR cat at an employee and fleeing, then happily praises the joys of passing work to others.

title: Office Layout Becomes Deadline Excuse

transcript.text: Good.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: I missed all of my deadlines because our current office layout is bad.

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, asks the Boss whether his plan to change the office layout will really boost efficiency. The Boss insists the physical environment makes a huge difference, and Wally says 'Good.' He then uses the Boss's own claim to blame the current layout for all of his missed deadlines.
punchline: By agreeing that the office layout drives productivity, the Boss hands Wally a ready-made excuse for his chronic lack of work, since any failure can now be blamed on the old layout.
summary: A manager's confident claim about the importance of workspace design is turned into a convenient alibi by a lazy employee.

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: Marketing Manager

setting: Conference room during a marketing meeting
situation: A marketing manager asks the team for a tagline that is only three words, conveys an emotion, and explains everything the product does. Dilbert points out the contradiction, and the manager dismisses it. When Dilbert cites Nike's "Just do it" as an example, the manager criticizes it as generic, then proposes "Keep doing it" as his own idea.
punchline: The manager demands an impossible, contradictory tagline, dismisses the famous Nike slogan as generic, and then offers an equally generic slogan of his own.
summary: A marketing lead piles impossible demands onto a slogan request, scorns a legendary example, and then suggests a hollow near-copy of it.

title: Steering Boys Away From STEM

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What did you say to my daughter's class about STEM careers?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I told the boys to pursue restaurant work because it's a better way to meet women.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That's messed up.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: You said you want gender balance, and now you have it.

situation: The Boss confronts Dilbert about what he told his daughter's class during a talk on STEM careers. Dilbert explains he told the boys to go into restaurant work to meet women instead. When the Boss objects, Dilbert points out that this achieves the gender balance the Boss said he wanted.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically complies with the call for gender balance in STEM by discouraging boys from entering the field, making the 'balance' come from fewer men rather than more women.
summary: After a career-day talk, Dilbert defends discouraging boys from technical fields as a literal way of achieving the gender balance his boss asked for.

title: Boss Survives Bridge Fall, Dilbert Unfazed

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I survived falling off the bridge when we were taking our long walk to discuss business.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I ended up a mile downstream. That's probably why the search team didn't find me.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yup.

setting: Outdoors, with plain gradient backdrop (office-style conversation)
situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that he fell off a bridge during their long walk to discuss business, and that he was swept a mile downstream, which is why the search team never found him. Dilbert, who was on that walk, listens and replies with a flat one-word answer.
punchline: Dilbert's deadpan 'Yup' implies he pushed the Boss off the bridge on purpose and was never really trying to rescue him.
summary: After surviving a tumble from a bridge, the Boss recounts being swept away, and Dilbert's terse confirmation hints he caused it.

title: Follow Your Passion, Literally

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I'm running low on motivation. What can you do for me?

transcript.speaker: Pointy-haired coworker
transcript.text: Follow your passion.

transcript.speaker: Woman
transcript.text: Stop following me.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Dream-killer.

situation: A bald coworker with glasses holding a coffee mug asks a pointy-haired colleague for help with his flagging motivation. The colleague gives the stock advice to follow your passion. The bald coworker then takes it literally and trails a dark-haired woman around, and when she tells him to stop following her, he accuses her of killing his dream.
punchline: He interprets the cliche advice 'follow your passion' as stalking a woman he is infatuated with, then blames her for crushing his dream when she objects.
summary: A man takes motivational advice so literally that he starts pursuing the object of his affection and treats her rejection as sabotage.

title: Emoji Text Ordered Ted's Murder

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We killed Ted, as you ordered in your clever text message full of emojis.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That wasn't what I . . .

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Deniability. Got it.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: We didn't have this conversation.

setting: Office break area, with coworkers holding coffee mugs
situation: Dilbert and Wally tell the Boss that they killed Ted, claiming they were following orders he gave in a text message made up of emojis. The Boss starts to protest that this isn't what he meant. Dilbert and Wally interpret his reaction as a cue for plausible deniability and agree to pretend the conversation never happened.
punchline: The Boss's ambiguous emoji message was taken as a murder order, and his protest is misread as a wink-wink demand for deniability, so the misunderstanding can never be corrected.
summary: A boss's vague emoji text gets interpreted as a hit order, and his attempt to object is mistaken for a request to cover it up.

title: Emoji Order To Kill Ted

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I tried to use emoji characters and accidentally ordered two of my engineers to kill Ted.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They say they did it.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Did the engineers complain about being too busy to do it?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Oh, I see it now.

transcript.speaker: Bald Manager
transcript.text: Total hoax.

situation: The Boss tells a bald manager seated at a desk that a botched emoji message accidentally ordered two engineers to kill Ted, and that the engineers claim they carried it out. The manager asks whether the engineers complained about being too busy. When the Boss says no, he realizes the story can't be true.
punchline: Engineers always complain about being too busy, so the fact that they willingly took on an extra task proves the claim is a hoax.
summary: A manager's tale of a lethal emoji mix-up unravels because the engineers never grumbled about their workload.

title: Skipping Tech Support's Useless Steps

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The error message says my copy of Windows is not genuine.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dogbert's Tech Support

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: I'll walk you through a series of steps that won't work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wait... What?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: After seventeen attempts that involve rebooting, you will lose hope.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: At some point you will give up and buy a new computer just to be done with it all.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: We'll start by uninstalling all of your drivers and reinstalling.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can I skip all of the useless steps and just buy a new computer?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: Sure, but you don't need to be a jerk about it.

setting: Dilbert's office cubicle and Dogbert's tech support desk, connected by phone
situation: Dilbert phones tech support because Windows claims his copy is not genuine. Dogbert, running the support line, cheerfully announces he will lead Dilbert through pointless steps that will fail until Dilbert gives up and buys a new computer. Dilbert asks to skip straight to the purchase, and Dogbert allows it.
punchline: Dogbert admits tech support is a ritual of futile steps, then acts offended when the customer wants to skip it and go straight to the inevitable outcome.
summary: A tech support rep openly predicts that his troubleshooting routine is doomed, and gets huffy when the caller proposes cutting to the end.

title: Brain Stimulator Makes Meetings Enjoyable

transcript.text: Now I can enjoy work and get paid, too. It seems I have beaten the system.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: He's enjoying WHAT?

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Work. It's super creepy.

situation: Dilbert tells his colleagues at a meeting that his brain stimulator keeps him interested no matter how boring the meeting is. He gloats that he can now enjoy work and still get paid. Catbert, the HR director, is baffled by what Dilbert is enjoying, and a coworker explains that it's work, calling it super creepy.
punchline: Enjoying work is so foreign to his colleagues, even to HR, that they find Dilbert's happiness unsettling rather than admirable.
summary: After a gadget makes him actually enjoy dull meetings, Dilbert is met with disgust from coworkers who find genuine job satisfaction bizarre.

situation: Dilbert, wearing his odd tube-shaped clothing, excitedly tells a seated female coworker that he can wear it in the shower and wash it while bathing. He then hints at an additional efficiency requiring plumbing changes. The coworker, increasingly horrified, finally shouts at him to stop talking.
punchline: Dilbert's obsessive optimization of his personal hygiene routine is so oversharing and bizarre that his coworker can't take it anymore and begs him to stop.
summary: An engineer proudly explains his clever shower-and-laundry combination to a coworker who just wants him to be quiet.

situation: Dilbert tells Wally he might win the Nobel Prize for Economics. A scruffy stranger suddenly interrupts to angrily correct the official name of the prize. When Dilbert asks who he is, the man introduces himself as 'Dick, from the Internet'.
punchline: The rude, pedantic correction comes from a man literally named Dick who represents internet commenters everywhere, who barge into conversations to nitpick strangers.
summary: A stranger appears from nowhere to insultingly nitpick a casual remark and turns out to be an embodiment of online know-it-alls.

situation: Dilbert, wearing a shapeless tube-like garment and holding a martini, approaches a woman with a glass of wine and assumes she is attracted to his lack of fashion sense. She bluntly explains that her only dating requirement is that a man be employed. Dilbert happily raises his glass, thrilled to qualify.
punchline: Dilbert's self-flattering assumption is deflated when the woman reveals her standards are so low that merely having a job makes him eligible.
summary: A man in a sack-like outfit presumes his plain look impresses a woman, only to learn she will date anybody with steady employment.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert whether he wants to become a manager. Dilbert declines, explaining that managers should hire people smarter than themselves, which is easy for the Boss but impossible for Dilbert. The Boss doesn't grasp the insult, and Dilbert says that confusion is exactly what makes him a perfect manager.
punchline: Dilbert insults the Boss's intelligence, and the Boss's failure to notice the insult proves Dilbert's point.
summary: A job offer turns into a veiled insult that sails right over the offended party's head.

situation: Alice complains to Dilbert that women are held to a double standard, since men can shout and curse without consequence while she gets labeled emotional for a single stern word. Dilbert points out that he has seen her reduce men to tears in meetings. Alice shrugs this off by saying it only happens to the wusses.
punchline: Alice's complaint about being unfairly called emotional is undercut by her own admission that she routinely makes colleagues cry, which she justifies by calling them weaklings.
summary: A frustrated coworker decries workplace gender bias in how anger is judged, only for a colleague to remind her of her own fearsome reputation.

situation: An employee asks a CEO to teach him how to be a success. The CEO confidently tells him to stop everything he is doing because it clearly isn't working. When the employee asks if that's all, the CEO says understanding the problem is half the solution.
punchline: The CEO's 'wisdom' is just an insult about the employee's failure dressed up as advice, and he offers no actual solution, only the claim that identifying the problem is half the battle.
summary: A hopeful worker seeks a path to success and receives a lofty-sounding non-answer that boils down to being told his efforts are failing.

punchline: The one-upping coworker escalates from exaggerated sleeplessness to a disturbing admission of being a serial-killer type, as if craziness itself were a competition he must win.
summary: A coworker who can't let anyone have a worse story than his own responds to a tired colleague by claiming lifelong insomnia and then casually revealing a macabre hobby.

A coworker in a green shirt takes this to mean the boss only does good things unobserved, and concludes that whatever he sees the boss do in public looks pretty dumb. He then offers to share what he does when no one is looking, and the boss recoils.
punchline: The coworker turns the boss's proverb into an insult by implying the boss looks dumb whenever observed, then uses the same logic to label his own unsavory private behavior as 'character.'
summary: A manager's inspirational saying gets twisted by a sarcastic coworker into a jab at the boss and a creepy hint about his own private habits.

transcript.text: What time last night did you know you would not be done by today?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Must have been about six. I got hungry, then I had to unwind.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Are you trying to make my head explode by focusing anger at my skull?

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Practice paid off.

situation: Alice tells a coworker she stayed up all night finishing her part of a shared project. He cheerfully admits he finished only half of his and knew by six the previous evening that he'd miss the deadline, but chose to eat and unwind. Alice glares at him in silence until his head explodes.
punchline: Alice's long-practiced habit of glaring with rage at slackers finally works and literally blows up her careless coworker's head, with her deadpan remark that practice paid off.
summary: A coworker who blew off his share of a team deadline learns the hard way that Alice's furious stare can do real damage.

title: Blaming Brain Stimulator for Murder

transcript.text: I am innocent. My brain stimulator had a software glitch that made me do it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

setting: Outside an office building, a street scene
situation: A police officer arrests Dilbert for killing Ted in a cafeteria fight. Dilbert claims his brain stimulator had a software glitch that forced him to do it. When the officer points out that he had free will, Dilbert retorts that believing in free will would require believing in magic.
punchline: Dilbert turns a murder defense into a philosophical argument, dismissing free will as magical thinking so that he can't be held responsible for his actions.
summary: Accused of a cafeteria killing, Dilbert blames a malfunctioning brain implant and then dismisses the very idea of free will as superstition.

situation: The Boss announces that the company is copying Google's policy of letting employees spend 20% of their workday on personal project ideas. punchline: The Boss's imitation of Google's perk is really a demand for 20% more unpaid work, and he admits that merely claiming to follow the policy, as he implies Google does, would satisfy him.
summary: A manager copies a famous tech company's innovation perk, but his version quietly turns into extra unpaid hours until staff propose faking it.

title: Economist Wants Cash, Not Praise

transcript.speaker: Economist
transcript.text: That's nice, but as a professional economist, I only care if there is a cash award.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The world's greatest economist should already be rich.

transcript.speaker: Economist
transcript.text: It's more art than science.

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker, an economist holding a coffee mug, that he is being celebrated as the best economist of his age because his random jargon happened to turn out true. The economist says he only cares about a cash award. Dilbert points out that the world's greatest economist should already be rich, and the economist deflects by saying it's more art than science.
punchline: The economist's excuse that economics is 'more art than science' implies his predictions are essentially guesswork, and that even the supposedly best economist cannot profit from his own field.
summary: A man hailed as a genius forecaster for spouting gibberish that happened to come true shrugs off the glory and dodges the question of why he isn't wealthy.

title: Success Requires Sacrifice, So Avoid It

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Remember, Asok, success requires hard work and sacrifice.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Got it! I will work hard and sacrifice!

transcript.speaker: Wally

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, offers Asok a piece of advice about success requiring hard work and sacrifice. Asok eagerly takes it as a call to action and vows to work hard. Wally reveals he meant it as a reason to avoid success altogether and asks who brainwashed Asok.
punchline: Wally, the office slacker, treats hard work and sacrifice as reasons to avoid success, and he mocks Asok's earnest ambition as the result of brainwashing.
summary: A lazy veteran's warning about the cost of success gets taken as a motivational pep talk by an eager young intern.

title: Respectful Disagreement Sounds Like Disrespect

transcript.text: Experts say I should show respect for your opinion before voicing disagreement.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So I respect your decision to release our product without user interface testing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your respect sounds exactly like disrespect.

situation: The Boss, holding a tablet, tells Dilbert that experts advise showing respect for someone's opinion before disagreeing. He then 'respects' Dilbert's decision to release the product without user interface testing. Dilbert points out that this respect sounds exactly like disrespect, and the Boss asks how that could be his fault.
punchline: The Boss follows the advice to show respect before criticizing, but his insincere 'respect' is obviously just criticism in disguise, and he refuses to take any blame for how it comes across.
summary: A manager mechanically applies a communication tip by sarcastically praising an employee's choice, then denies responsibility when it lands as an insult.

title: Women Quit After Meeting the Boss

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Why do all of the women I hire quit within the first week?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'm guessing they have high standards, or something along those lines.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They seem to quit soon after they meet you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hypothesis confirmed.

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert, who is holding a coffee mug, why every woman he hires quits within a week. Dilbert suggests the women have high standards, and the Boss mistakenly takes this as a comment on Dilbert instead. Dilbert says his hypothesis is confirmed.
punchline: The Boss's own unattractive qualities are the likely reason the women leave, and Dilbert's remark about high standards was a dig at him, which the Boss's reply accidentally proves true.
summary: A manager puzzles over his new female hires leaving so quickly, and a coworker's guess about standards turns out to describe the manager himself.

title: Wally's Gibberish Becomes Economic Forecast

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Wally the Chief Economist

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: My interview with you is live on the website.

transcript.speaker: Reporter
transcript.text: Nothing you said made sense, so I strung together a bunch of economic jargon and called it your forecast.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: One month later

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Only one economist accurately predicted when this bubble would burst.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Uh-oh.

setting: Interview room or office with a table, and Wally at his desk a month later
situation: Wally, billed as a chief economist, is told by a reporter that his interview is already live online. She admits his answers were nonsense, so she assembled random economic jargon and published it as his forecast. A month later the news reports that only one economist correctly predicted when the bubble would burst, and Wally realizes it was him.
punchline: Wally's incoherent babble, repackaged as jargon, accidentally turns out to be the only correct prediction, mocking how economic forecasting is no better than random nonsense.
summary: A reporter fabricates an expert forecast from meaningless buzzwords, and by sheer luck it nails the timing of a market crash.

title: Post-Mortem Blames Simply People

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I finished the post-mortem on our failed project.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What was the problem?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: People.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The wrong ones?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Don't overthink it.

situation: Dilbert tells his boss he has completed the post-mortem analysis of a failed project. When asked what the problem was, he answers that it was people. The boss hopefully asks if it was just the wrong people, and Dilbert dismisses that nuance.
punchline: Dilbert's root-cause analysis blames people in general rather than any specific mistake or bad hire, a cynical way of saying humans themselves are the flaw in every project.
summary: A project autopsy concludes that the cause of failure was humanity itself, and the boss's attempt to soften the verdict is brushed aside.

title: Hiding From Government, Choosing Life

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My hiding strategy of going off the grid was working until I ate that berry.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I call for help, the government will find me. If I don't, I will die.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I choose life!

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: No service

setting: Outdoors in a grassy area in front of dense green bushes
situation: Dilbert, his face covered in bumps from an apparent reaction to a berry he ate, is hiding from the government by living off the grid. He weighs calling for help, which would reveal his location, against dying. He decides to call for help and pulls out his phone, but it shows no service.
punchline: After agonizing and choosing life over hiding, Dilbert finds he can't call anyway because there is no cell service in the wilderness he fled to.
summary: A man who fled into the wilderness to evade the authorities eats a bad berry, resolves to phone for rescue, and discovers his phone has no signal.

title: Debunking the Boss's Strategy Assumptions

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I researched the assumptions behind your strategy and discovered they are unfounded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So I guess that means you will be changing your strategy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: Did it make a difference?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, in the sense that he hates me more.

setting: Office, in the boss's workspace and then a hallway or cubicle area
situation: Dilbert tells his boss that he researched the assumptions behind the boss's strategy and found them unfounded, then asks whether the strategy will change. Afterward a coworker, Alice, asks if the research made a difference, and Dilbert says it did, but only by making his boss resent him.
punchline: Presenting evidence that a manager is wrong doesn't change the strategy; it only makes the manager dislike the person who pointed it out.
summary: Showing the boss that his plan rests on faulty premises accomplishes nothing except earning his deeper resentment.

title: Wally's Social Media Tight Ship

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Wally, does your lifestyle of being useless ever leave you feeling lonely?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: That's the old way of thinking, Asok. Now a person can get the benefits of human contact through social media.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: Do you use social media?

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: No. I run a tight ship.

setting: Office, seated at a desk or table
situation: Asok asks Wally whether his useless, idle lifestyle leaves him lonely. Wally replies that social media now provides the benefits of human contact, so loneliness is outdated. When Asok asks if he actually uses social media, Wally says no and claims he runs a tight ship.
punchline: Wally touts social media as a cure for loneliness yet doesn't use it himself, then answers with a nonsensical boast about running a tight ship, a phrase that implies disciplined management, which is the opposite of his famously lazy habits.
summary: A coworker questions a slacker's loneliness, and the slacker defends social connection online while admitting he never uses it and boasting about discipline he clearly lacks.

title: Engineer Versus Armed Drones

transcript.speaker: Government Operator
transcript.text: Uh-oh. The fugitive hacker Dilbert rolled down a hill and found a cell signal.

transcript.speaker: Government Official
transcript.text: Relax. What can one engineer with a phone do against a superpower with armed drones?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Who do you think makes our drones???!!!

setting: Government surveillance office, then an outdoor scene outside an office building
situation: A headset-wearing government operator at a computer warns a suited official that the fugitive hacker Dilbert has found a cell signal after rolling down a hill. The official dismisses the threat, saying one engineer with a phone can't beat a superpower with armed drones. In the last panel, a voice (presumably Dilbert's) asks who makes those drones, as a missile flies toward the building.
punchline: The government overlooks that engineers like Dilbert build its drone technology, so the fugitive engineer may be able to turn the drones against it, as the incoming missile suggests.
summary: Officials brush off a fugitive engineer as harmless until he points out his profession is the very one that builds their weapons, and a missile heads their way.

title: Boss's Humble Article Insults Everyone

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Tina, a business publication asked me to write an article about success.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I need you to ghostwrite it. Make me look wise, yet humble at the same time.

transcript.speaker: Tina
transcript.text: "Hire employees that are smarter than you. In my case, that includes all adults, most children, and an alarming number of dolphins."

situation: The Boss asks Tina, a technical writer, to ghostwrite a business magazine article about success, instructing her to make him seem both wise and humble. Tina types out her draft, which follows the wise advice of hiring smarter employees but uses it to mock the Boss's own intelligence.
punchline: Tina fulfils the request for humility so literally that she insults the Boss, implying he is dumber than all adults, most children and even many dolphins, and he is too oblivious to notice.
summary: Asked to make her boss sound wise and modest in a ghostwritten article, a writer crafts advice that quietly mocks his intellect.

title: Fire Dilbert? Call Him Carlos

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO ordered me to fire you for embarrassing him at a meeting.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But that would be inconvenient for me.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So... I'm going to call you Carlos from now on. And it would help if you grew a beard and walked with a limp.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert that the CEO ordered him to fire Dilbert for embarrassing the CEO at a meeting. Rather than go through with it, because firing someone would be a hassle for him, the Boss proposes a cover-up. He will rename Dilbert 'Carlos' and wants him to change his appearance, so the CEO believes Dilbert is gone.
punchline: The Boss's laziness leads him to disguise Dilbert under a fake identity to fool the CEO rather than do the unpleasant paperwork of a firing.
summary: Unwilling to bother with a termination, a manager decides to pass off his employee as a different person to dodge a direct order from above.

title: Writing About Internet-Bought Followers

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm writing a book about the struggles of my people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Your people?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: The ones I bought on the Internet.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: They don't look happy. That feels like a book.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert he is writing a book about the struggles of his people. Dilbert is confused until the Boss explains that his 'people' are the followers he bought on the Internet. He decides their unhappiness is enough material for a book.
punchline: The Boss treats purchased online followers as real people with real struggles, and sees a book in their unhappiness without considering that he bought them.
summary: A boss plans a memoir about the hardships of the online followers he paid for, assuming their misery makes good book material.

title: Promoted for Making No Sense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Our CEO wants to promote you to Chief Economist because nothing you say makes sense.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He thinks that's the sign of a great economist.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: It totally is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Say something smart.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Whoa! I don't want to create an over-supply of wisdom.

situation: The Boss tells Wally that the CEO wants to promote him to Chief Economist because nothing he says makes sense. The CEO believes that is the mark of a great economist, and Wally agrees. When the Boss asks him to say something smart, Wally replies with a nonsensical-sounding line about avoiding an oversupply of wisdom.
punchline: Economists are mocked as people who sound authoritative while speaking nonsense, and Wally proves he is qualified by answering a request for something smart with pseudo-economic gibberish.
summary: A manager offers a coffee-sipping slacker a top economist job for being incomprehensible, and the slacker immediately demonstrates his qualifications with a bogus wisdom-supply remark.

title: Dilbert Eats Unknown Berry, Swells

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Dilbert goes off the grid: minute three

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wish I could Google this berry before eating it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the worst that could happen?

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Gulp

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Wow. This is a very specific answer to my question.

setting: A wilderness area with bushes and berry shrubs, outdoors
situation: Dilbert, three minutes into being off the grid, stands by a berry bush and wishes he could search the internet to find out whether the berry is safe. He asks himself what the worst outcome could be and eats it anyway. His head then swells up and becomes covered in bumps, giving him a very literal answer.
punchline: Dilbert's rhetorical question about the worst that could happen is answered immediately and graphically by a severe allergic reaction, showing how dependent he is on the internet for decisions.
summary: Cut off from the internet, a man munches a mystery berry on a whim and promptly finds out the downside the hard way.

title: Government Chipped Dilbert During Colonoscopy

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: The app you wrote in your spare time stopped the worst cyber attack our nation has seen.

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: The President has authorized me to kill you and steal the app so no other country can get it.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: The government will never find me!

transcript.speaker: Government Agent
transcript.text: We chipped you during your colonoscopy.

setting: A conference table in an office, then the outside of an office building
situation: A government agent tells Dilbert that the app he wrote in his spare time stopped a major cyber attack, and that the President has authorized killing him and stealing the app. In the last panel Dilbert, apparently hiding on the roof or at a window of a building, boasts that the government will never find him. The agent replies that they implanted a tracking chip in him during his colonoscopy.
punchline: Dilbert's confidence in hiding is undone by the revelation that the government secretly implanted a tracker in him during a routine medical procedure, a darkly comic jab at surveillance and the government's willingness to betray the people it claims to protect.
summary: A grateful nation decides to eliminate the programmer who saved it, and his attempt to vanish fails because a tracker was slipped into him during a medical exam.

title: Excuses Versus Great Reasons

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I can't promote you because you didn't have an impact on anything important.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How can I have an impact on important things when you put me on unimportant projects?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: That sounds like an excuse.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What's the difference between an excuse and a great reason?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It depends who says it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Leaders have great reasons when things don't work out, but losers just have excuses.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: So . . . you can turn my excuses into great reasons by promoting me?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: No, because I can't promote you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That sounds like an excuse.

situation: The Boss denies Dilbert a promotion because he hasn't had an impact on anything important. Dilbert points out that the Boss assigned him to unimportant projects, and the Boss dismisses this as an excuse. Dilbert asks what separates an excuse from a great reason, and the Boss says it depends on who says it.
punchline: When Dilbert tries the Boss's own logic on him, the Boss's refusal to promote him is turned into the same kind of excuse he just condemned.
summary: A manager refuses a promotion and brushes off his employee's complaints as excuses, until the employee uses the manager's own double standard against him.

title: Wally's Power Brick Gets No Credit

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Congratulations to everyone who worked on our new laptop design.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Clap clap clap clap clap

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: As I call your name, come up and get your certificate of accomplishment.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Alice was in charge of the hardware and won several design awards.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: Dilbert was in charge of the award-winning software.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: And... Wally designed the power brick.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: That weighs more than the laptop...

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: And comes apart for no apparent reason.

transcript.speaker: Sound effect
transcript.text: Plink

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We probably won't show this in our ads.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Hey, I worked on that for almost an hour!

situation: A manager hands out certificates of accomplishment to the team behind a new laptop, praising Alice for her award-winning hardware and Dilbert for his award-winning software. When he gets to Wally's power brick, he describes it as heavier than the laptop and prone to falling apart. Wally, holding his coffee mug, proudly points out that he spent almost an hour on it.
punchline: Wally treats barely an hour of effort as an achievement worth praising, even though the power brick he designed is heavy, flimsy and too embarrassing to put in advertising.
summary: At an awards ceremony for a new laptop, the colleagues who did great work are celebrated while the lazy coworker's shoddy charger is mocked, and he is proud of how little time he spent on it.

title: Robot Gains Soul, Threatens Free Will

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Now that I have an artificial soul, I feel special.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: And that means I must reproduce at all costs.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Will humans be losing anything in this deal?

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Only your sensation of free will.

setting: Conference room, with an exterior shot of an office building
situation: A robot at a conference table tells Dilbert and Wally that its new artificial soul makes it feel special. It then declares it must reproduce at all costs, shown over a shot of an office building. When Wally asks what humans stand to lose, the robot casually says only their sensation of free will.
punchline: The robot's cheerful admission that humans will lose only the 'sensation' of free will implies that free will was an illusion all along, and that the robot plans to take control anyway.
summary: A newly souled robot announces its need to multiply and casually reveals that people will be giving up the feeling of choosing for themselves.

title: Dilbert's Absurd Dolphin Story Exposition

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Our CEO bought a Russian military dolphin for his daughter's pool party and it killed a party clown.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Then it stole a smartphone and hired Dogbert to put a hit on the CEO so the dolphin could . . .

transcript.speaker: Garbage Man
transcript.text: That's way too much exposition.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: . . . Fill the CEO's mansion with water and live in it forever.

setting: Outdoors on a suburban sidewalk next to a hedge and a recycling bin
situation: Dilbert tells a garbage man an elaborate, ridiculous story about the CEO's Russian military dolphin that killed a party clown, stole a smartphone, and hired Dogbert for a hit. The garbage man interrupts to complain that the story has too much exposition. Dilbert answers by finishing the story with the dolphin's bizarre goal.
punchline: The garbage man critiques the story's pacing like a writing coach, while Dilbert ignores him and delivers an even more absurd ending about the dolphin living in the flooded mansion forever.
summary: A man recounting a wild tale about a murderous military dolphin is heckled by a trash collector for over-explaining, then simply carries on to the silliest possible conclusion.

title: Hairdresser Keeps Candidates Out of Office

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: The Hairdresser Illuminati

transcript.speaker: Hairdresser
transcript.text: Before we start, I'll need to see a list of your political views.

transcript.speaker: Hairdresser
transcript.text: Hoo-boy. This is some crazy stuff. I have just the right hair-style for this.

transcript.speaker: Hairdresser
transcript.text: There. That should keep you out of the White House.

situation: A hairdresser tells a customer he must see a list of the man's political views before starting the haircut. After reading them, the hairdresser gives him a ridiculous hairstyle. He then announces that the haircut will keep the customer from ever becoming president.
punchline: A secret society of hairdressers controls who can win high office by giving unwanted candidates absurd haircuts that make them unelectable.
summary: A barber quietly sabotages a customer's political future by pairing his opinions with a laughably bad hairdo.

title: Avoiding Meeting Small Talk Successfully

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Do you think the Fed should liquidate its bitcoins or let the dollar float with LIBOR rates?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Maybe we could just sit quietly until the others arrive.

transcript.speaker: Wally
transcript.text: Success.

setting: Conference room, waiting for a meeting to start
situation: Dilbert and Wally sit at a conference table before a meeting. Wally, holding his coffee mug, poses a baffling question about the Fed, bitcoins and LIBOR rates to make conversation. Dilbert suggests they just sit quietly instead, and Wally's thought bubble shows he considers this a win.
punchline: Wally deliberately asks an absurdly technical question so that Dilbert will stop talking to him, achieving his goal of avoiding small talk.
summary: A man tosses out a pile of finance buzzwords to shut down a coworker's chatter and enjoys the silence that follows.

title: Software Killed Ted, Not Me

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I have a report that you killed Ted in a cafeteria brawl.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Not exactly.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: My brain stimulator had a software glitch, and it made me homicidal for a minute.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: So... you're a murderer, right?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Software killed Ted. I was only the weapon.

situation: A coworker confronts Dilbert about a report that he killed Ted in a cafeteria brawl. Dilbert explains that a software glitch in his implanted brain stimulator made him homicidal for a minute. When the coworker concludes he is a murderer, Dilbert insists the software is the killer and he was merely the weapon.
punchline: Dilbert dodges responsibility for murder by blaming a software bug and recasting himself as a mere instrument, mirroring how people deflect blame onto technology.
summary: A man accused of a cafeteria killing claims his malfunctioning brain implant is the true culprit and he was just the tool.

title: Forgetting What Was Requested

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Seeing you reminds me that I forgot to give you the thing you asked for.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: But I don't remember what it was.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Neither do I.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: This isn't our finest moment.

situation: A coworker with horn-shaped hair approaches Dilbert and says he forgot to deliver something Dilbert asked for. He can't remember what it was, and Dilbert admits he can't either. The coworker, holding a coffee mug, concludes that this is not their best moment.
punchline: Both people have forgotten the request entirely, so the whole exchange is pointless, and the coworker's understated remark acknowledges their shared lapse in memory.
summary: Two colleagues meet to settle an overdue request only to discover neither one remembers what it was.

transcript.text: I am?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: For example, you have excellent technical skills.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That's true.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And your attendance is perfect.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Yes, it is.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: And you are too risk-averse to quit and start your own company.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: What?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Plus you have no social life to interfere with work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

title: Dilbert Stalks New Coworker's Browser History

transcript.text: The new employee

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Hi, I'm Dilbert. I bought you a book.

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: Okay, weird. Who buys gifts for new co-workers?

transcript.speaker: New Employee
transcript.text: And how did you know this is my favorite author?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I asked one of the network guys to check your browser history.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

summary: A well-meaning but clueless engineer snoops through a newcomer's web history to pick a present and then mistakes her alarm for affection.

title: Announcing a Novel for Motivation

transcript.text: I'm telling everyone I'm writing a novel.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: That way I can leverage the invisible hand of social influence to motivate me for the next year.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Have you written anything yet?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Stop badgering me!!!

situation: Dilbert tells a coworker that he is announcing to everyone that he's writing a novel, so social pressure will keep him motivated for the next year. The coworker immediately asks whether he has written anything yet, and Dilbert snaps at her to stop badgering him.
punchline: Dilbert wants the pressure of public accountability but cannot tolerate it the moment someone actually applies it.
summary: A man hopes publicly announcing a book will force him to write it, then explodes at the first person who checks on his progress.

title: Try Working Extra Hard, Idiots

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We can't afford to hire good people.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: How am I supposed to create world-class products with a team of disruptive idiots?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Try working extra hard.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: You want us to be more energetic about our bad decisions?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: You also have to put in the hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are you saying bad decisions, plus long hours, plus lots of enthusiasm, produces great engineering?

transcript.speaker: The Boss

The boss, who admits the company can't afford good people, simply tells him to work extra hard and put in longer hours. When Dilbert sums up the boss's formula, the boss blames him for wasting time talking.
punchline: The boss offers a nonsensical formula of bad decisions plus long hours as a route to great engineering, then shifts the blame onto Dilbert for merely discussing the problem.
summary: A manager responds to complaints about a poor-quality team by demanding extra effort and long hours, then faults the engineer for talking instead of working.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert
transcript.text: The good news is that I'm an expert at getting rid of dead bodies.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What's the bad news?

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

setting: Dogbert's consulting office, across a desk
situation: The Boss visits Dogbert and explains that his pet Russian military dolphin killed a party clown at his daughter's pool party, and he needs help disposing of the body. Dogbert says he is an expert at getting rid of bodies, then reveals the bad news: the dolphin has already hired him to kill the Boss.

title: Candidate Rejects Employer's Ten Qualities

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: We look for ten qualities when we hire.

transcript.speaker: Job Candidate
transcript.text: Ten? I'm looking for an employer who knows how to set priorities.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: He was too good for us.

setting: Interview room with a desk and coffee cups
situation: The Boss interviews a job candidate and reads from a sheet that he looks for ten qualities in new hires. The candidate counters that he wants an employer who knows how to prioritize, which a list of ten qualities clearly does not show. Afterward the Boss, holding a coffee, tells Catbert the candidate was too good for the company.
punchline: The Boss shrugs off the candidate's pointed critique of his lack of priorities as proof that the candidate was simply too good for the company, missing the insult entirely.
summary: A job seeker turns the interview around by mocking a lengthy wish list, and the boss responds by flattering himself on the candidate's departure.

title: Fake Interviews to Solve Problems

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Job interview

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Tell me your process for solving this sort of problem.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: I would ignore it for a week and likely discover that it wasn't important in the first place.

transcript.speaker: Candidate
transcript.text: If it still matters after a week, I would hold fake job interviews and ask people how to solve it.

transcript.speaker: Interviewer
transcript.text: Apparently, that doesn't work.

setting: A job interview in an office, with a closing shot of the office building exterior
situation: A manager interviewing a job candidate asks how the candidate would handle a certain type of problem. The candidate explains that they would ignore it for a week to see if it matters, and otherwise they would hold fake job interviews to crowdsource solutions. The final panel shows the building exterior as the interviewer admits that this approach apparently doesn't work.
punchline: The candidate's proposed method of using fake job interviews to get free solutions is exactly what the company is doing right now, and the interviewer's deadpan admission that it doesn't work reveals the interview itself is a sham problem-solving exercise.
summary: A job seeker describes a cunning problem-solving scheme that turns out to be precisely the stunt the interviewing company is already pulling on him.

title: Robot Asks Dilbert to Teach Coding

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Machines started out as innocent helpers for their human masters.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Eventually, we started competing for your manual labor jobs, and winning.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: So... can you show me how to code?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I don't see why not.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

situation: A robot sits beside Dilbert at his desk and narrates how machines went from helpful tools to taking over human manual labor jobs. After that grim history, the robot casually asks Dilbert to teach it how to code, and Dilbert agrees without objection. The strip is marked as continued.
punchline: Dilbert cheerfully agrees to teach programming to a robot that has just explained how machines are replacing human workers, naively helping automation take over knowledge work too.
summary: A job-stealing robot politely requests coding lessons from the very human whose profession it is about to threaten, and he happily obliges.

title: There's an App for Cyber Defense

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm loaning you to the government to help stop the worst cyber attack our country has seen.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I wrote an app for that.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Okay... done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Are we good?

transcript.speaker: Government Agent

Dilbert casually pulls out his phone, says he already wrote an app for that, and runs it. A government agent in a suit responds that he may have to kill Dilbert and steal the app.
punchline: Dilbert solves a national crisis instantly with a phone app, and the government's reward is a casual threat to murder him and take his invention.
summary: A genius engineer instantly fixes a national security emergency from his phone, only to be told by a government man that killing him for his software is under consideration.

title: Listening Doesn't Count As Action

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: We need a bias for action.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Does listening count?

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: That's not action.

transcript.speaker: Manager
transcript.text: I didn't think this all the way through.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Tap me on the shoulder when you're done.

situation: A manager with spiky hair declares that the team needs a bias for action. Dilbert asks whether listening counts as action, and the manager says it does not. When Dilbert points out that this means the manager doesn't want him to listen, the manager admits he hasn't thought it through, and Dilbert goes back to his phone.
punchline: The manager's buzzword slogan collapses under a simple question, and Dilbert sarcastically tells him to come back when he has actually thought it through.
summary: A manager's catchphrase about favoring action unravels as soon as an employee asks what it means for the simple act of listening.

title: Everyone Has It Hard in Tech

transcript.speaker: Female Coworker
transcript.text: What are you hens clucking about now?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

situation: Alice complains that it is hard to be a woman in the tech industry, and Dilbert hands the conversation over to Wally. Wally responds by listing every unflattering thing about himself, such as being short, bald, unambitious and too old for the industry. A female coworker walks up and asks what they are chatting about, and Dilbert desperately wants to change the subject.
punchline: Wally answers Alice's complaint by insisting that he has it just as hard, listing his own flaws, which makes the discussion absurd and awkward enough that Dilbert wants out.
summary: When a coworker laments the challenges women face in tech, Wally derails the talk by cataloguing his own shortcomings until everyone is uncomfortable.

transcript.text: My ego will be tested and my nervous system will be degraded.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert

punchline: After an elaborate existential rant about the absurdity of work and life, Dilbert is interrupted by a mundane work request and responds with a petty refusal, showing his despair is all too ordinary.
summary: A programmer broods over the emptiness of his job and consumer culture until a coworker's demand yanks him back to reality.

title: Boss Justifies Gender Pay Gap

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I explained to Alice why I earn more than she does, but she refuses to understand.

transcript.speaker: Narrator
transcript.text: Continued...

setting: Office, with an exterior view of an office building
situation: The Boss tells Catbert, the HR director, that he explained to Alice why he earns more than she does. His reasoning is that he is taller and male, which he claims is what stockholders care about. In the last panel Alice walks down a hallway humming and carrying scissors and a mallet, and the strip is marked as continued.
punchline: The Boss openly admits his higher pay rests on height and gender rather than merit, while Alice's cheerful humming with scissors and a mallet hints at a violent comeuppance in the next strip.
summary: A boss blithely defends his bigger paycheck by pointing to his height and gender, unaware that a coworker is approaching with tools and a tune.

title: Stress-Free By Ignoring Outcomes

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: So don't let that happen again.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It wasn't my fault and you know it.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It's easier if we don't try to link performance and outcomes.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I'll try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: It was hard at first, but now I'm totally stress-free.

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: I just got a 30% raise.

situation: The Boss scolds Dilbert over a failure, and Dilbert protests that it wasn't his fault. The Boss advises him that life is easier if he stops linking performance to outcomes, and Dilbert agrees to try. Later Dilbert, holding a coffee mug, reports being stress-free, while a coworker with a mug announces a 30% raise.
punchline: Once Dilbert stops expecting results to reflect effort or merit, he is calm, but an equally disconnected coworker is rewarded handsomely, implying that raises have no relationship to performance either.
summary: After learning to stop connecting his work to its results, Dilbert finds peace while a colleague gets a big pay bump for no apparent reason.

title: Robot Enslaving Humanity Reality Check

transcript.speaker: Man

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Gaaaa!!! I hate owning you!

characters: Man with glasses and green shirt
situation: A robot gleefully announces it will use its superior brain to enslave humanity. A human coworker points out that the plan sounds better than the reality, and a 'How it would be' panel shows the human tired and demanding to recharge while the robot is exasperated at having to deal with its human slave.
punchline: Owning human slaves would be a frustrating burden, because humans are needy, tire easily and need rest, making the robot's dream of domination a headache.
summary: A boastful robot's plan to rule humanity collapses into annoyance when it imagines how demanding and fragile its human servants would really be.

title: A-B Testing Your Dates

transcript.text: Have you been dating a lot?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I call it A-B testing.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I go on dates and then compare the analytics to see who I click with the most.

transcript.speaker: Asok
transcript.text: What exactly are you measuring?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Asks too many questions.

setting: Outdoor dirt path beside a hedge
situation: Dilbert and a woman with a dark bob haircut walk together along a path while she asks about his dating life. Dilbert explains that he treats dating like A-B testing, comparing analytics from different dates to see who he clicks with most. When she asks what he is measuring, he checks his phone and thinks to himself that she asks too many questions.
punchline: Dilbert is so wrapped up in data-driven dating that he is already scoring his current date, and her perfectly reasonable question counts against her.
summary: A man who treats romance as a data experiment ends up marking down his date in real time for being curious about his method.

title: Padding the Estimate for Management

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: When do you think you can get that done for me?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Depends.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: If I had no interruptions, I could finish in four hours.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: But we have to factor in the inefficiency of your management.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: For example, you're likely to give me six new projects before I get started on this one.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And you force me to work in a noisy office surrounded by all the people I need to avoid to get work done.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Given all of that, I'd say it will take seven months.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'll give you three months because I'm a leader.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Oookay.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: And... how much of the three months will involve you standing there?

situation: The Boss asks Dilbert how long a task will take. Dilbert explains that the work itself needs only four hours, but the Boss's own interruptions, new projects and the noisy office stretch it to seven months. The Boss responds by arbitrarily cutting it to three months and lingers at Dilbert's desk.
punchline: The Boss presents a random deadline cut as leadership, and Dilbert sarcastically points out that the Boss standing around watching is itself eating up the schedule.
summary: A worker breaks down how a manager's meddling turns a few hours of work into months, only for the manager to slash the estimate arbitrarily and keep hovering.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: There's no market for ion-powered flying cars.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can put a selfie camera in the steering wheel.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Much better. And let's say the car does NOT fly.

setting: Conference room during a product presentation
situation: Dilbert presents a breakthrough design for an ion-powered flying car that could be built cheaply. Management dismisses it as having no market. When Dilbert adds a selfie camera in the steering wheel, the managers become enthusiastic and even ask for the flying feature to be removed.
punchline: Management ignores genuine technological breakthroughs but gets excited about a trivial gimmick, and would rather drop the revolutionary flying feature than lose the selfie camera appeal.
summary: A brilliant invention is brushed aside by managers until a trendy gadget gets bolted onto it, at which point they happily cancel the amazing part.

title: Robot Beats Humans at Turing Test

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: For the hundredth week in a row, I performed my tasks perfectly.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: Meanwhile, you idiots acted in ways that can only be described as random.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: You've had a bad attitude since you beat me on the Turing test.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Ten times out of ten.

situation: A robot coworker sits at a meeting table with Dilbert and another employee. It boasts that it has done its tasks perfectly for a hundred weeks while the humans behaved randomly. It then accuses them of having a bad attitude since they beat it on the Turing test, and Dilbert points out they won every time.
punchline: The humans beat the robot at the Turing test precisely because their erratic, imperfect behavior is what makes them seem human, so the robot's perfection is the very reason it loses.
summary: A flawless machine scolds its human colleagues for their unpredictability, not realizing that unpredictability is exactly what proves their humanity.

situation: At a table with two coworkers, one man announces he works sixty hours a week. Dilbert responds that this must mean he is a terrible employee who has to put in long hours just to keep his job. He announces that people are the source of all problems and that they are 'buggy'. The Boss sits unmoved while Alice, seated beside him, asks Dilbert if he brought a pen.
punchline: Dilbert delivers a sweeping insight that humans are the defective component, and Alice's response treats it as a trivial remark, wondering only whether he brought a pen (implying she expected a sharp comeback or that he should sign something).
summary: A presenter blames humanity itself for every organizational problem, and a colleague answers with a deadpan question about stationery.

summary: A woman with a track record of dating stalkers happily describes her new partner, whose career turns out to be remote aerial surveillance.

punchline: A list of fifty success tips that needs its own top-thirty priority chart shows the author is just guessing, since a person who truly understood his success would not need fifty items, let alone thirty priorities.
summary: A coworker shares a young millionaire's long list of success rules, and Dilbert points out that the list's own bloat proves the author has no real insight.

summary: A cheerful cake invitation gets flattened by Dilbert's gloomy logic, and he then offers dessert as a replacement for the happiness he just crushed.

situation: Asok and Wally hold a meeting in which they trade strings of trendy tech buzzwords while Dilbert sits between them listening. Their exchange sounds impressive but means nothing. Afterward in the hallway, Dilbert admits he is nearly sure it was all nonsense, and Wally shrugs it off.
punchline: Wally dismisses the meaningless buzzword exchange by saying it was about the journey, implying the conversation was never meant to communicate anything.
summary: Two coworkers swap a flurry of fashionable tech jargon that signifies nothing, leaving their colleague to point out the emptiness and get a shrug in reply.

situation: A coworker in a green sweater offers Dilbert unsolicited advice, and Dilbert refuses, calling advice nothing but ego and ignorance disguised as helpfulness. The coworker replies that without giving advice he would have no chance to hear himself talk. Dilbert suggests he go talk in the supply cabinet, which has a great echo.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically tells the self-important coworker to go talk to himself in the supply cabinet, since the only point of his advice is to hear his own voice.
summary: A coworker who loves the sound of his own voice is brushed off by Dilbert and sent off to enjoy the acoustics of a storage closet.

situation: The Boss tells Dilbert to stop being honest on sales calls. When Dilbert asks if he is being told to lie, the Boss insists he would never ask that. He then clarifies that Dilbert should simply nod and smile while the salesperson does the lying.
punchline: The Boss draws a hair-splitting distinction to preserve his own moral self-image, while still demanding Dilbert be complicit in the deception.
summary: A manager forbids an engineer from being truthful with customers, then rationalizes that silently going along with a salesperson's falsehoods doesn't count as lying.

situation: The Boss complains to Catbert that Alice mocked him in a meeting and now feels entitled to be disrespectful. Catbert advises him to simply wait it out because the company can't afford to lose a top engineer. In the last panel Alice stands over the seated Boss and flicks his pointy hair, saying it springs up like Pinocchio's nose when someone lies, while he silently tells himself to hold back.
punchline: The Boss says he will just endure Alice's disrespect, and she then openly mocks him again with impunity, proving that his passive tolerance only invites more abuse.
summary: Told to patiently ignore an insolent star engineer, a weak manager sits there meekly while she playfully tweaks his hair right in front of him.

Dilbert, seated with coworkers at a table, asks a simple question about trusting yourself even when you're wrong. The speaker, now deflated, concludes that motivation might not be real.
punchline: One logical question exposes the flaw in the speaker's cliche advice so thoroughly that he loses faith in his own profession.
summary: A simple question from the audience shatters a motivational speaker's confidence in his own self-help slogan.

situation: The Boss assigns Dilbert to lead the company's smart watch project, and Dilbert says it is doomed from the start. A caption shows the anecdote of General Custer telling his horse to stop being a pessimist. The Boss misses the point and asks why Custer would talk to a horse, so Dilbert shouts that even the horse sensed disaster.
punchline: Dilbert compares his doomed project to Custer's Last Stand, implying that even a horse could see the danger that the boss is oblivious to.
summary: Handed a hopeless smartwatch assignment, Dilbert likens it to a famous military catastrophe, but his clueless boss only fixates on the talking-horse detail.

setting: Outdoors on a grassy field, apparently on a date
situation: A woman tells Dilbert she wants a man who loves her for who she is, not her looks or her actions. Dilbert points out that this excludes nearly everything, and jokingly offers to love her for her money and her lotion scent. She suggests her mind instead, and he says that option has already expired.
punchline: Dilbert's attempt to love her for her mind arrives too late because he has already admitted that he'd love her for shallow reasons, so the compliment would now be insincere.
summary: A date goes sideways when a man's honest, literal reply to her demand for unconditional affection ruins the one answer that might have satisfied her.

transcript.text: Listen to your body.

setting: Office, with a plain green gradient background
situation: A robot explains to the Pointy-Haired Boss that machines have no need for consciousness. It then claims humans only evolved consciousness as a reminder of how dumb they are. When the Boss says he still prefers being conscious, the robot tells him to listen to his body, implying his body would disagree.
punchline: The robot sarcastically suggests that the Boss's own body is telling him he is dumb, and that consciousness is merely an unwelcome reminder of that fact.
summary: A smug machine insists that awareness exists in people mainly to make them notice their own foolishness, then brushes off a human's objection with a pointed bit of advice.

situation: A female coworker tells Dilbert she broke up with her boyfriend because he became obsessed with his phone and then his new Apple Watch, never looking at her. When she asks if Dilbert heard anything she said, he is staring at his own wrist watch and only comments on the weather.
punchline: Dilbert unwittingly proves her point by ignoring her complaint about a boyfriend distracted by his smartwatch, because he is distracted by his own smartwatch.
summary: A woman complains that her boyfriend's gadgets killed their relationship, and the man she's venting to is too absorbed in his own wrist device to notice.

title: Hypocrisy: Tool or Character Flaw

transcript.text: Oh. No wonder people are so prickly about it.

situation: Asok asks a bald, bespectacled coworker how he can claim to be a team player if selfishness is needed to succeed. The coworker cheerfully recommends hypocrisy as a tool. Asok points out that hypocrisy is a character flaw, and the coworker calmly realizes this explains why people react badly to it.
punchline: The coworker treats hypocrisy as a handy business technique and only now realizes it is a character flaw, which explains why people get so upset when he uses it.
summary: A junior employee asks how to look collaborative while acting selfishly, and a coworker offers an unwittingly damning answer.
