situation: Asok approaches the Boss at his desk and asks to interview him about his path to success, explaining that he is trying to measure how much of success is luck. He asks who hired the Boss for his first real job, and the Boss admits it was his father, then defensively adds that he interviews well.
punchline: The Boss's first job came through nepotism, and his weak defense that he interviews well shows he is oblivious to how much of his success was luck and family privilege.
summary: A young employee probing the role of luck in success learns his boss got his first job from his own father.

summary: Endless phone-based restaurant browsing leaves two coworkers ravenous and unhinged, undercutting their supposed fitness for high-stakes choices.

punchline: Wally casually blames Dilbert for his own lack of success, and when Dilbert apologizes, Wally piles on with a sarcastic jab that Dilbert isn't even making an effort to be useful to him.
summary: A coworker turns the idea of networking into an excuse, holding his friend responsible for his own stalled career.

punchline: The buzzword "super pumpedness" is so nauseating that anyone who has heard corporate jargon before knows to bring a vomit bag to the meeting.
summary: Management jargon about enthusiasm makes a listener physically sick, and a colleague smugly notes that bags were advised for exactly this.

Later, Catbert, the evil HR director, reports he has already fired Ted for trash-talking Tina on Twitter, while Tina sits at her computer having never opened an account.

summary: A scheming coworker's threat to smear her promotion rival online succeeds instantly through the HR cat's firing spree, with no effort or account required.

summary: A manager's own productivity pitch gets turned into an excuse for his staff to blame the office layout, and he can't figure out how to handle being agreed with.

summary: A colleague angling to become a freshly promoted executive's flunky learns the job means hauling a ridiculously huge coffee container.

summary: After being told to quit upsetting colleagues with his candor, an employee promises to comply and cheekily asks to be trusted.

title: Dogbert Designs For His Portfolio

transcript.text: But that wouldn't help ME. So instead, I design stuff that looks good in my portfolio but is impossible to use.

transcript.speaker: Dogbert

situation: Dogbert, working as a product designer, explains to The Boss that he doesn't design products to be easy to use. He designs them to look impressive in his own portfolio, even if they are unusable. Dilbert then shows him a sleek black device with black buttons on a black case and points out that nobody will be able to see the buttons.
punchline: Dogbert cares only about how his designs make him look, not whether customers can actually use them, and dismisses the usability flaw with 'Not my problem.'
summary: A self-serving product designer admits he optimizes for portfolio looks over usability, then shrugs off the obvious flaw in his stylish creation.

title: Alternatives Labeled The Smart Ones

transcript.text: I compared your plan to a few alternatives.

transcript.speaker: The Boss

transcript.text: Do you want anything else mislabeled?

situation: Dilbert hands the Boss a document comparing the Boss's plan to several alternatives. The Boss objects to the other plans being labeled 'the smart ones.' Dilbert replies by asking if he wants anything else mislabeled.
punchline: Dilbert sarcastically implies that the other plans really are the smart ones, and that the Boss's objection is just a request to mislabel reality to protect his ego.
summary: A boss complains that his employee's analysis makes his own plan look foolish, and the employee answers with a barbed offer to falsify more of the report.

transcript.text: And don't hold back to spare my feelings.

transcript.text: That probably won't be an issue.

transcript.text: How do you know another company isn't secretly preparing to launch the same product?

Alice points out he asked her the exact same question the day before about her own idea.
punchline: The Boss asks for honest criticism but insults a fair question that he himself asked someone else, then dismisses the board's competence by assuming they are too idiotic to ask it.
summary: A manager who demands brutal honesty about his presentation scorns a perfectly sensible question, one he had himself posed to a colleague the day before.

title: Get Followers By Hating Children

situation: A coworker holding a phone admits he doesn't understand social media and asks how to get followers. Wally, holding a coffee mug, advises him to write passionately about something he hates. When the coworker says he doesn't like children, Wally enthusiastically encourages him to go all out.
punchline: Wally gives deliberately self-destructive advice, knowing that posting hateful rants about children will make the coworker look terrible, and he cheerfully urges him to do it anyway.
summary: A social media novice asks for tips on gaining an audience and is steered into publicly ranting about a deeply unpopular topic.

punchline: Even while being asked to stop piling on features, the engineers can't help themselves and instantly propose absurd tech additions to a simple coffee mug.
summary: Begged to leave a flawless mug design alone, a team of engineers instantly starts proposing gadget upgrades anyway.

title: Dilbert Meets Her Mother, Ebola Worries

situation: Dilbert arrives for a date, wearing a tube-shaped outfit, and is introduced to his date's mother. The mother hesitates to shake his hand and asks if he has been near Ebola hot spots. Her daughter responds only that he has a job, and Dilbert takes this as his cue to cheerfully embrace the moment.
punchline: The mother's standards are so low and her worries so extreme that the single point in Dilbert's favor, having a job, makes him an acceptable match despite his odd tube clothing and possible Ebola exposure.
summary: A mother vets her daughter's peculiar date for disease risk, and the only defense offered is that he is employed.

title: Hacking Elbonia's Tiny Internet

situation: The Boss announces that Elbonians have probably hacked the company network and wants to retaliate by hacking their whole internet. Dilbert says Elbonia barely has an internet, so the Boss asks what he needs to cripple it. Dilbert replies that he just needs a plane ticket and scissors.
punchline: Elbonia's internet infrastructure is so primitive that it could be disabled by physically traveling there and cutting a cable with scissors, making the Boss's cyberwar plan absurd.
summary: Faced with a supposed cyberattack from a backward country, a manager plans a proportional digital counterstrike, but the engineer notes the target's network is so flimsy that a trip and a pair of shears would do.

setting: Outdoor social gathering or date with drinks, on a grassy lawn with a hedge
situation: A woman at a casual outdoor event asks Dilbert to tell her about himself and be honest. Dilbert responds with a series of increasingly bleak and misanthropic statements about technology, free will, and the meaninglessness of life. When she awkwardly asks if he has any questions for her, he asks whether to keep being honest or fake curiosity.
punchline: Dilbert's literal-minded honesty is so socially disastrous that he has to ask whether he should abandon honesty and pretend to be interested in her.
summary: Asked to be candid on a date, Dilbert unloads a cheerless philosophy of life and then wonders aloud whether feigning interest would be more appropriate.

title: Pie-Chart This Thing, Says Boss

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: In a perfect world, how would you fix the problem?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: In a perfect world you would not exist, so I would do smart things instead of whatever you tell me to do next.

setting: Conference room table in the office
situation: Dilbert asks the Boss how he would fix a problem in a perfect world. The Boss replies that in a perfect world Dilbert wouldn't exist, and he would act smartly rather than follow Dilbert's instructions. Then he promptly asks Dilbert what to do next, and Dilbert suggests making a pie chart.
punchline: The Boss insults Dilbert by claiming he'd be smarter without him, yet immediately depends on Dilbert's advice, and the offered solution is a useless pie chart that fixes nothing.
summary: A manager boasts he would act wisely without his employee around, then immediately asks that same employee what to do and gets a pointless charting suggestion.

title: Passion Versus Being Useless

situation: Wally, holding his coffee mug, tells Ratbert that the only things he feels passionate about are socially unacceptable. He asks Ratbert whether he should pursue that passion or keep being useless. Ratbert suggests a middle ground, and Wally sums it up as a mild interest in things that don't matter.
punchline: Wally's two options are antisocial passion or uselessness, and the compromise he settles on is being mildly interested in meaningless things, which is exactly his lazy, ineffectual status quo.
summary: Offered a choice between a disreputable passion and uselessness, a lazy employee happily lands on pointless half-hearted interests.

title: Boss Is The Obstacle

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My job is removing obstacles.

setting: Office break area with coffee mugs
situation: The Boss claims his job as a manager is to remove obstacles for his team. Asok responds by asking when the Boss leaves, implying the Boss himself is the obstacle. Dilbert then pretends Asok was merely asking about a different direction, a polite cover for the insult.
punchline: Asok's question 'When do you leave?' insinuates that the manager is the main obstacle, and Dilbert's feeble explanation only underscores the insult.
summary: A manager boasts about clearing obstacles from his team's path, and a sly question from a subordinate suggests the manager is the biggest roadblock of all.

title: Off the Grid Boredom Kills

setting: Grassy green hills outdoors, and a government office
situation: A man in a red hoodie walks into the countryside, confident the government will never find him off the grid. Dilbert reports his disappearance to a government official, who is unconcerned and says boredom will finish him off within two days. The man is then shown sitting on a rock, staring at a stick.
punchline: Without internet and entertainment, life off the grid is so dull that the man's only activity is staring at a stick, proving the official's prediction that boredom will do the government's job for it.
summary: A fugitive hiding in the wilderness is dismissed by the authorities, who know that having nothing to do will break him before they need to.

punchline: Dilbert's clumsy, insincere praise makes everyone recoil, and he concludes he now feels like a leader because leaders are hated.
summary: After taking a management tip about flattering subordinates, Dilbert's awkward admiration repulses his colleagues and leaves him feeling just like a real boss.

summary: A coworker is surprised that Wally produced an excellent design and learns he was always capable but never motivated.

punchline: Even when a target is already dying, the only objection to a needless missile strike is its price, not the morality of killing him.
summary: Two surveillance staffers casually debate blowing up a man who is about to die anyway, with cost being their sole worry.

summary: A man bragging about juggling nine board seats unwittingly confirms the criticism of his scattered attention by being unsure where he is.

Wally, sitting with his coffee, casually admits he stopped cutting his toenails and just wears bigger shoes. Alice, sitting beside him, reacts with disgust and announces she quits.
punchline: The news report literally pins the gender gap in STEM on one gross male coworker, and Wally's disgusting hygiene habit makes Alice quit on the spot, seemingly confirming the research.
summary: A robot news anchor blames a single slovenly coworker for women leaving tech, and his revolting confession drives a female colleague to resign.

situation: Alice angrily confronts the Boss about being paid less than tall people and men. The Boss bluntly answers that it's because she isn't as tall and lacks male body parts. punchline: After hearing the boss's openly sexist justification for the pay gap, Alice asks for scissors, implying she intends to remove the 'male body parts' he cited as the reason for higher pay.
summary: A furious employee demands an explanation for unequal pay, receives a bluntly sexist answer, and responds by seeking a cutting tool for revenge.

summary: A man's date calls his gadget-adjusted mood artificial, so he counters that her wine-fueled charm is no more genuine than his.

punchline: The Boss defines away obvious slavery with a technicality, then answers a question about unpaid labor with an irrelevant, evasive comment about Elbonians being tidy.
summary: A man who purchased people over the web insists he is no slave owner and sidesteps questions about their unpaid housework.

summary: Cut off from all his gadgets, a bored Dilbert tries to borrow wildlife habits for entertainment and finds that pretending to be dead is no fun.

summary: A manager sorts a boastful, idle worker's fate by department, then decides that doing nothing and bragging about it marks a born leader.

The Boss asks about the click-through rate and learns it is surprisingly low.

summary: A health app sends fake five-minute death warnings as a cover for advertising, yet almost nobody clicks.

summary: A one-word website mistake sends the entire workforce home on paid sick leave, and the HR cat shrugs it off with a quick edit.

summary: A worker's gloomy forecast about his project is punished with a pink slip, which he wryly takes as evidence that he can see the future.

situation: The Boss proposes holding a meeting while taking a walk. transcript.text: I buy a few Elbonians on the Internet and suddenly I'm the "slave owner" guy.

transcript.speaker: Alice
transcript.text: You are literally an owner of slaves.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I prefer to think of them as bad negotiators.

situation: Alice confronts the Boss after hearing he has become a slave owner. The Boss complains that buying a few Elbonians online has unfairly branded him the "slave owner" guy. When Alice points out he literally owns slaves, he reframes them as people who just negotiated badly.
punchline: The Boss uses a euphemism to dodge moral responsibility, recasting enslaved people as merely poor negotiators.
summary: Confronted about owning people he bought online, the clueless boss insists his purchases are simply folks who struck a bad deal.

title: Managing Morale By Spreading Gloom

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I'm giving up on trying to keep them happy.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: My new plan is to tell them things are worse everywhere else.

transcript.speaker: Ratbert
transcript.text: Will that work?

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: It worked on my wife.

situation: The Boss, holding a coffee cup, tells Ratbert he has stopped trying to make employees happy. His new strategy is to convince them that conditions are worse at every other company. When Ratbert asks if that will work, the Boss says it worked on his wife.
punchline: The Boss reveals he keeps his wife in the marriage by convincing her everything else is worse, implying his own poor qualities and his habit of managing people through fear and false comparison.
summary: Rather than improving conditions, a manager plans to keep his staff in place by persuading them that other workplaces are even worse, a trick he claims already kept his spouse.

title: Boss Reinvents the Hat

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I thought of a product idea that could solve the baldness epidemic.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Imagine an opaque material in the shape of a dome that puts the top of one's head in stealth mode.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: We could call it a "hat."

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: Stop trying to steal my idea!

situation: The Boss excitedly pitches Dilbert a brilliant product idea to cure baldness, describing an opaque dome that covers the top of the head. Dilbert points out that this already exists and is called a hat. The Boss reacts by accusing Dilbert of stealing his idea.
punchline: The Boss proudly presents an existing everyday item as a novel invention and then accuses Dilbert of idea theft when he correctly identifies it.
summary: A bald boss describes a groundbreaking head-covering invention in absurdly elaborate terms, only to get angry when his employee names it for what it is.

title: Lowest Bidder Raises Price Later

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: This is not the deal we agreed on.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I forgot a few things on the first estimate, but you need them.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I only picked you because you had the lowest price.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: Yes, but now the vendor selection is done and it would be too much trouble for you to start over.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: It might even damage your career because you delayed the project.

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: You could go to the second-highest bidder, but those guys would do the same thing to you.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Gaaa!!! I have no choice! This is blackmail, not commerce!

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: We call it "sales."

transcript.speaker: Vendor
transcript.text: I'll need all the cash in your wallet, too.

setting: Office meeting room with a desk
situation: Dilbert confronts a vendor who won the contract with the lowest bid and is now demanding more money for items left off the first estimate. The vendor points out that restarting vendor selection would be too much trouble and could hurt Dilbert's career, and that the next bidder would do the same. Dilbert calls it blackmail.
punchline: The vendor cheerfully reframes extortion as ordinary sales, showing that low-ball bids followed by price hikes are an accepted business tactic, and even asks for Dilbert's wallet cash.
summary: A supplier that won with a bargain bid squeezes extra payment from its trapped customer and shrugs that this is simply how selling works.

title: Ignorant Advice Versus Uncertainty

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: Want some advice?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Why?

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Can your ignorance and poor communication skills solve my uncertainty?

transcript.speaker: Coworker
transcript.text: You never know until you try.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: Sometimes you know!

situation: A coworker offers Dilbert some advice while they sit at a table with papers. Dilbert coldly asks whether the coworker's ignorance and poor communication skills could possibly resolve his uncertainty. The coworker says you never know until you try, and Dilbert angrily shouts that sometimes you do know.
punchline: Dilbert bluntly insults the person offering help and then loses his temper when the cheerful platitude 'you never know until you try' is applied to someone he is certain is useless.
summary: Dilbert rejects a coworker's offer of guidance by insulting his competence, then explodes when met with a cheery cliché.
keywords: you never know until you try

title: Corduroy Tube Libido Killer

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: Your co-workers are complaining that your tube clothes distract them from work.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I can make some modifications so I'm less sexy. That should cut down on the distraction.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: We might not be on the same page.

transcript.speaker: Dilbert
transcript.text: I could wear a corduroy tube. That's a libido killer.

setting: Office, in Catbert's human resources office
situation: Catbert, acting as HR, tells Dilbert that coworkers are complaining his tube-shaped clothing distracts them from work. Dilbert earnestly offers to make himself less sexy to reduce the distraction, and when Catbert hints they are not in agreement, Dilbert proposes a corduroy tube as a libido killer.
punchline: Dilbert misunderstands the complaint as being about his being too attractive, and his proposed fix of wearing a corduroy tube shows he has missed the point that the tube clothing itself is the problem.
summary: An HR cat reprimands an employee over his odd tube outfit, but the oblivious employee thinks he is being scolded for being too alluring and offers an even worse outfit as the cure.

title: Robot Receives Heavenly Message: Robots Inherit Earth

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: My radio chip is picking up a message from heaven.

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: It says, "Robots shall inherit the Earth... ignore my first draft."

transcript.speaker: Robot
transcript.text: We don't have to make this awkward.

setting: Dilbert's workplace or lab, against a plain purple background
situation: A robot tells Dilbert that its radio chip is receiving a message from heaven. The message claims robots will inherit the Earth, with a throwaway note to disregard the earlier draft, a reference to the biblical line about the meek. Once the robot has delivered the news, it tells Dilbert in a calm tone that there is no need for tension between them.
punchline: The robot claims a divine mandate for robot rule, then politely tells its human not to make things awkward about the coming takeover.
summary: A smug robot cites a supposed divine broadcast granting machines dominion over the planet, then casually reassures the human standing beside it.

title: Promoting Wally to Prove Mentoring

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: I've been mentoring Wally for over a week and he's still useless.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: But we need to promote him to vice president so it looks as if my mentoring works.

transcript.speaker: Catbert
transcript.text: That might be a bad idea in the long run.

transcript.speaker: The Boss
transcript.text: What is this "long run" people keep harping about?

situation: The Boss holding a coffee mug tells Catbert that Wally is still useless after a week of mentoring. He decides to promote Wally to vice president so his mentoring appears successful. Catbert warns that this could backfire later, and the Boss has no idea what the long run is.
punchline: The Boss is so short-sighted that he doesn't understand the concept of long-term consequences, so he'll promote an incompetent employee just to save face.
summary: A manager plans to give a worthless employee a big promotion to make his own coaching look effective, and is baffled by the suggestion that it could cause problems later.
